en: Preface to the *Abridged Essentials of the Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* Now, the three realms are illusory and false, produced solely by the mind. Apart from the mind, there are no phenomena; apart from phenomena, there is no mind.

Therefore, within the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*), one is free from the mark of names, free from the mark of verbal expression, and free from the mark of mental conditions. Thus spoke the World-Honored One.
At the moment of his parinirvāṇa, the Buddha held up a flower to show the assembly to manifest that there is no dharma that can be preached;
thus, one knows that there is no fixed dharma for a Tathāgata to speak—how, then, could he rely extensively upon the vehicles of the teachings (śāsana-yāna) to compose treatises?

Nevertheless, within the gates of skillful means (upāya-mukha), not a single thing is abandoned: sometimes he emits light and rains down flowers, sometimes he raises an arm or bends his fingers, and sometimes he raises an eyebrow.
Whether it be the blinking of an eye, a cough, opening the mouth, speaking plainly or in secret, or whether it be meditative concentration or wisdom—all are Buddha-activities.
Therefore, within the gate of arising and ceasing, all speech, writing, and the activities of daily life accord with the True Dharma.
Observing this, one cannot but compose a treatise; once the treatise is completed, it simultaneously encompasses both the Sudden and the Gradual, just as a great [ocean contains all rivers].

The ocean does not reject even small streams; yet those who have not transcended the mind, intellect, and consciousness cannot fathom its depths. When a beginner unrolls this scroll, it is as if facing a blank wall.
Desiring that they might seek the meaning within the text and forget the words once the ultimate meaning is realized, these commentaries on the *Śāstra* had to be composed.

Now that the commentaries have appeared, each person races with their own interpretations, vying with one another to display superiority or inferiority; among those who follow these commentaries, it is impossible to know who is right.
Who is it? Who is not it? How deep? How shallow? Understanding arises merely following words, like overgrown weeds difficult to eradicate.

If one wishes to remove this profusion and grasp the essential framework, then by examining the waves one discerns the water, and by touching the smoke one recognizes the fire; thus, these swift and essential points must necessarily be recounted.
The Master Cong of Yanmen received the transmission of this treatise from Master Mei of Kaixian; for one month, his shadow did not leave the room.
That this commentary has thus achieved such an understanding may be called a thorough penetration of both letter and meaning, like splitting firewood with an axe.

It is my hope that sentient beings possessing the faculty of faith will, by means of this, clarify the treatise; and by means of the treatise, realize the fundamental meaning of the Tathāgata. This is like borrowing a path to return home or using a finger to see the moon;
it is my wish that I shall not fail those who composed this treatise to instruct, benefit, and gladden others, so that the lineage of the Buddha may never be severed.
If this were not the case, then both the commentator and the recipient would be submerged together; the mere trap and snare would constitute a slander against the Buddha and sentient beings.
In the spring of the Bingchen year of the Wanli era, the Layman of Xiangzhou, Li Tengfang, wrote this preface to the *Essential Guide to the Treatise on the Awakening of Faith*.

When I first underwent tonsure and donned the dyed robes, I frequented lecture halls, traversing through both winter and summer to investigate the teachings of the *Dharmalakṣaṇa* and *Dharmatā* schools.
Although the various masters did not possess the countenance of Guṇamegha, I was ultimately like a deaf person listening for the sound of mosquitoes from beyond a hundred paces.
It was not until the winter of the Wushen year that I inquired into the Dharma with Master Kaixian, whereupon we met like a needle and its eye; since then, several cycles of the seasons have passed.
In the summer of the year of the Tiger, I again took up the principle of "clarifying the mind and seeing its nature" to seek further instruction from my teacher.

The teacher commanded me to read the *Awakening of Faith* thoroughly so that I might master this meaning. I immediately shut myself away from the world for over ten days, diligently investigating this treatise.

Suddenly, I began to perceive the meanings of the discourse as clearly as looking at the palms of one's hands; what it expounds allows sentient beings to clearly mirror their own mind-nature. Therefore—
The Dharma of the One Mind opens two gates: the gate of True Suchness and the gate of arising and ceasing.

By establishing the gate of True Suchness, it reveals the essence of unchanging nature to clarify that the wondrously pure nature is fundamentally neither delusion nor enlightenment, and belongs to neither the ordinary person nor the sage.

By establishing the gate of arising and ceasing, it reveals the function of following conditions to clarify that the source of the eight consciousnesses can manifest the ordinary and the sage, as well as the causes and effects of cultivation, realization, delusion, and enlightenment, thereby causing all beings—
All sentient beings clearly perceive their own nature as pure, wondrous, and signless;

they illuminate the source of the mind, which is perfectly interfused and capable of manifesting all things, thereby ensuring they do not fall into the views of nihilism, eternalism, annihilationism, or substantialism. Thus, based on what I have perceived, I have taken up the pen to compose these annotations.
They are now carved into woodblocks to inform my fellow practitioners. At that time, a guest passed by me and said: "In the past, Master Zang of Taiyuan and Master Xuan of Changshui..."
The Master had exhaustively examined the entire Tripitaka and its various treatises, and after devoting his spirit to them for several years, he finally completed these commentaries and records.

How is it that you, bypassing this extensive work, are able to explain this treatise in just a few thousand words? Is this not like peering at the heavens through a tube or fathoming the ocean with a clam shell?
I replied: "It is not so. Observe carefully the Bodhisattva’s intention: he wished to enable sentient beings to take pleasure in concise texts while encompassing much meaning."

The Master composed this treatise for this very purpose. Now, the commentator has exerted himself to exhaustively extract the teachings on both Nature (svabhāva) and Characteristics (lakṣaṇa) in order to broaden its meaning.
Although the Dharma is not fixed such that it may be treated either briefly or extensively, students who encounter these vast texts cannot help but retreat like those facing the ocean;
how then can they hope to accord with the fundamental intent of the author of the treatise? I, however, [do not...]* *Note: The original text appears to be incomplete at the end.*
I, Min, have merely extracted the essential outlines from this treatise so that readers may readily perceive its core intent upon opening the volume.

Nevertheless, as individual capacities for understanding vary, there may be those who attain comprehension through the extensive text itself; thus, it would not be improper for them to explore thoroughly the commentaries and records of the masters of Changshui.
As for me, how could I dare claim that my own interpretation is the definitive truth?
Written by Zhengyuan of Mount Lu on the day the Buddha attained enlightenment in the year Wuli Jia-yin (1574), at the Shizhao Mountain Hermitage.
*An Easy Compendium of the Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, Fascicle One.
Composed by Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha;
with the assistance of Prince Vasunāga as interpreter.
Annotated by the Śramaṇa Zhengyuan of Mount Lu.
There are five vehicles: the human vehicle, the celestial vehicle, the śrāvaka vehicle, the bodhisattva vehicle, and the Tathāgata vehicle.
Here, the term "Mahāyāna" (Great Vehicle) is used to distinguish it from the vehicles of humans, devas, and śrāvakas, directly indicating the Tathāgata vehicle; therefore—

The treatise states: To explain the fundamental meaning of the Tathāgata so as to prevent the seeds of humans and devas, as well as the seeds of the two vehicles, from arising, and to cause one to dwell solely within the true causal correspondence of the Tathāgata-lineage—this Mahāyāna doctrine consists generally of two kinds:
first, the Dharma; second, the meaning (artha). The Dharma is the mind of sentient beings; this mind encompasses the mundane world.
The supramundane dharmas rely upon this mind to manifest the meaning of Mahāyāna; furthermore, there are three aspects: first, the greatness of essence (*tathatā-mahattva*);
second, the greatness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-mahattva*); and third, the greatness of function (*kāritra-mahattva*).

These names are derived from their own nature because they are vertically exhaustive and horizontally pervasive, unimpeded and perfectly interfused, and do not correspond to the "small" [i.e., the Hīnayāna]. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "It is not because of a small emptiness that it is called..."
The Great Emptiness and Nirvāṇa are likewise; they are not called Great Nirvāṇa because of minor characteristics.

Furthermore, this mind is called a "vehicle" (yāna) because it proceeds from cause to fruit, realizing and attaining the essence, characteristics, and function [of the Buddha-nature]. As the text says:
"This is what all Buddhas have fundamentally mounted," and "All Bodhisattvas mount this Dharma to reach the stage of the Tathāgata. Therefore...

That which can be mounted is initial enlightenment (*ādikṣaya-bodhi*); that which is mounted is original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*). The non-duality of the initial and the original is called ultimate enlightenment (*niṣṭhā-bodhi*).
As the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-śāstra* states: "Because it mounts upon the great nature, it is called the Mahāyāna.

Those who give rise to faith [in this] are all sentient beings who, although they possess this Mahāyāna mind, are deluded and do not awaken; they either believe in the Hīnayāna or sink [into ignorance].
Because of the heterodox paths, the Bodhisattva elucidates the mind-dharma of the Mahāyāna so that sentient beings may give rise to right faith in the Mahāyāna.
As the treatise says: "There is a dharma capable of giving rise to the faculty of faith in the Mahāyāna; therefore, it should be explained as 'arising.

'Arising' means manifesting; 'faith' means patient acceptance and delight. That which manifests patient acceptance and delight through a single-minded focus on the Mahāyāna is called the arising of faith. This refers to...
When faith arises, it must necessarily be caused internally by fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) and conditioned externally by the teacher’s instruction.

Because cause and condition are in harmony and internal and external factors mutually support one another, it is able to manifest [the truth]. As the treatise says: "One whose causes and conditions are complete is able to give rise to a mind of weariness toward suffering.
Regarding the meaning of giving rise to faith in the existence of *nirvāṇa*, there are also two kinds. The first is for...
First, it is to cause those sentient beings whose roots of goodness are mature to become capable of non-retrogressive faith;
second, it is to cause those sentient beings whose roots of goodness are slight to cultivate faith.

There is nothing that does not cause all sentient beings—whether entering the path suddenly or gradually—to deeply believe in the mind-dharma of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), for within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions there is neither two nor three. Thus says the Treatise.
It is called a *śāstra* because it discriminates between the heterodox and the orthodox, thereby revealing the True Teaching (*saddharma*). Question:

As the *Śāstra* states, "The Mahāyāna Dharma is precisely the mind of sentient beings; since the mind is fundamentally identical, why are there distinctions such as the Human Vehicle, the Celestial Vehicle, the Śrāvaka Vehicle, the Bodhisattva Vehicle, and the Tathāgata Vehicle?
Answer: The mind is fundamentally without distinction; it is only that the obstructions (*āvaraṇa*) vary in depth.
As the *Awakening of Faith* (Yuánjué lùn) briefly states: "It manifests and clarifies the distinctions among the five natures of sentient beings.
Because sentient beings, by relying on this mind-dharma, are able to uphold the five precepts, it is called the Vehicle of Humans (*manuṣya-yāna*).

Because they rely on this mind to cultivate the ten wholesome deeds while simultaneously eliminating the outflows of desire, it is called the Vehicle of Devas (*deva-yāna*). Because they rely on this mind to sever and eliminate afflictive hindrances..."

Because it transcends death within the limits of分段 (fen-duan) [birth and death], it is called the Śrāvaka Vehicle; because one diligently severs the two obstacles through the wisdom of the two emptinesses by means of this mind, it is called the Bodhisattva Vehicle;
and because one exhaustively severs the two obstacles and eternally eliminates the two deaths by means of this mind, it is called the Tathāgata Vehicle.
Thus, we know that within the gate of arising and ceasing (生滅門), there are five distinct natures (五性) regarding the severance of obstacles.

How could the Gate of True Suchness (tathatā-mukha) establish a distinction between ordinary beings and sages? Therefore, when the Patriarchs see through this, they do not maintain even the remaining vehicles;
if they perceive the existence of the Tathāgata-yāna, they cast it beyond the Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa).
Question: As the Treatise says, the arousal of the mind (cittotpāda) possesses three types, namely: the arousal of the mind through the perfection of faith (śraddhā-sampanna-cittotpāda)...

Regarding the resolve through understanding (*adhigama-citta*), the resolve through practice (*pratipatti-citta*), and the resolve through realization (*sākṣātkriyā-citta*): why is this work titled specifically "Arousing Faith" (*Qixin*)?

Answer: The most difficult aspect of arousing the resolve lies in faith. If faith is perfected, then the stages of the three levels of worthies (*traya-śaikṣa*) of understanding and practice, and the ten levels of sages (*daśārya*) of realization, follow as naturally as pushing open a door and the bolt falling out.
Thus, throughout the forty-nine years of the World-Honored One’s preaching of the Dharma, his great disciples...
Because they still did not believe that their own minds are Buddha, the World-Honored One emitted light and manifested auspicious signs at the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra,

emerged from meditative concentration to proclaim his virtues, and responded to three requests with three refusals, using indirect and circuitous means none of which were other than to cause those of the three faculties to directly perceive before them and straightway believe that their own minds are Buddha;
yet once the assembly of the three faculties had entered into faith, the World-Honored One immediately proclaimed his passing into extinction.
The original aspiration for transcending the world is finally fulfilled. Viewed from this perspective, how could faith easily arise?
Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Faith is the source of the Way and the mother of merit;
it nurtures all roots of goodness, severs the net of doubt, enables one to emerge from the river of craving, and reveals the unsurpassed path to Nirvāṇa."
I take refuge in those who have exhausted the ten directions— the most supreme ones, those of all-encompassing knowledge, those with unimpeded mastery over form,
the Great Compassionate Saviors of the world— and in their physical bodies, their marks, the *dharmatā*, the ocean of *tathatā*, the treasury of immeasurable merit, and their authentic practice;
for the purpose of causing sentient beings to eliminate doubt, abandon false attachments, give rise to right faith in the Mahāyāna, and ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is never severed.
This consists of eight lines of reverential homage preceding the main body of the treatise, followed by four lines explaining the purpose for composing it.
There are briefly six meanings to this homage to the Triple Gem: first, acknowledging their benevolent virtue; second, requesting their protection; third, causing faith to arise;

fourth, establishing a formal model; fifth, manifesting their supreme excellence; and sixth, revealing their benefit to sentient beings. This homage concludes with the phrase "I take refuge. (Total: ten lines)
The first phrase, "Pervading all," encompasses the three phrases below: the Dharma-jewel, the Saṃgha-jewel, and the most supreme activity; these constitute the taking of refuge in the Buddha-jewel.
The two phrases, "The ocean of the true suchness of the dharma-nature," constitute the taking of refuge in the Dharma-jewel.

The single phrase, "Practicing according to reality," constitutes the taking of refuge in the Saṃgha-jewel. Within this, the phrase "and that body" pervasively subsumes the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha.
The meaning [of "refuge"] is to manifest the Three Jewels as being of one essence. "To take refuge" (*śaraṇa*) means to rely upon, to surrender, and to turn toward.
"Life-force" (*jīvita*) refers to the essential means of governing all the sense faculties; among all that which protects a person, nothing takes precedence over this.

By raising up this non-dual life-force to serve the Unsurpassed Honored One, the term "ten directions" (*daśadig*) manifests the vastness of those toward whom one turns in reverence, rather than being restricted by limited dimensions.
The "most excellent function of the ear" refers to the characteristic of the purity of wisdom (*jñāna-viśuddhi-lakṣaṇa*) and the characteristic of inconceivable activity (*acintya-karma-lakṣaṇa*).

"Excellence" (*śreṣṭha*) means surpassing the small; "supreme" (*parama*) means transcending the causes. Because this most excellent functional activity exhausts the consciousness-mind (*vijñāna-citta*) and perfectly accomplishes the four wisdoms (*catur-jñāna*), it is called "universal knowledge" (*sarvajña*).
This is the mastery of mind (*citta-vaśitā*). Through this correct universal knowledge, one realizes that all phenomena are suchness (*tathatā*); thus, the great and the small [are non-dual].
Because the various faculties are unimpeded and function interchangeably, it is said that the mastery over form (*rūpa*) is the mastery over phenomena (*dharma*).
Since form is thus mastered, it is identical to principle (*li*); as the mind is mastered, it is identical to wisdom (*jñāna*).

When the wisdom that accords with principle is one with the mind, and when mind and form are non-dual, one realizes fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), which is termed "self-awakening perfected. Thereupon, one further gives rise to subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

Arousing compassion for those of the same essence, universally rescuing the world from suffering, and extensively gathering in all sentient beings, one is therefore called a "Great Compassionate Savior of the World.
This refers precisely to the intention of being able to awaken others; because one has perfected self-awakening and is able to awaken others, one is called a Buddha.
Although both self-awakening and awakening others belong to the functioning of wisdom (*jñāna*), it is from this functioning that one returns to the ultimate source.

Because it is the essence, it is called "and that body. Since the characteristics of that body are already designated as being subsumed within the essence by means of wisdom, yet it is further called "and that body," this is to demonstrate that the nature of wisdom is itself form (*rūpa*).
Furthermore, to realize fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is precisely to realize the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhoga-kāya*);
subsequently giving rise to subsequently-attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) is simply to manifest the three types of transformation bodies (*nirmāṇa-kāya*).

Therefore, it is said that this refers to "his body. However, according to the treatise, it is divided into three bodies; the two phrases "supreme activity" and so forth refer specifically to the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body).

As the text states: "Because the nature of wisdom is form (*rūpa*), it can manifest according to the mind infinite *saṃbhogakāyas* of infinite bodhisattvas throughout the worlds of the ten directions, each distinct from the others, yet all without any limitation."
There is no contradiction; this is precisely as the old commentary explains it by taking "universal knowledge" (*parijñā*) to mean the purity of mental action (*manas-karman*).
Since "mind" refers to the seven consciousnesses, once they are said to be "pure," they are transformed into the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*).

Furthermore, the body manifested by the Wisdom of Equality is also a *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body). Thus, we know for certain that the *saṃbhogakāya* is named such because its form is universally known and unimpeded. This is the resolution.
The Great Compassionate One of the world is the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body). As the text says:

"All Buddhas and Tathāgatas, originally while on the stage of the causal ground, gave rise to great compassion and established great vows, desiring to deliver all realms of sentient beings without limit as to the number of kalpas, until the end of the future.
That which is perceived by the minds of ordinary people and those of the two vehicles is called the *saṃbhogakāya* (response body).
The body that is firmly known as the "Transformation Body" (nirmāṇakāya) by virtue of its great compassion for saving the world is, in its essential nature, the "Dharmakāya.
Thus, one returns from the two bodies—the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya) and the Transformation Body—to the Dharmakāya.

Furthermore, that "body" refers to the aforementioned two bodies, while the two characters "essence" and "nature" refer to the Dharmakāya; this is because the Reward and Transformation Bodies are not separate from the Dharmakāya.
How is it known that the essence and characteristics are called the *dharmakāya*? As the text states:

"Furthermore, regarding the essence and characteristics of true suchness (*tathatā*), from the very beginning its self-nature has been fully endowed with all merits," which is termed the *tathāgatagarbha* and also the *tathāgata-dharmakāya*.
Thus, we know for certain that the essence and characteristics are designated as the *dharmakāya*. Although the *dharmakāya* is without marks (*animitta*)...
Furthermore, the reason the *dharmakāya* is designated by its marks (*lakṣaṇa*) is that this *dharmakāya* is the very substance of form (*rūpa*). As the text states:

"Because the nature of form is itself wisdom, the substance of form is formless and is called the *jñānakāya*; because the nature of wisdom is itself form, it is called the *dharmakāya*, which pervades all places.
These two lines—"the ocean of the *dharmatā* and *tathatā*"—refer to the Jewel of the Dharma.

Furthermore, it is named the "Dharma-Jewel" based on its essence (*tattva*) and its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Because it relies upon the essence, it is called the "Ocean of the True Suchness of Dharma-nature" (*dharmatā-tathatā-samudra*);
because it relies upon the characteristics, it is called the "Treasury of Immeasurable Merits. As the text states:

"First is the greatness of essence (*tattva-mahātmya*), meaning that the true suchness of all phenomena is equal, neither increasing nor decreasing. Second is the greatness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-mahātmya*), meaning that the Tathāgatagarbha is fully endowed [with all virtues]."

Because it possesses immeasurable qualities of nature, this True Suchness (Tathatā) is called "Buddha-nature" when included within the category of sentient beings, and is called "Dharma-nature" when included within the category of insentient things.
That which is above is the Buddha Jewel, which is precisely Buddha-nature; that which is here is the Dharma Jewel, which is precisely Dharma-nature.
Therefore, it is termed the "Ocean of True Suchness of Dharma-nature. True Suchness is characterized by being unchanging while following conditions.

Because it possesses the two meanings of "changing" and "conforming to conditions," it is likened to the ocean; for while the ocean produces waves in accordance with the wind, the nature of water is not lost.

Furthermore, although not a single dharma is established within the essence of True Suchness (tathatā), it nonetheless fully possesses immeasurable merits that accord with its nature, being able to encompass and sustain them;
therefore, it is called a "Treasury" (garbha). It is like the Sangha Jewel when practiced according to reality.

"Those who practice according to reality" refers to those who cultivate by means of the internal permeation of the essence and characteristics of their own minds, and who act in accordance with the Dharma taught by all Buddhas;

this specifically indicates Bodhisattvas of the Dharmakāya stage practicing in truth, thereby distinguishing them from humans, devas, Śrāvakas, and Bodhisattvas of provisional stages. The above concludes the homage to the Triple Gem; hereafter follows:

The four lines beginning with "desiring to cause sentient beings" correctly state the purpose for composing this treatise. The first two lines cite the intended audience (the *adhikāra*) so that they may abandon faults;
the latter two lines clarify the benefits to be obtained, namely becoming capable of realizing Buddhahood.

Although the root dispositions (*gotra*) of sentient beings are manifold, they do not exceed those who doubt and lack faith, or those who, despite having faith, fall into the net of heterodoxy. Therefore [this treatise is composed].

The Bodhisattva reveals the mental dharmas of the Mahāyāna and extensively establishes skillful means of counteraction so as to eliminate doubt, engender faith, cause one to abandon the heterodox and follow the orthodox, and give rise to the faculty of faith in the Mahāyāna.
By causing one to dwell securely within the lineage of the Tathāgata, he ensures that the life of wisdom continues in succession and is never severed.

Regarding the question of why, in the act of taking refuge and paying homage, the transformation body is mentioned first and the Dharma second: [it is because] the transformation body is the primary means for introducing beings to the Dharma.

The *Shen ye* replies: Because the formless Dharma-body is difficult to direct one's reverence toward, one first takes refuge in the body with form and thereby gathers oneself back into the essence that is formless.
Furthermore, those in the stage of the Three Worthies perceive only the two bodies of retribution and transformation;

even when they subtly contemplate the Dharma-body at the level of the Ten Grounds, although they gradually realize the Dharma-body, it is not yet ultimate, and they see only the physical marks of the retribution body.

Because it is adorned, one knows that function is subsumed within essence and that phenomena are ultimately identical with nature; therefore, one first pays homage to the *nirmāṇakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*, and subsequently proceeds to the *dharmakāya*.
The treatise says: "There is a dharma capable of giving rise to the faculty of faith in the Mahāyāna; for this reason, it should be explained. This explanation consists of five parts."
What are these five? First, the section on causes and conditions; second, the section on establishing the thesis; third, the section on detailed explanation;
fourth, the section on practicing with faith; and fifth, the section on the benefits of encouraging practice.

This indicates the general purport of the treatise. The two characters "dharma" (fa) refer to the one hundred Mahāyāna teachings subsumed within this treatise, as well as the three divisions—establishment of tenets (*siddhānta*), explanation (*vyākhyā*), and cultivation of faith (*śraddhā-pratipatti*)—expounded by this treatise.
That which is revealed and manifested by these Mahāyāna teachings and the three divisions of this treatise is the *tathatā* (true suchness) of sentient beings.
This is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Although sentient beings possess this mind, they have long been deluded and have not returned to it.
Because Bodhisattvas wish to cause sentient beings to perfectly realize this mind, they employ the Dharma of the One Mind to open the two gates of True Suchness (*tathatā*) and Arising-and-Ceasing.

This enables sentient beings, within the nature of True Suchness, to abandon the causes and conditions of arising-and-ceasing and give rise to the correct faith of the Mahāyāna, thereby becoming capable and able to bear [the burden].
One enters directly into the stage of the Tathāgata; for this reason, this treatise should be expounded. Because it must be taught in a systematic order, it is divided into five parts:

first, the Section on Causes and Conditions (*nidāna*), which corresponds to the introductory section (*nidāna*) of other sūtras; second, the Section on Establishing the Meaning (*arthavyavasthāpana*); third, the Section on Exegesis (*vyākhyāna*);

fourth, the Section on Cultivating Faith (*śraddhābhāvanā*), which corresponds to [the section on] faith in other sūtras; and fifth, the Section on the Manifestation of the Result (*phalasaṃdarśana*).

This constitutes the Main Body (the *shengzhengfen*). Fifth is the Section on Encouraging Practice and its Benefits, which corresponds to the Dissemination Section (*liutongfen*) found in other sutras.
However, the essential meaning of these five sections will be explained in detail below; therefore, they are not annotated here at length.
In the first section, the Exposition of Causes and Conditions (*nidāna*), it is asked: "By what causes and conditions was this treatise composed? It is answered:
"There are eight such causes and conditions.

This constitutes the first [of the eight], the Exposition of Causes and Conditions, which is the reason for the origination of this fundamental treatise; the preceding verses serve as its introduction.

Desiring to cause sentient beings to eliminate doubt, abandon false attachments, give rise to right faith in the Mahāyāna, and ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is never severed, [the Buddha] has not yet pointed out:
for what kind of sentient beings; by what dharma; how to sever the web of doubt;
by what gate of contemplation to counteract false attachments; what meaning to explain in order to give rise to right faith; and how to maintain continuity.
Because the lineage of the Buddhas is never interrupted, this provisional question is posed; the answer sets forth eight kinds of causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) to clarify the preceding intent.
The meaning of these eight kinds will be explained in the text below.
What are the eight? First, the general characteristic of causal conditions: that is to say, it is for the sake of causing sentient beings to leave all suffering behind.
First, because they have attained ultimate bliss and do not seek worldly fame, profit, or honor;
second, because they wish to explain the fundamental meaning of the Tathāgata so that all sentient beings may understand it correctly without error;

third, because they wish to enable those whose roots of goodness are matured to become capable of non-retrogressive faith in the Mahāyāna Dharma; fourth, because they wish to enable those whose roots... [text truncated]

Fifth, it is to demonstrate expedient means for the sake of sentient beings with weak and few roots who cultivate faith, thereby eliminating the obstacles of evil karma, well-guarding their minds, remaining far removed from delusion and pride, and escaping the net of heterodoxy.
Sixth, it is to demonstrate the cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* as an antidote to the mental faults of ordinary people and those of the two vehicles.
Seventh, it is to demonstrate the expedient means of single-minded mindfulness so that one may be born in the presence of the Buddha.

First, because it is certain that one will not retreat from the mind of faith; and eighth, because it is for the purpose of demonstrating benefits and exhorting the practice of cultivation—it is due to such causes and conditions that this treatise was composed.
Regarding the general characteristics, the overall intent for composing this treatise for the sake of sentient beings is as follows: all suffering does not exceed [the following]...
The two obstacles are the causes of suffering that can summon the two types of death as their resultant fruits of suffering.

The afflictive obstacle (*kleśāvaraṇa*) continues the birth-and-death of fragmented segments (*prādeśika-saṃsāra*), giving rise to the suffering of being bound by karma; it acts as the cause for the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), which continues the birth-and-death of transformation (*pariṇāmi-saṃsāra*) and corresponds to subtle suffering.
Regarding ultimate bliss, there are also two meanings: first, the joy of awakening to the Dharma through unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhi*); second, [the bliss of cessation].
Sentient beings do not obtain the bliss of the unexcelled nirvāṇa of quiescence due to the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*),
nor do they obtain the bliss of awakening to the dharmas of unexcelled bodhi due to the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Out of compassion for these sentient beings, the Bodhisattva extensively gathers and teaches the vehicles (*yāna*), revealing skillful means (*upāya*) to cause them to be free from [these obstructions].

Although one attains the bliss of nirvāṇa and bodhi from the suffering of afflictions and the known, and though one universally benefits sentient beings to attain ultimate happiness, one does not personally dwell upon the appearance of saving beings;
therefore, it is said that one does not grasp at worldly fame, profit, or honor.
Nevertheless, in order to cause sentient beings to leave suffering behind and attain happiness, one must necessarily explain the fundamental nature of the Tathāgata.
The meaning of this is that the Tathāgata’s root is precisely the self-nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Now, in order to explain and clarify this so that sentient beings may develop deep faith in the self-nature of True Suchness and enter directly into the resultant awakening of the Tathāgata—thereby preventing them from falling into the vehicles of the Two Vehicles or the paths of externalists—it is said:
"To cause all sentient beings to have correct understanding without error. This is intended to explain the root of the Tathāgata.
The meaning of "fundamental" (*mūla*) is precisely to establish the basis for the two-part exposition of dependent origination.

Third, it is to enable sentient beings whose roots of goodness are mature to become capable of non-retrogression; fourth, it is to cause those sentient beings with meager roots of goodness to cultivate faith.
This collectively inherits the preceding intent to ensure that all sentient beings attain correct understanding without error. Thus, it is excellent.

Those whose faculties are mature have already completed ten thousand kalpas and fulfilled the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), entering the stage of the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*) within the path of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*);
thus, their prior faith becomes capable of non-retrogression. Those with minor roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*) have not yet passed ten thousand kalpas, as their correct faith is not yet perfected;
they are made to advance in cultivation so that the ten faiths may be fulfilled. Therefore, it is said: "cultivating the mind of faith."
These two meanings precisely constitute the dependent origination for the analysis of the characteristics of setting out upon the path.
Fifth, the following is provided generally for those whose roots of goodness are slight and who practice faith;

"those with slight roots of goodness" refers generally to those whose past habitual tendencies involve heavy obstructions and deep defilement by false views, and thus first employ skillful means such as prostration and repentance to eliminate them.
Because the obstacles of evil karma are light, one should well protect the mind so that internally it is free from delusion and pride, and externally it escapes the net of heterodoxy.

Next, the meaning of *śamatha* (calm abiding) is shown to eliminate the fault of ordinary beings who cling to existence, and the meaning of *vipaśyanā* (insight) is shown to counteract the fault of those of the Two Vehicles who indulge in emptiness.

Having transcended the levels of ordinary beings, the Two Vehicles, and external paths, one finally achieves correct faith; yet, fearing there may be timidity or lack of manifestation, [the teaching continues].

Previously, seeing that it is difficult for beings to practice *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, the Buddha further revealed the Dharma-gate of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*), enabling these sentient beings to be reborn according to their vows and reach the stage of non-retrogressive faith.
These three meanings constitute the causal origin (*nidāna*) for the section on practicing faith.
Eighth, showing the benefits and exhorting practice specifically constitutes the section on exhorting practice for the sake of benefit.

The origin of this [teaching] is as follows: in that text, the benefits and harms are extensively set forth to exhort the cultivation of relinquishment (*prahāṇa*), which serves generally to spur the accomplishment of the various preceding practices.
Question: Since these dharmas are already fully contained within the *sūtras*, why is it necessary to state them again? Answer: Within the *sūtras*...

Although such a teaching exists, because the faculties and practices of sentient beings are unequal and their conditions for reception and understanding differ— namely, that while sentient beings possess sharp faculties when the Tathāgata is in the world,
and the teacher’s physical and mental karma is superior so that a single utterance of the perfect voice is understood differently by various types of beings,
no further discussion is required— if, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, there are sentient beings who can extensively hear it through their own power;
Furthermore, among those who attain understanding, there may be sentient beings who, by their own power, attain much understanding from hearing little;
there may be sentient beings who lack the power of their own minds and attain understanding through extensive treatises;

and there may be sentient beings who, finding extensive textual discourse cumbersome, delight in concise summaries that encapsulate many meanings within few words and are thus able to attain understanding.
Thus, this treatise should be expounded because it intends to comprehensively encompass the boundless meanings of the Tathāgata’s vast and profound Dharma.
Furthermore,
this single question clearly demonstrates that [the purpose] is to enable sentient beings to leave suffering behind and attain happiness, rather than seeking worldly fame.
Because of the desire for gain and honor, this question and answer can be understood according to the text; however, within the response, the text is divided into three points.
From the phrase "Although such a teaching exists in the Sūtra" onwards, it briefly explains the purpose of composing this treatise.

Specifically, from the phrase "While the Tathāgata was in the world" onwards, it clarifies that there was no need to compose the treatise because the individuals capable of receiving it possessed superior physical, mental, and karmic faculties.

The capacities [of those] to be reached are sharp, their roots are deep, and their understanding is profound; yet, as for the excellence of the physical, mental, and karmic [faculties], the single manifestation of the perfect voice constitutes the three wheels:
the physical refers to the wheel of physical marks, the mental refers to the wheel of mental attention, and the perfect voice refers to the wheel of sound.

If, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, [the text] now correctly explains that the faculties and practices of the assembly are unequal and the conditions for their reception and understanding are distinct:

Therefore, this treatise is composed. Although the purpose of composing a treatise is vast—encompassing all sentient beings—the primary emphasis lies in the profound essence of mind, wherein the teaching and the capacity of the recipient meet so that the benefit of transformation is extensive.

Because it condenses many meanings into few words, it is said to "comprehensively encompass" the boundless meanings of the Tathāgata’s vast and profound Dharma; for this reason, this treatise ought to be composed.
Having already explained the section on causes and conditions, the section on establishing the doctrine is now presented next. Regarding the Mahāyāna, there are generally two kinds.
What are these two? First, the phenomena (dharma); second, the meaning (artha).

The introduction, consisting of the explanation of the causes and conditions, is now concluded. We shall now set forth the formal proposition (*pratijñā*) to clarify the essential meaning of the main body of the teaching.
"Formal proposition" refers to the fundamental meaning of the Tathāgata established within the section on causes and conditions;
this fundamental meaning is precisely what is called the Mahāyāna. This Mahāyāna possesses immeasurable meanings, but we shall now address its core essentials with few words.

Regarding the summary of manifold meanings, there are two types of comprehensive summaries for the immeasurable meanings, namely: first, the Dharma (the teaching), and second, the meaning (the significance).
The essential purport of these Dharma and meaning will be explained in the subsequent text.
That which is called "Dharma" refers to the mind of sentient beings; this mind encompasses all mundane and supramundane dharmas.
Based upon this mind, the meaning of Mahāyāna is revealed. Why is this so?

Because the aspect of the True Suchness (*tathatā*) of this mind reveals the essence of Mahāyāna, while the aspect of the arising and ceasing through causes and conditions of this mind can reveal the self-nature and characteristics of Mahāyāna.
Because of this usage, the statement "dharmas are the very mind of sentient beings" is intended to reveal that dharmas are identical to mind. Therefore, he explains it himself:
"This mind encompasses all mundane and supramundane dharmas; 'mundane' refers to the phenomena of the six classes of ordinary beings, including both their primary and secondary environments."
The supramundane is the principle of the four noble wisdoms; it is truly said that the entire world of causes and effects, down to its subtlest atoms, takes its substance from the mind.

Because the essence and characteristics of this wondrous mind are unobstructed, and both defilement and purity rely upon it equally, whether following the flow or returning against the flow, one merely turns this mind.
Therefore, if one follows defilement and falls into non-awakening, one then encompasses the mundane world.

If the dharmas of the mundane and supramundane realms follow the initial awakening (*pratipakṣa-ādi-bodhi*) that returns to the source and the unchanging fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*), they are subsumed within it.
Although it is explained that this mind encompasses all mundane and supramundane phenomena, it still relies upon the gate of birth-and-death (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*) for its manifestation;

thus, the subtlety of the ultimate single mind has not yet been fully realized. Therefore, the following section immediately demonstrates the meaning of the three great aspects (*tri-mahā-dharma*) to exhaustively reveal its profound essence.
This reveals that the essence of the mind is truly wondrous and pure in nature, such that not a single dharma exists therein;
it is only within the realm of appearances and functions that all dharmas are subsumed. By "relying on this mind," it is clarified that there is no objective referent external to the mind.

This mind possesses the meanings of both emptiness and non-emptiness, as well as immutability and conformity with conditions. If one examines it from the perspective of the substance of true emptiness and immutability:

Since both ordinary beings and sages are not established and cause and effect are simultaneously extinguished, it is said that "this mind is the aspect of True Suchness (*tathatā*)," which indicates the essence of Mahāyāna.
As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "The originally enlightened, luminous mind was originally neither water nor fire.

If one considers its function of non-empty accordance with conditions, ordinary beings and sages all manifest, and cause and effect coexist; therefore, it is said that "this mind is the cause of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*)."

The causal characteristics (*nimitta*) are able to demonstrate the essence, nature, and function of the Mahāyāna; as the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "If you manifest clarity through emptiness, then emptiness appears;
if you manifest clarity through both, then both appear. However, the characteristic of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the gate of non-arising;
it does not stand by means of a gate of arising or dependent origination. Therefore, it speaks only of the essence, while the causes and conditions of birth and death pertain to the latter.
The gate of arising does not depart from the gate of non-arising; yet, while arising, it contains non-arising. Therefore, it is called the "essence, nature, and function.
As for what is called "meaning," there are three kinds. What are these three? First is the greatness of essence (*tathatā-mahattva*), which refers to all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*).

First, because True Suchness (*tathatā*) is equal and neither increases nor decreases; second, because its characteristic is greatness (*lakṣaṇamahattva*), meaning the Tathāgatagarbha is fully endowed with immeasurable inherent merits (*guṇa*);
and third, because its function is greatness (*vṛttimahattva*), meaning it can produce all causes and fruits of mundane and supramundane goodness.
It is that which all Buddhas have fundamentally mounted, and all Bodhisattvas ride upon this Dharma to reach the state of a Tathāgata.
Because it is the ground.

Although the preceding section has revealed its essential nature (*svabhāva*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and functions (*vṛtti*), this section correctly explains their meaning. First, as for the greatness of essence (*tattva-mahat*):

because this mind-essence can serve as the basis for both ordinary beings and sages, although not a single dharma is established therein, it does not fall into nihilistic emptiness (*uccheda-śūnyatā*).
Thus, regarding the meaning of emptiness: because all phenomena have nothing that can be discarded, as they are all truly real;
and because there is nothing that can be established, as they are all identical to suchness (*tathatā*). Therefore, it is said that "all phenomena are themselves suchness.
Since all phenomena are suchness, mind and form are non-dual, and subject and object are both eliminated; thus, it is said they are "equal, without increase or decrease. This is the second aspect.

This greatly reveals that the characteristics of this mind are able to manifest all phenomena—both mundane and sagely, defiled and pure. Although the myriad dharmas all appear within it, they do not fall into the realm of existence;
this is the meaning of "not empty in accordance with reality" (*tathatā-śūnyatā*), because all merits and virtues abide in dependence upon the mind.

Thus, it is said that the Tathāgatagarbha is the entire substance of the mind, and is therefore called "intrinsic merit" (*svabhāva-guṇa*). Third, the greatness of function (*vṛtti-mahattva*) is revealed.
The function of this mind is able to accomplish the dharmas of cause and effect for both ordinary beings and sages;

because it accords with this great function by maturing the roots of goodness of sentient beings through the manifestation of the two bodies—the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*—it is said to be "able to give birth to all mundane and supramundane wholesome causes and effects.
Mundane wholesomeness refers to the dharmas of cause and effect pertaining to humans, devas, and the *śrāvaka* vehicle; supramundane wholesomeness... [refers to the dharmas of the Mahāyāna].

That is to say, it is the goodness of the practices and understandings of the three stages of worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*), the wisdom and principles of the ten stages of sagehood (*daśārya-bhūmi*), and the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of the Tathāgata.
Although unwholesome dharmas are not separate from the mind, because they contradict reality, they do not constitute its function.

The aforementioned dharma-meanings are all termed the "Greatness of the Mind-nature" (*citta-prakṛti-mahattva*). From here below, the meaning of the Vehicle (*yāna*) is correctly revealed; as for the Vehicle, it fully encompasses everything from cause to fruition.

Regarding the two meanings of "proceeding from fruit toward cause": first, it means that those who have attained the fruit have already realized the *dharmakāya* by riding upon the essence and characteristics (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*) of *tathatā*, and furthermore, they manifest the *sambhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* by riding upon the function (*vṛtti*) of *tathatā* to extensively benefit sentient beings; thus it is said that this is "what all Buddhas have fundamentally ridden upon.
Second, it means that those on the path of the cause likewise ride upon the essence and characteristics of *tathatā* as their internal causal perfuming (*adhyātma-hetu-vāsanā*).
Gradually realizing the Dharma-body and further employing the function of True Suchness as an external condition for cultivation and practice in order to awaken sentient beings,
it is said that "all Bodhisattvas ride upon this Dharma and reach the stage of a Tathāgata."
Having explained the section on establishing the thesis, the section on the analysis of the interpretation is now presented. There are three types of analysis; what are these three?
First, the elucidation of the correct meaning; second, the counteracting of erroneous attachments; third, the detailed classification of the characteristics of the path toward enlightenment.
This is the formal explanation of what was briefly indicated in the preceding section on the Establishment of the Thesis regarding the fundamental meaning of the Tathāgata.

All sentient beings who fail to attain unsurpassed bodhi, or even deviate into the paths of the Lesser Vehicle or externalists, do so because they cannot distinguish between the real and the delusory;
since their false attachments are difficult to eliminate, they practice in a confused manner and thus achieve nothing.

Because it pertains to the fruits of sainthood (*āryaphala*), this commentary explains the three kinds of correct paths so that practitioners may first clarify the correct principles to distinguish between the two gates of *tathatā* (suchness) and arising-and-ceasing;
next, they treat erroneous attachments to eliminate the two views of self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-dṛṣṭi*).

From the beginning of the arousal of the resolve (*cittotpāda*) to the end of its directed application, it clarifies the stages of the path and the basis for the progressive cultivation of the resolve.
These three points are intended to ensure that one does not encounter divergent paths but enters directly into the oceanic fruition of the Tathāgata.
Regarding the revelation of the correct principle: based on the single dharma of the One Mind, there are two gates.
What are these two? First is the gate of the True Suchness of the mind; second is the gate of the arising and ceasing of the mind. These two gates each comprehensively encompass all dharmas.
How is this meaning established? Because these two gates are inseparable.
To explain that the single dharma of the one mind possesses both the gates of True Suchness (*tathatā*) and arising-and-ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*), it correctly interprets the preceding statement:
"This mind encompasses all mundane and supramundane dharmas," and "Based on this mind, the meaning of the Mahāyāna is revealed. This is the [meaning of] the mind.
The gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*) explains the aspect of the mind as True Suchness, thereby demonstrating the essence (*svabhāva*) of Mahāyāna.

The gate of the arising and ceasing of the mind explains the aspect of the causes and conditions for the arising and ceasing of this mind, being able to demonstrate the essence, characteristics, and function (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa-kārya*) of Mahāyāna itself.
Both True Suchness and arising and ceasing are called "gates" because a single mind fully possesses and encompasses both.
Regarding the meaning that encompasses both "entry" and "exit": because the True has no separate substance other than the substance of the delusory, it is named "True";
thus it is said, "Illusion and delusion are called 'phenomena,' yet their nature is the True, the essence of wondrous enlightened clarity.

Because the delusory has no separate function other than the function of Wisdom, it is named "delusory"; thus it is said, "The mind of wondrous enlightened clarity. Since it is called "delusory," how is this so?
Regarding the meaning of "entering and exiting" based on causes: when sentient beings are deluded, they exit the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*) and enter the gate of arising and ceasing;

thus it is said they "turn their back on awakening and unite with the dust. When they awaken, they exit the gate of arising and ceasing and enter the gate of True Suchness; thus it is said they "extinguish the dust and unite with awakening.
These two gates each encompass all phenomena because these two gates are not mutually exclusive.

Therefore, because the True Suchness Gate (tathatā-mukha) is the universal characteristic that permeates both the defiled and the pure, and there is nothing apart from it that constitutes defilement or purity, it can comprehensively encompass all dharmas.
As for the Arising and Ceasing Gate (utpāda-nirodha-mukha), it specifically manifests defilement and purity;
since the dharmas of defilement and purity include everything without exception, it also comprehensively encompasses all dharmas. "All dharmas" refers precisely to the eighteen [elements].

These eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are the phenomena of the realm. Within the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*), they are subsumed under a single characteristic and a single flavor, both being termed "empty essence.
Because the nature of the faculties and the nature of the objects pervade the Dharma-realm, when subsumed within the gate of arising, they are termed the three subtleties and the six coarsenesses;
when subsumed within the gate of cessation, they are termed the phase of pure wisdom and the inconceivable phase. Although there is defilement and purity, [they are ultimately one].
These distinctions, in total, do not go beyond being established based on the one mind. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:

"If one is utterly unable to know that arising and ceasing, going and coming, are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha—the eternally abiding, wondrously luminous, immovable, and all-pervading nature of wondrous True Suchness"—then one will understand that the two gates are inseparable, and thus it is clear that each encompasses all phenomena.
The suchness of mind is precisely the essence of the Dharma-gate of the Great Universal Characteristic of the Single Dharma-realm;
that is to say, the nature of the mind is neither born nor extinguished. All phenomena exist only through the differentiation of deluded thought;

if one is free from mental conceptualization, then there are no signs of any objective realms. Therefore, all phenomena have, from the very beginning, been free from the characteristics of verbal expression.
Being free from the marks of names and free from the marks of mental objects, it is ultimately equal, without change or variation, and indestructible;

because it is solely the one mind, it is called True Suchness (*tathatā*). This is because all verbal expressions are merely provisional names without reality, following after deluded thoughts and being ultimately unattainable.
This is the correct explanation of the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Because within the nature of True Suchness, mind and form are mutually fused and emptiness and existence are equal;
because it is called the One Dharma-realm (*ekadharmadhātu*) wherein principle and phenomena are perfectly encompassed and defilement and purity universally rely upon it;

and because it is the substance of the Great Universal Dharma-gate—according to the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya*, "Dharma-realm" has the meaning of being the cause of the noble dharmas—it is said to rely upon...
Because it gives birth to the noble dharmas, it is called the "Great Universal Characteristic of the Dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu*);
this means that it encompasses all phenomena and sustains immeasurable meanings. A "Dharma-gate" (*dharmamukha*) refers to that which the noble wisdom universally traverses.
Its "essence" (*tattva*) serves as the basis for all phenomena. "Universal" means that the self-nature of *tathatā* is the cause of pure dharmas and is where all noble ones collectively abide.

The Master Yu says: As the *Awakening of Great Perfect Enlightenment* states, there is a great *dhāraṇī* gate called "Perfect Enlightenment," from which flow forth all pure *tathatā*, *bodhi*, *nirvāṇa*, and the *pāramitās* for the instruction of bodhisattvas.
That which is called the "nature of mind being neither born nor extinguished" further explains the meaning of the great universal characteristic of the single *dharmadhātu*. If there is...

If there were arising and ceasing, there would necessarily be the distinctions of abiding and changing; how then could it be considered one or great? Because the nature of the mind is fundamentally pure, it does not arise through delusion;
because it is not extinguished by means of cultivation, the mundane world is not destroyed and the supramundane is not exhausted.

Therefore, it is called the "Great Universal Characteristic of the Single Dharma-realm. This refers to all phenomena, which, when examined from below, reveal that the nature of the mind is fundamentally non-existent.
Arising and ceasing exist because all phenomena possess differentiation only by depending upon deluded thought; thus we know that true nature is without arising and manifests only through delusion.
If one is separated from deluded thought, then phenomena are as they are. As it is said: "All dharmas are originally tranquil, yet people themselves create clamor.
Just as when the diseased eye is removed, empty space no longer produces flowers, for this reason the conclusion below clarifies the nature of the mind.
Fundamental purity is free from all names and characteristics; yet the characteristics of names and verbal expressions are precisely the aforementioned "all dharmas.
The characteristics of mental objects are precisely the aforementioned "relying solely on deluded thought.

Since all dharmas exist only by relying on deluded thought and possess their distinctions, they cannot be found at all within the nature of *tathatā*. Therefore, they are all detached from them; being detached from names, [they are also detached from characteristics].

Because it is the characteristic that transcends the distinctions of verbal expression, it is called "equality. Because it is free from the characteristics of mental conditioning and arising-and-ceasing, it is called "unchanging and indestructible.
Since these three characteristics are both abandoned and their distinctions eliminated, there remains only the pure, singular, true essence—the reality of awakened nature.
Therefore, it is called "the single mind," and thus named "True Suchness" (Tathatā). This is what was referred to in the preceding text as "the One Dharma."
The essence of the Dharma-gate of the Great Universal Characteristics of the Realms is seen here in the nature of the mind, which is neither born nor extinguished.
The following passage explains the meaning of being free from these three characteristics: all verbal expressions and names lack such an essence;
they are established merely according to the conditions of the deluded mind. Yet even this delusion lacks an essence and cannot be apprehended at all.
Because within the essence of *tathatā* (suchness) all things are entirely devoid [of characteristics].
That which is called "suchness" is likewise without marks; it is the ultimate limit of verbal expression, wherein words are used to dispel words.
This essence of suchness has nothing that can be dispelled, because all phenomena are entirely suchness. Furthermore, there is nothing that can be established, because all [phenomena]...
Since all phenomena are identical to suchness, one should know that because all phenomena are ineffable and inconceivable, they are called "true suchness" (*tathatā*).
Having previously used the phrase "free from the characteristics of names, words, and so forth" to reveal that true suchness is without marks, here again—
The commentary states: That which is called *tathatā* (suchness) likewise has no marks.
One speaks of "truth" by means of "delusion," as if there were a nameable entity called *tathatā*. Yet, if one is separated from delusion, even truth does not exist.

Although this is the ultimate limit of verbal expression, because words are used to dispel words, even the name and concept of *tathatā* are dispelled, and the essence of *tathatā* remains solitary and prominent; therefore, it is so stated.
This essence of *tathatā* (suchness) has nothing that can be discarded, because all phenomena (*dharma*) are entirely suchness;
since phenomena are themselves suchness, there is nothing to be discarded. Although all phenomena cannot be discarded, not a single phenomenon corresponds to the conceptualizing mind;
therefore, it is said that there is also nothing that can be established, because all phenomena are identical to suchness. Since phenomena are thus...

Since it is originally such as it is, there is nothing that can be established; yet, because it cannot be discarded, it does not fall into nihilism. Furthermore, because it cannot be established, it does not fall into eternalism.

Once both nihilism and eternalism are transcended, it is only then called "True Suchness" (*tathatā*). One should know that the phrase "all phenomena" below summarizes and establishes the meaning of what precedes.
The intended meaning is that True Suchness is without marks (*animitta*), such that both names and language are discarded, and all phenomena are fundamentally such as they are.
To enable those who study the Mahāyāna to thoroughly penetrate this meaning, it is said: "One should know that all dharmas are ineffable and inconceivable;
therefore, they are called True Suchness (tathatā). "Ineffable" means causing one to depart from the characteristics of names and verbal expression;
"inconceivable" means causing one to depart from the characteristics of mental objects.
Question: If this is the meaning, how do sentient beings accord with it and thereby attain entry? Answer:

If one knows that although all phenomena are spoken of, there is neither a speaker nor anything to be spoken; and although they are contemplated, there is neither a contemplator nor anything to be contemplated—this is called "accordance.
To be free from such contemplation is called "attaining entry."
The above explains the fundamental meaning of the Tathāgata. This dialogue is intended precisely to ensure that sentient beings attain correct understanding without error.

If this is the meaning, it refers to the aforementioned true suchness (*tathatā*) and the nature of mind (*cittatā*), which are free from the characteristics of verbal expression and so forth, up to the point where all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are ineffable and inconceivable; therefore, they are called "true suchness" (*tathatā*). That is to say:
Regarding this meaning, how can one accord with and enter it? "Accordance" refers to skillful contemplation (*upāya-vipaśyanā*); "entry" refers to correct contemplation (*samyag-vipaśyanā*).

Since True Suchness (*tathatā*) is beyond words and mental conceptions, one should approach it by means of the state that transcends speech and enter it by means of the state where deluded thoughts are severed.
Therefore it is said: "Although it is spoken of, there is neither a speaker nor anything to be spoken; although it is contemplated," [there is neither a thinker nor anything to be thought].
Furthermore, there is neither a subject that can contemplate nor an object that can be contemplated; this is called "conformity.

Since there is neither a subject nor an object of speech, one conforms to *tathatā*, for all phenomena are ineffable. Since there is neither the characteristic of a subject nor an object of contemplation, one conforms to *tathatā*, for all phenomena are inconceivable.
Although one does not abide in the speaker and the spoken, nor in the contemplator and the contemplated, it is nevertheless...
The wisdom of expedient contemplation (*upāya-vipaśyanā*) is not yet empty of mental activity; it is merely called "conformity" (*anuloma*).

Only when correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*) stands before one and the characteristics of thought naturally depart can one enter into the nature of *tathatā*. Therefore, it is said: "If one is free from thought, this is called entering.
The full meaning of this "entering by being free from thought" is entirely revealed below in the section on the principle of "Awakening" (*bodhi*). Question: This...
Question: To clarify the self-nature of True Suchness (tathatā), why is it said that all phenomena are free from the characteristics of verbal expression and so forth? Answer:
This is to clarify the fundamental meaning of the Tathāgata and to reveal the principle that nature and characteristics are not distinct.

In the contemplative wisdom of the Hīnayāna, one views nature as existing apart from characteristics and characteristics as existing apart from nature; however, this Mahāyāna dharma-gate holds that nature is precisely characteristics and characteristics are precisely nature.

Thus, their nature is fundamentally non-dual in essence, as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "This Dharma abides in the station of the Dharma; the characteristics of the world are eternally constant.
If one seeks this nature apart from its characteristics, it is like pushing away the waves to seek the water, or leaving the echo to search for the sound.
Furthermore, regarding suchness (*tathatā*), there are two meanings based on conventional linguistic discrimination. What are these two?

First, it is emptiness according to reality (*yathābhūta-śūnyatā*), because it can ultimately manifest the true reality. Second, it is non-emptiness according to reality (*yathābhūta-aśūnyatā*), because it possesses its own essence, being fully endowed with the qualities of untainted nature (*anāsrava-dharma*).
The above has revealed the essence of *tathatā* by departing from characteristics such as verbal expression;

this has clarified the meaning of *tathatā* through reliance on verbal expression and conceptualization. However, because understanding arises based on words, one must not grasp at them with attachment.

There are two kinds of "meaning" (*artha*), namely: the aforementioned self-essence, characteristics, and function. Naming it according to its essence, it is "emptiness as it truly is" (*yathābhūta-śūnyatā*). It is...
The names [of emptiness and non-emptiness] correspond to their functions and are thus "as-it-is" (*yathābhūta*) and not empty;

furthermore, based on the preceding principle that neither can be discarded nor established, these two meanings exist. Since they cannot be established, this is the meaning of "emptiness as it is"; since they cannot be discarded, this is the meaning of "non-emptiness as it is.
The name "emptiness as it is" is used because it is able to ultimately realize that all phenomena are the true emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
The true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is not the same as the nature of delusion, which lacks substance;
it is called "non-empty according to reality" because, although all pure dharmas share the same essence of empty quiescence, they nevertheless accomplish immeasurable qualities of nature.
That which is called "emptiness" is because, from the very beginning, it has been dissociated from all defiled dharmas;
that is to say, it is free from the differentiated characteristics of all phenomena because it lacks false mental conceptions.

One should know that the self-nature of *tathatā* (suchness) is neither characterized by existence, nor by non-existence, nor by being neither existent nor non-existent, nor by being neither not-existent nor not-non-existent, nor by having both existence and non-existence as its characteristic, nor by having a single characteristic.
It is not of different characteristics, nor of non-different characteristics, nor of non-different characteristics, nor of both identical and different characteristics;

this is stated in summary because, based on all sentient beings, their deluded minds give rise to moment-to-moment discrimination that is entirely inconsistent with reality, and thus they are said to be empty.
If one were free from the deluded mind, there would truly be nothing that could be called empty.
That which is called "emptiness" clarifies that within the essence of *tathatā* (suchness), all characteristics are absent.
Because it has been intrinsically pure from the very beginning, its self-nature does not accord with any defiled phenomena;
all defiled phenomena exist solely based on deluded thought. Since this essence of true emptiness is utterly devoid of deluded thought, all [forms of] differentiation...
Because all marks are entirely detached, one should know that [the following] explains in detail the detachment from the marks of differentiation among all dharmas...

[The section on] the general summary below correctly reveals that by means of a mind free from false conceptualization, the marks of differentiation among all dharmas do not transcend existence and non-existence, or identity and difference;
these are precisely what the heterodox teachers cling to, because they possess a mind of false conceptualization.
The conceptualization of thought is what ordinary people take to be their own nature; even the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) cannot purify it.
This true reality transcends all ordinary beings, outsiders, and the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle; it is solely the True and devoid of delusion. Therefore, none of these [concepts] apply.
This collectively reveals that within the essence of True Emptiness, one is free from mind, thought, and consciousness, and cuts off all worldly and saintly artifices. If one is free from...

In the section below on "the deluded mind," the meaning of "as-it-is" (yathābhūta) is correctly explained to reveal that while all that exists is empty, the essence of true emptiness is in fact not empty.

That which is called "not empty" has already revealed that the substance of phenomena is empty because it is devoid of delusion; this is precisely the True Mind, which is eternally constant and unchanging.

When the transformation into pure dharmas is fulfilled, it is called "not empty"; yet there are no marks to be grasped, because this is a realm free from conceptual thought, realized only through direct correspondence with realization.
To say it is "not empty" reveals that within the characteristics and functions of True Suchness (tathatā), all dharmas are present; although they are fully complete...
Since all phenomena do not depart from the essence of true emptiness, it is said that the essence of phenomena has already been revealed as empty and devoid of delusion;
this is precisely the true mind, eternally constant and unchanging, wherein pure dharmas are fully perfected.

It is by relying upon this eternally constant and unchanging true mind, in which pure dharmas are fully perfected, that the meaning of "non-empty according to reality" is first established. This refers to what was stated in the preceding text:
This is because its own essence is fully endowed with the qualities of the untainted nature (*anāsrava-dharma*).

Although it is perfected in pure dharmas, there is no mark of purity to be grasped, for it is a realm free from discursive thought (*niṣprapañca*), accessible only through realization and correspondence. However, where there is thought, one clings to various phenomena;
since there is no longer a "thinker," how could there be anything to be grasped? It is simply that wisdom and principle are united, accessible only through realization and correspondence.
In reality, there is neither a subject that realizes nor an object to be realized. This section on the Gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is divided into two parts;

in principle, they are of one essence. The preceding section revealed the principle of True Suchness and was thus titled "The Essential Body of the Great General Characteristic Dharma-Gate of the Single Dharma-Domain.
This present section clarifies the meaning of True Suchness and therefore opens up two kinds of emptiness. However, since there is no meaning outside of the principle, they are one.
The Dharma-realm Great Universal Dharma-gate subsumes the two meanings of emptiness and non-emptiness.
Since there is no principle outside these meanings, emptiness and non-emptiness both return to the essence of the Dharma-realm Great Universal Dharma-gate.
Within this essence, emptiness as it truly is is the empty Tathāgatagarbha; non-emptiness as it truly is is the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha. This...

Since these two meanings both converge upon the essence of the Great Universal Dharma-gate of the Single Dharma-realm, this Great Universal Dharma-gate of the Single Dharma-realm is precisely the Tathāgatagarbha that is both empty and non-empty.

Thus we know that when it is empty yet not empty, and not empty yet empty, the two extremes do not stand and the Middle Way is also obliterated; only then is the wondrous purport of True Suchness fully exhausted.
Thus, the fundamental meaning of the "coming" [of the mind] is finally established.
Regarding the arising and ceasing of the mind: because it relies upon the *tathāgatagarbha*, there is a mind that arises and ceases.

This is what is called the non-dual union of the unborn and undying with that which arises and ceases; being neither identical nor different, it is named the *ālayavijñāna*. This consciousness possesses two meanings.
How is it that they can encompass all phenomena and give rise to all phenomena? There are two aspects: first, the meaning of awakening; second, the meaning of non-awakening.
That which is above, the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*), is neither defiled nor pure, neither arising nor ceasing; it is the nature of primordial equality.
Sentient beings, being without distinction, are themselves Nirvana; they do not depend upon extinction. Ordinary people and Maitreya share the same ultimate limit (*ekānta*).

In this gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-dvāra*), there is delusion and awakening, cultivation and realization, wisdom and consciousness; there is the clarification of principle and the engagement with phenomena.
Thus, the gate of arising turns wisdom into consciousness by depending on non-awakening (*avidyā*); it is deluded regarding principle and pursues phenomena. The gate of cessation [is the reverse].

By means of initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*), the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are transformed into wisdom (*jñāna*), whereby phenomena are realized as identical to principle (*tattva*).
Previously, the Gate of True Suchness (*tathatā-mukha*) was shown to lead practitioners of the Mahāyāna to first perceive that self-nature is pure and ultimately devoid of even a single thing;

now, this clarifies the Gate of Arising and Ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*) so that one may clearly understand how one’s own mind manifests according to karma. Having thus perceived nature and clarified the mind, one realizes the principle.
The task of perfecting the Buddha-way through the integration of phenomena is now complete. This mind of arising and ceasing relies upon the *tathāgatagarbha*;
thus, that which undergoes arising and ceasing is shown to have no intrinsic substance, being established based on the mind.

It is said that the mind of arising and ceasing relies upon the non-arising, non-ceasing mind because the non-arising, non-ceasing mind begins to function as arising and ceasing when stirred by the wind of ignorance. Therefore, it is taught that the mind of arising and ceasing relies upon the non-arising, non-ceasing mind.
Now, regarding the arising of the three subtleties and six coarsenesses based upon the Tathāgatagarbha:

it is said that because the characteristics of form and emptiness mutually oppose and supplant one another within the Tathāgatagarbha, the Tathāgatagarbha accordingly manifests as form and emptiness, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.

Therefore, within this [Tathāgatagarbha], there arise the movement of wind, the clarity of space, the brightness of the sun, and the darkness of clouds. Thus begins the discussion of initial awakening (*ādikṣaya-bodhi*) and ultimate awakening (*niṣṭhā-gata-bodhi*).
Regarding the cessation based on the *tathāgatagarbha*: it refers to uniting the wondrous clarity that is neither extinguished nor born with the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Since the *tathāgatagarbha* is solely wondrous enlightened clarity that perfectly illumines the *dharmadhātu*, within it, the one becomes the infinite and the infinite becomes the one.
Thus, one knows that although the functions of wisdom regarding birth-and-death, ordinary beings, and sages differ, they all collectively do not depart from the *tathāgatagarbha*.
This is manifested from the *ālayavijñāna*. To explain: the following correctly interprets that the mind of arising and ceasing depends upon the *tathāgatagarbha*.

That which is neither born nor extinguished is the *tathāgatagarbha*; because the *tathāgatagarbha*—the intrinsically pure mind (*cittaprakṛti*)—and its activity of arising and ceasing are inseparable, they are termed "conjoined" (*saṃyukta*).
Being neither identical nor different, it is named the *ālayavijñāna*.
They are "not one" because the essence of the true and the deluded do not inherently follow one another;
they are "not different" because the true and the deluded harmonize with each other according to conditions.
