Furthermore, they are "not one" because when the evolving consciousnesses of birth and death are extinguished, the essence of this storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) does not actually perish, thereby avoiding the fault of nihilism; they are "not different" because...

When stirred by the wind of ignorance, this ocean of the *ālayavijñāna* gives rise to the waves of consciousness; thus, it avoids the fault of permanence and remains free from these two extremes, being neither identical nor different [from the mind].

The *ālayavijñāna* is translated as "store-consciousness" (*zàngshí*) because it possesses the capacity to store (*nengcáng*), that which is stored (*suocáng*), and is itself clung to as a self (*wǎ'ài zhícáng*).
Since this consciousness is a synthesis of the real and the false, it serves as the basis for...
If based on the True, all phenomena are subsumed and returned to their own nature, whereby one attains the designation of "Awakening.

If based on the delusory, all phenomena arise, giving rise to the characteristic of grasping, whereby one attains the designation of "Non-awakening. These two meanings will be explained in the text below;

there is no need for further elaboration here. Question: Since the natures of the True and the delusory are inherently at odds with one another, in what sense can it be said that [the latter] "depends" on [the former]?

Because of the *tathāgatagarbha*, there is the mind of arising and ceasing. Since its substance is not distinct [from it], the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara-citta*) is called the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Due to the movement of the wind of ignorance, this [mind] arises and ceases. Apart from the *tathāgatagarbha*, this mind of arising and ceasing has no substance;
it is like still water which, when blown by the wind, manifests the appearance of motion. This motion...
Just as the characteristic of water ceases to exist when separated from the still body of water, the principle herein is likewise; this should be contemplated.

As for the meaning of "awakening" (bodhi), it refers to the essence of the mind being free from thought. This characteristic of being free from thought is equal to the realm of empty space, having nothing [to be grasped].
The single characteristic that pervades the entire Dharma-realm is precisely the Tathāgata’s equal Dharma-body; based on this Dharma-body, it is termed "original enlightenment" (*mūla-avabodha*).
Why is this? The meaning of original enlightenment is spoken in contrast to the meaning of "initial enlightenment" (*ādi-avabodha*); for initial enlightenment is identical to original enlightenment.
The meaning of initial enlightenment exists by depending upon original enlightenment, and it is because of non-enlightenment (*a-avabodha*) that [the distinction of initial enlightenment] is taught.

Initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) is called ultimate awakening (*atyanta-bodhi*) because it awakens to the source of the mind; it is not ultimate awakening because it does not awaken to the source of the mind.
What is the meaning of this? It is like an ordinary person who, perceiving that a preceding thought has arisen as evil, is able to restrain the subsequent thought so that it does not arise.
Although this is called "awakening," it is still non-awakening. This is because, for example, the contemplative wisdom of the two vehicles has only just begun to arise.
When Bodhisattvas at the stage of "Intent" (āśaya-bhūmi) realize that mindfulness and its variations are without distinct characteristics, they abandon coarse conceptualization and attachment;

this is called "similar realization" (*sādṛśa-abhisamaya*), because it accords with the realization of Dharmakāya Bodhisattvas who realize that mindfulness in the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) is without the characteristic of abiding, having departed from the coarse characteristics of conceptualized mindfulness;
thus it is called "partial realization" (*prādeśika-abhisamaya*), as it fulfills the skillful means (*upāya*) to the end of the Bodhisattva stages.
When the mind is awakened through a single thought-moment, the initial arising of the mind is found to have no initial characteristic;
because one has distanced oneself from subtle thoughts, one perceives the nature of the mind, which is eternally abiding—this is called ultimate awakening.
This is the correct explanation that the gate of cessation relies upon the *tathāgatagarbha*.

The passage beginning with "The essence of mind is free from thought" provides a general explanation of the meaning of awakening (*bodhi*), while the section beginning with "As for ordinary people" specifically clarifies the meaning of awakening. That it is both general and specific is because it accords with the capacities of those who follow the sudden and gradual approaches.
However, since wisdom and principle are of one suchness, they are inherently equal and inherently all-pervading; by virtue of this oneness...

When one contemplates this obscurity and dullness, the nature and its manifestations diverge and phenomena and principle conflict; thus, the Dharmakāya transmigrates through the five paths and is called a "sentient being.
All of this arises from non-awakening. That which is called "awakening" is none other than returning to the essence where principle and wisdom are of one suchness;
because it is fundamentally free from thought, it is termed "awakening. The meaning of awakening refers to the fact that the substance of the mind is detached from thought.
This term "awakening" (*jue*) already contains the subsequent categories of awakening: semblance awakening (*xiangsi jue*), partial awakening (*suifen jue*), and ultimate awakening (*jiujing jue*).
This term "thought" (*nian*) already contains the subsequent four characteristics of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing (*sheng-zhu-yi-mie*).

Since one is already free from the characteristics of thought, one realizes the essence of the Great Universal Dharma-Gate of the Single Dharma-Domain (*eka-dharmadhātu*), wherein there is no phenomenon not subsumed and no principle not contained; therefore, it is called "equality" (*pingdeng*).

The realm of empty space is all-pervading; the single characteristic of the *dharmadhātu* is precisely what is called the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata. The *dharmakāya* is the meaning of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena.

This means that it extends horizontally across the three periods of time and penetrates vertically through both the ordinary and the sagely, remaining eternally non-dual whether in bondage or beyond hindrances.

Therefore, based upon this *dharmakāya*, it is designated as "original enlightenment" (*mūla-avabodha*). Because of the *dharmakāya*— [Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a larger commentary on the *Awakening of Faith*. The translation reflects the philosophical content of the extant portion.]

Because the principle of awakening is not newly produced, it is called "original" (*ben*). As the *Awakening of Mahāyāna Faith* states: "When all illusions are extinguished, there is no place where the Way is realized, nor is there anything attained;
for the original nature is inherently perfect. Why is this? The following section poses two simultaneous inquiries regarding these two meanings.

First, it inquires about the meaning of "original awakening" (*benjue*). Therefore, the commentary explains: "The meaning of original awakening is spoken in contrast to the meaning of initial awakening (*shijue*). Thus it is said.
The "Original" (ben) serves as a verification of what was stated above regarding "Awakening" (jue). Why does it conclude by saying, "therefore it is called Original Awakening" (benjue)?
The commentary explains: because initial awakening (shijue) is identical to original awakening, it is concluded by means of original awakening.
When original awakening is spoken of in contrast to the meaning of initial awakening, it is because within the essence of true awakening, there is fundamentally no "original."
The name "awakening" (*bodhi*) arises from the nature of awakening following defilement; thus, there is "initial awakening.

Although initial awakening involves the departure from the marks of thought and the perfect realization of the *dharmakāya*, this principle of the *dharmakāya* is fundamentally complete in itself and is not produced by initial awakening; therefore, it is called "original.
That initial awakening is identical to original awakening is because the meaning of initial awakening is precisely the fundamental substance.
Since the function of wisdom does not exist as a separate entity, it is said to be identical to the original awakening (*mūla-awakening*).

Regarding the meaning of initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*), the text further explains below that because one relies on original awakening and follows the conditions of ignorance (*avidyā*) to produce deluded thoughts, there is non-awakening;
and because of this non-awakening, the function of wisdom suddenly arises. It is taught that there is initial awakening when awakening removes the marks of these thoughts. Thus, we know for certain.

Because of thought (*citta*), there arises the distinction between the beginning and the fundamental; yet, if one is free from thought, they are fundamentally equal and identical within a single awakening (*bodhi*).
Thus, regarding the beginning of the arousal of awakening and the ultimate end of that awakening, there are differences in depth and distinctions in thought.
Furthermore, because it directly reveals the source of the ultimate, it is said: "Moreover, because it awakens to the source of the mind, it is called ultimate awakening (*atyanta-bodhi*)."

Because one does not awaken to the source of the mind, it is not ultimate awakening. What is the meaning of this? The two points—the awakening to the source of the mind and the non-awakening to the source of the mind—are both examined together.
From the passage "As with ordinary people" onwards, the text correctly explains the non-awakening to the source of the mind.

It says that one who is aware when a prior thought arises as evil and is able to stop a subsequent thought from arising has entered the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*) and has severed [delusion].
The "characteristic of the arising of karma" and the "characteristic of suffering bound by karma" from among the six coarse characteristics are transcended by a single stage of ignorance.
Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "When desire and love are dried up and the faculties and objects do not meet, the remaining physical form no longer continues to be born.

Therefore, one knows that if one is able to awaken to the arising of evil in the preceding thought-moment, then the desire and love of the present moment will be dried up, and the faculties and objects [will no longer meet].
If one can occasionally arrest subsequent thoughts so that they do not arise, then the continuity of future bodies will no longer persist;

although the signs of karma may manifest in the present, they will not give rise to subsequent continuations, and the residual physical substrate will still possess the four phases of birth, abiding, change, and extinction.

Furthermore, the forty-one grades of ignorance remain latent within the *ālaya-vijñāna*, and thus it has not yet interfused with the Tathāgata’s dharma-stream. Therefore, the text concludes with "although... (sui).

Furthermore, it is called "awakening" precisely because it is non-awakening. This explains the meaning of the "similar awakening to the source of the mind," as clarified below regarding the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas).

Although the contemplative wisdom of the Two Vehicles has not yet fully realized the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), the power of their insight has already exhausted self-clinging (*ātma-grāha*).
Since self-clinging is exhausted, they no longer give rise to the marks of grasping; therefore, they are included here alongside those who have first resolved upon the Bodhi-mind.
The "Sas" and so forth refer to the three stages of the provisions (*sambhāra*) as well as the four stages of application (*prayoga*).

This Bodhisattva in the stage of worthiness (*satpuruṣa-bhūmi*) seeks to abide in consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) and practices the two contemplations of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

Gradually suppressing and gradually eliminating the two types of dualistic grasping—grasping at a self and grasping at phenomena—they sever the thirty grades of the ignorance of differentiated characteristics (*visabhāga-lakṣaṇa-avidyā*), thereby transcending the six coarse [stages] and the grasping at signs (*nimittodgrahaṇa*) and the conceptualization of names (*nāman-vikalpa*).

It is also said that "to awaken to the difference in thought" refers to awakening to the characteristic of difference, which is ignorance (*avidyā*). Since thought lacks the characteristic of difference, wisdom arises;

to eliminate the delusions that manifest [from it] means that although the differences in thought have already been exhausted and are no longer grasped, there still remain eleven grades of ignorance (*avidyā*) latent within the fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). Thus, the realm of the *dharmakāya* has not yet been fully awakened to and realized.
The conclusion states: "Because one has already abandoned the coarse marks of conceptual attachment, it is called 'similar awakening' (*sābhāsā-bodhi*).

It is called 'similar' because, while performing the wisdom of the contemplation of the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena on a level similar to the *bhūmis*, one has not yet fully realized the two innate attachments to a self and to phenomena;
hence it is termed 'similar awakening. It is like the Bodhisattva of the Dharma-body..."

The term "Sa" (薩) below signifies the meaning of awakening to the source of the mind according to one's respective capacity. Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) refer to those in the noble stages of the ten grounds (*bhūmi*);

because from the first ground onward they realize that the Dharma-body is all-pervasive, and thus through the tenth ground they all equally attain this realization, they are all called Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body.
These Bodhisattvas abide in *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) and cultivate the dual entry into both the characterized (*sanimitta*) and the uncharacterized (*animitta*).

Through the gradual subduing and gradual severing of the two innate attachments to self and dharmas via the cultivation of contemplative insight, the ten grades of the ignorance of the abiding-phase (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa-avidyā*) are extinguished.

This transcends the six coarse states (*ṣaḍ-audārika*) among the middle [three] and the three subtle states (*tri-sūkṣma*): the state of cognitive wisdom (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*), the state of continuity (*anubandha-lakṣaṇa*), and the state of the perceiving subject (*darśana-lakṣaṇa*) within the state of objective environment (*viṣaya-lakṣaṇa*).
By awakening to the abiding through the wisdom of the dual emptiness contemplation, one immediately awakens to the ignorance of the abiding-phase; thus, thought ceases to exist.
The dwelling in the mark (*lakṣaṇa*) clearly manifests that the obstructions have been exhausted and wisdom appears as purely signless (*animitta*). Thus, the ancient masters said:

"In the Stage of Extreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), the two obstructions of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) are eliminated; however, the innate (*sahaja*) grasping at self and phenomena is not yet severed.

Although the innate dual grasping at self and phenomena is abandoned stage by stage, the ignorance of the arising-mark (*utpatti-lakṣaṇa-avidyā*) is still not fully exhausted, and the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) has not yet manifested."
Because it is an initial emergence, the concluding phrase states: "It is called 'partial awakening' (*prādeśika-bodhi*) because it is free from the characteristics of coarse conceptualization.
It is called "partial" because, in each stage (*bhūmi*), one awakens to and abandons one hindrance and two delusions, thereby partially realizing the ten kinds of *tathatā*.

This refers to the meaning of "awakening to the source of the mind," which is correctly elucidated below in the section on the "Exhaustion of the Bodhisattva Stages. This bodhisattva is the stage immediately following Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*).
The mind severs the first grade of the *utpatti-lakṣaṇa-avidyā* (ignorance characterized by arising), which is the *karma-lakṣaṇa* (aspect of karma) among the three subtle states.

At this point, because the causes are exhausted and the fruits are fulfilled, it is said that "the stages are ended" (*bhūmi-kṣaya*). Because the myriad practices are already perfected, it is said that "expedient means are complete.

"A single thought-moment of resonance" (*ekakṣaṇa-samprayoga*) occurs because, through the emptiness of the *vipākavijñāna* (retributive consciousness), the Vajra-wisdom of a single thought-moment arises and accords with the principle of *tathatā* (suchness).
When one responds, one realizes that the initial arising of consciousness lacks clarity and cannot be apprehended; thus it is said that the mind has no initial characteristic (*ādi-lakṣaṇa*).

Reaching this point, both demons and Buddhas are empty, and defilement and purity are equally forgotten. The nature of the mind is purely true, and its wondrous virtue is brilliantly radiant; therefore, the conclusion states:

"Because one is far removed from subtle thoughts, one attains the vision of the nature of the mind; this mind is eternally abiding and is called ultimate awakening (*atyanta-bodhi*). The preceding section concludes here.

In the first three stages, because the perception of mental activity (*saṃjñā*) has not been exhausted and the True [Nature] has not yet fully manifested, it is not said that one "sees the nature" (*jìng xìng*).
Now, because one is far removed from subtle mental activity, the True [Nature] is immediately revealed; therefore, it is said that one "sees the mind-nature.

In the preceding three stages, awakening had not yet reached its source, and the arising and ceasing of the karmic consciousness (*karmavijñāna*) were not called "permanent abiding. Now, because one awakens to the source, the wind of ignorance has ceased, and the nature [is permanently abiding].

Because the waves of the ocean have subsided, it is called "eternally abiding. Within the first three stages, because one has not awakened to the source of the mind, one seeks to extinguish thoughts and looks toward reaching the other shore;

thus, it is not called ultimate. Now, having awakened to the source of the mind—which is fundamentally free from the marks of thought and is originally but the One Mind—one begins to be no different from the original state; therefore, it is called ultimate awakening. Question: Since ignorance...

Question: Why, when dividing [the characteristics] into four according to their coarseness and subtlety, are the two characteristics of arising and ceasing each assigned one grade, while the characteristic of abiding is divided into ten grades, and the characteristic of difference is further divided into thirty grades? Answer:

Ignorance originally has no fixed number of grades; rather, "grades" are spoken of only in reference to the stages at which they are abandoned. Furthermore, as for the characteristic of cessation, it resides in the state of *kṣānti* (receptivity).

The characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*) is severed at the stage of Wisdom (*prajñā-bhūmi*); the characteristic of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*) is severed at the stage of Sages (*ārya*), while the characteristic of difference (*anyathātva-lakṣaṇa*) is severed at the stage of Worthies (*pṛthagjana*).

Because there is no duality between the stages of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and the severance [of the remaining characteristics], the two characteristics of arising and cessation are each divided into one part. The characteristic of difference is severed during the stage of Worthies, and the characteristic of abiding is severed during the stage of Sages.

The stage of Sages is divided into the ten *bhūmis*, while the stage of Worthies is divided into the positions of Abiding (*sthiti*), Practice (*caryā*), and Direction (*mukha*), each forming its own tenfold set. This is because, at each successive stage, awakening eliminates [the respective delusions].
The aspect of abiding is divided into ten categories, while the aspect of differentiation is divided into thirty categories.
Therefore, the Sūtra states: "If there are sentient beings who can contemplate non-thought, they are then heading toward Buddha-wisdom.
Furthermore, as for the arising of the mind, there is no initial characteristic that can be known; thus, to speak of knowing an initial characteristic is precisely to say that there is none.
For this reason, all sentient beings are not called "awakened," because from the very beginning their thoughts have continued in succession, never having been separated from thought;
therefore, it is said that ignorance is without beginning. If one attains the state of non-thought, then one knows the arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing of the marks of the mind.
Because of the equality of non-thought, there is in reality no distinction between "beginning awakening" (*ādi-bodhi*), for the four marks occur simultaneously.
"Yet all existences are without self-establishment, being fundamentally equal and identical to one awakening.
This summarizes the preceding meaning. "Therefore, in the Sūtra, the following concludes the 'similar awakening' and the 'partial awakening.
"Therefore, all sentient beings... concludes "non-awakening. "If one attains non-thought... concludes [the ultimate awakening].
Ultimate awakening is also said to be the ability to contemplate non-thought (*amanasikāra*) by turning toward the Buddha-wisdom; it does not mean entering the Buddha-wisdom by abandoning thought.

Therefore, it was previously stated that awakening to divergent thoughts while abiding in mindfulness—yet not having attained the distancing from the subtle marks of thought—is only called "similar" or "partial" awakening.
Furthermore, as for the arising of the mind, there is no initial mark; although this is an explanation...
By clarifying the initial characteristic, the intention to manifest non-thought (*amanasikāra*) is revealed;

furthermore, it is explained that all sentient beings are in a continuous succession of thoughts from moment to moment, never departing from thought, and thus there is "beginningless ignorance" (*anādikālikāvidyā*).

Moreover, it causes the practitioner to know this and abandon this, whereby they realize the Tathāgata’s equal Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); hence, the conclusion states: "If one attains non-thought..."
One who thus knows the characteristics of the arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing of the mind attains non-thought;

because the four wisdoms are perfectly luminous, one knows that characteristics such as arising and ceasing are all like flowers in the sky. Since there is no distinction among the four characteristics, how could there be one who perceives the characteristic of cessation?

This is called non-awakening (*abodha*). One who perceives the characteristic of change is called "similar awakening" (*sādṛśa-bodha*). One who perceives the characteristic of abiding is called "conforming [awakening]" (*anuvartana*).
If one asks whether the awakening that perceives the characteristics of arising is called ultimate awakening (*niṣṭhābodhi*), it is said:

"Because of non-thought (*amanasikāra*) and so forth, there is in reality no difference in initial awakening (*ādikṣānti-bodhi*). "Non-thought and so forth" refers to the absence of the characteristics of thought regarding arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing.
"There is no difference in initial awakening" means that initial awakening exists simultaneously with these four characteristics; they are all [identical].
Since there is no self-existence, the thought that is perceived is already empty; how then could the wisdom that perceives be different?
Therefore, it is said that they are fundamentally equal and identical as one awakening.
Furthermore, when original awakening follows defilement, two kinds of characteristics arise through discrimination, yet these are not separated from that original awakening.
What are these two? First, the characteristic of the purity of wisdom; second, the characteristic of inconceivable activity.
Although the preceding text clarifies the beginning of the arousal of the mind and its ultimate consummation, it has not yet detailed the characteristics of the three bodies and four wisdoms.
Now, the "characteristic of the purity of wisdom" refers to the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, which realizes the Dharma-body. It is inconceivable...
The characteristics of the karmic activities are precisely the Wisdom of Perfect Accomplishment, the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation, and the Wisdom of Equality, as well as the two bodies:

the Body of Recompense and the Transformation Body. These two types of characteristics arise following defilement; this refers exactly to the wondrous nature being perfectly luminous and free from all names and marks.
Because of delusion there is birth, and because of birth there is extinction. Birth and extinction are called delusion; the extinction of delusion is called the True.
These are designated as the two names for the twofold transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*): supreme enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhi*) and great nirvāṇa (*mahā-nirvāṇa*).

Now, the characteristic of the purity of wisdom (*jñāna-viśuddhi-lakṣaṇa*) refers to the convergence of defiled discrimination back to the pure essence; the characteristic of inconceivable activity (*acintya-karma-lakṣaṇa*) arises precisely from that pure essence as the functional operation of wisdom.

Regarding the characteristic of the purity of wisdom (*jñāna-viśuddhi-lakṣaṇa*): it refers to the manifestation of the pure wisdom of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), which occurs because one has fulfilled the skillful means of practicing according to reality through the power of the permeation of the Dharma.

Consequently, the characteristics of the synthetic consciousnesses (*saṃghāta-vijñāna*) are destroyed and the characteristics of the continuous mind (*saṃtati-citta*) are extinguished. As for the meaning of this principle:
all characteristics of the mind and consciousness are entirely ignorance (*avidyā*). Yet, the characteristics of ignorance do not depart from the nature of awakening (*bodhi-svabhāva*).
It is neither destructible nor indestructible, like the water of the great ocean which, stirred by the wind, possesses both the characteristics of water and the characteristics of wind;
yet these characteristics do not abandon one another, for while the water is not of a moving nature, when the wind ceases, the movement ceases, yet the moist nature remains undestroyed.
In this way, the intrinsically pure mind of sentient beings is stirred by the wind of ignorance, such that the mind coexists with ignorance.
Because they are formless and inseparable, the mind is not of a mobile nature; if the continuity of ignorance ceases, then that cessation is the indestructible nature of wisdom.
This means that for one who practices according to reality by relying on the power of the Dharma, it is by relying on the power of internal perfuming through True Suchness (*tathatā*) and...

Beyond the external conditioning of the teachings of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one practices according to reality from the stage of the worthy (*ārya*) up to the holy ones, until reaching the final thought-moment of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
When the skillful means are thus fulfilled, the seeds of the two hindrances, the seeds of outflows (*āsrava*), and the inferior untainted seeds (*anāsrava*) are all simultaneously emptied.
Thereupon, the Great Perfect Circle (*mahā-vimala-maṇḍala*) arises at once, and then all...

Because consciousness suddenly exhausts the dharmatā and the fundamental reality is pure and true, it is said that "the characteristics of the synthetic consciousness are destroyed and the characteristics of the continuous mind are extinguished, so that the wisdom of the Dharma-body manifests in its pure clarity. Here, "synthetic consciousness" refers to the eighth consciousness;
it is what was previously described as the *ālaya-vijñāna*, characterized by the synthesis of the unborn and undying with the born and dying, termed the "continuous mind."
This refers to the seventh consciousness. Later in the text, it uses the term "mind" (*manas*) to refer to the "successive consciousness. What is the meaning of this?

Below, the text raises this question to clarify that while the characteristics of consciousness are completely extinguished, the nature of wisdom (*jñāna-svabhāva*) is indestructible. This meaning is self-evident through the dharma and its metaphors, as can be understood from the text itself.
As for the statement, "neither destructible nor non-destructible," it is because of the non-awakened characteristics of the various consciousnesses.
The nature of fundamental awakening that does not depart from its accompaniment of defilement is neither identical nor different [from it]. Because it is not different, it cannot be destroyed;
because it is not identical, it is not indestructible. Based on the meaning of being neither different nor indestructible, it is said that ignorance is itself illumination.
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Illumination and ignorance are non-dual in their nature; there is no duality between them."
Nature is itself the true nature (*dharmatā*). If one speaks from the perspective of its meaning as being neither one nor indestructible, it is because ignorance (*avidyā*) can be extinguished;
thus, it is like the Nirvāṇa-sūtra which says: "By the extinction of ignorance, the lamp of Bodhi is attained.
Since the awakened nature remains unimpaired even when ignorance is utterly extinguished, for this reason it is said to be neither destructible nor indestructible.
Question: Since all consciousnesses must be purified to realize the *dharmakāya*, for what reason are only the seventh and eighth consciousnesses extinguished?

Answer: The five pure material sense-faculties (*pañca-rūpīndriyāṇi*) are the immediate objective portions (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses. Once the substance of the eight consciousnesses is transformed, their objective portions are likewise transformed accordingly.

When the objective portions of the five sense-faculties are transformed, the consciousnesses that take those five faculties as their support are also transformed. Thus, the six [consciousnesses] are transformed.
Consciousness takes the seventh consciousness as its root; since the root-consciousness is purified, the consciousnesses that depend upon it are also purified.
Thus, one knows that when the eighth and seventh consciousnesses cease, the sixth and fifth consciousnesses cease of their own accord, without needing to be mentioned.
Regarding the characteristic of inconceivable activity: by relying on the characteristic of pure wisdom, it is able to produce all supreme and wondrous realms—
namely, the characteristics of immeasurable merit— which are eternally uninterrupted, spontaneously correspond to the faculties of sentient beings,
manifest in various ways, and thereby bring about benefit.

It is called "inconceivable" because it manifests based on this reliance upon fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), and is not something that can be deliberated upon by the ordinary mind or consciousness.

Because one has already realized the *dharmakāya* by relying on the aspect of the purity of wisdom, and subsequently gives rise from within the essence of the purity of wisdom of the *dharmakāya* to the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*),
manifesting the two bodies— the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*— to perform infinite and supreme Buddha-activities, it is said [to be inconceivable].
Relying on the characteristic of the purity of wisdom, one is able to manifest all supreme and wondrous objects as the reality of things as they are.
As the *Treatise on the True Nature* states: "The bodies of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are like space and without marks;

for the sake of those of superior wisdom, they manifest as the objects of the six sense faculties, displaying subtle and wondrous forms, emitting sublime sounds, causing [beings] to smell the fragrance of the Buddha’s precepts, and partaking of the flavor of the Buddha’s sublime Dharma."
Because it causes the awakening of samādhi-contact and brings knowledge of the profound and wondrous Dharma, it is called the "Wondrous Realm";
this refers to the characteristics of immeasurable merit. The following clarifies the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body).

Since this *saṃbhogakāya* is that which is evoked by immeasurable adornments and immeasurable merits, it is constantly perceived by those of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), and because it is enjoyed by their bodies, it is eternal.
There is no cessation; this follows the capacities of sentient beings and clarifies the manifestation of the *nirmāṇakāya*.

Because this *nirmāṇakāya* manifests in various forms according to each class of being and teaches the Dharma in accordance with their spiritual faculties, it causes all sentient beings to leave suffering behind and obtain benefit.
Furthermore, regarding the essential nature and characteristics of awakening (*bodhi*), there are four kinds of great meanings that are equal to empty space, like a pure mirror.
What are these four? First, the Mirror of Suchness-Emptiness (*yathābhūta-śūnyatā-ādarśa*): it is far removed from all marks of the objective realm of the mind;

no phenomena can appear therein, for it does not possess the meaning of cognitive illumination. Second, the Mirror of Causal Infusion (*hetu-vāsana-ādarśa*): this refers to suchness as non-empty (*ayathābhūta-aśūnya*), wherein all worldly...

The intermediate boundaries all appear therein, neither emerging nor entering, neither losing nor perishing, eternally abiding in a single mind because all phenomena are identical to the true nature of reality.
Furthermore, it cannot be defiled by any defiled phenomena; its essence of wisdom is immovable, being fully endowed with the untainted and permeating sentient beings.
Third is the mirror of the emergence of phenomena, which refers to the emergence of non-empty phenomena.
Fourth is the mirror of the permeation of conditions:
because it is based on the emergence from the dharmas, it universally illumines the minds of sentient beings, causing them to cultivate roots of goodness and manifesting according to their thoughts.

These four kinds of meanings collectively encompass the two kinds of meaning regarding the conceptual differentiation of the discourse on the *tathatā* (suchness) gate, as well as the two aspects of the meaning of awakening within the *utpādanirodha* (arising and ceasing) gate. First, the mirror of reality-as-it-is and emptiness;
second, the mirror of causal perfuming—these are the two kinds of meaning within the *tathatā* gate. Third, the mirror of the emergence of phenomena; this is wisdom.
The fourth is the mirror of the perfuming of conditions, which is the inconceivable aspect of karmic activity (*acintya-karma-lakṣaṇa*).

The phrase "because the essence of awakening is equal to empty space" reveals that the nature of awakening is transparent and all-pervasive throughout all phenomena, and furthermore, is capable of containing all phenomena.
Furthermore, the analogy of a "pure mirror" clarifies that the nature of awakening is spiritually penetrating and able to respond to all phenomena, and furthermore, is able to manifest them.

All phenomena are one: they are like the mirror of reality-as-it-is (yathābhūta-śūnyatā), which is far removed from all marks of the objective sphere of the mind and has no phenomena that can manifest.
This is because within the nature of awakening, there is primordial emptiness and stillness; all mental objects and states of mind are fundamentally non-corresponding.
It is like a clear, bright sky or a pure, luminous mirror, severed from all forms and characteristics and free from all names and words, by virtue of all phenomena.
The fundamental suchness (tathatā) is empty in its very essence; it is not made empty through the contemplation of *śamatha*.
Therefore, it is said that this does not have the meaning of "awakened illumination. Second, regarding the mirror of causal perfuming (*hetu-vāsanā-maṇḍala*), which is truly not empty:

although all objective realms appear within it, this is because within the essence of true awakening, despite being fundamentally empty and quiescent from the beginning, it does not obstruct the manifestation of all phenomena.
All phenomena appear within it, just as the substance of empty space is not composed of manifold characteristics yet does not obstruct the manifestation of those various characteristics.
It is also like a mirror the size of a pellet that can reflect a mountain ten thousand fathoms high; although it manifests dust and worlds, its essence is inherently quiescent.
Therefore, it is said that there is no exiting or entering. While phenomena arise and perish according to conditions, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is non-existent.
Because there is arising and ceasing, it is said that [the mind] is neither lost nor destroyed, but is the eternally abiding single mind.
Since all phenomena are themselves the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and not something artificial, through the samādhi of realization, one understands that phenomena are precisely the mind.

The above concludes the explanation of how "true non-emptiness" acts as the cause for manifesting phenomena. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "that which cannot be defiled by any defiled phenomena," [the following] is the direct [explanation].

This clarifies the meaning of being permeated by causes (*hetu-vāsanā*). Because within the nature of awakening (*bodhi-svabhāva*) there is fully present the pure cause free from outflows (*anāsrava-śukla-hetu*), which internally permeates its own essence (*antar-bhāva*) in a constant and uninterrupted manner;
and because it is able to accumulate immeasurable merits in accordance with that nature;

it is said that "it cannot be defiled by any defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*)," that "the essence of wisdom (*jñāna-svabhāva*) is immovable," and that it "fully possesses the permeation of the outflow-free and thereby permeates sentient beings. (3)

The mirror of the transcendence of phenomena refers to the wisdom that realizes non-empty phenomena as being free from the hindrance of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the hindrance of cognitive objects (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), thereby transcending the characteristic of composite existence.

This means realizing that all phenomena are the true nature (*tathatā*), which is fundamentally devoid of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

Since one has transcended the imagined nature, one emerges from the hindrance of afflictions; since one thoroughly understands the dependent nature, one emerges from the hindrance of cognitive objects—thus transcending both obstacles.
Since mental phenomena have been eliminated and mastery over them is attained, the mind and its phenomena are in a state of harmonious detachment;

it is pure, wondrously luminous, truly eternal, and uniquely manifest. It is like empty space cleared of dust, or like a mirror cleansed of grime; therefore, it is said to be "pure, luminous, and clear.
Fourth is the mirror of the permeation of conditions: because it issues forth from the Dharma, it universally illumines the minds of sentient beings, causing them to practice.
Regarding the manifestation through the recollection of roots of goodness: this refers to first attaining the Dharma-body by relying on the Dharma to transcend the two obstacles;

subsequently, through the perfuming of pure conditions, one manifests the two bodies—the recompense body and the transformation body—to universally illuminate the mental activities of sentient beings.

According to their capacities, one manifests teachings to cause them to cultivate roots of goodness. Within this, there is nothing that can be called a speaker or a spoken teaching, nor a savior or one saved.

The void responds to sounds like a bright mirror manifests images. Of these four kinds of awakening, the first two belong to the meaning of original awakening (*mūla-awakening*), which does not depend on artificial cultivation;

the latter two belong to the meaning of initial awakening (*ādi-awakening*), which must be realized through enlightenment. However, when cultivating the latter two meanings, one must do so in accordance with the former two meanings.
Third is the mirror of the departure from phenomena (*dharmaviniḥsṛta-ādarśa*), which refers to departing in reliance upon the Dharma.

1. Being free from the hindrance of afflictions and the hindrance to knowledge, and being free from the characteristics of composite phenomena, it is correctly termed "one" because it is like a mirror of emptiness that accords with reality, wherein one practices by remaining far removed from all mental objects and characteristics.

4. It is the mirror of the permeating influence of conditions, which universally illumines the minds of sentient beings, causing them to cultivate roots of goodness and manifesting according to their thoughts;
this is correctly based on the second [nature], which is like a mirror of non-emptiness that accords with reality.
The manifestation of the adorned forms and appearances of all worlds is neither emerging nor entering, neither lost nor destroyed.
If one realizes only the former two meanings but does not cultivate the latter two, although one has been a Buddha from the beginning, it is like the nature of gold remaining within ore.
If one cultivates only the latter two meanings without attaining the former two, then even if one's practice is vast...

A kalpa is like gold being separated from its ore; if one can achieve perfect realization through these four meanings and cultivate both practice and understanding together, it is like gold extracted from ore that no longer becomes mixed with impurities.

Thus, we know that these four meanings are intended to comprehensively encompass the two types of emptiness within the True Suchness Gate (*tathatā-mukha*) and the two types of characteristics within the Awakening Gate (*bodhi-mukha*) of the Arising and Ceasing Gate (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*). This has profound significance.
What is called the meaning of non-awakening refers to the failure to know, as it truly is, that the *tathatā*-dharma is one. Consequently, non-awakening arises in the mind, giving rise to thoughts;

yet these thoughts lack intrinsic characteristics and do not depart from original awakening (*mūla-awakening*). It is like a person who becomes lost because they rely on directions: if they were separated from directions, there would be no such thing as being lost.
Sentient beings are likewise: they are deluded by relying upon awakening; if they were separated from the nature of awakening, there would be no delusion.
Thus, there is nothing that is not non-enlightenment; because of the existence of the deluded mind of non-enlightenment, one is able to know names and meanings and can speak of true enlightenment.
However, if one were separated from the mind of non-enlightenment, there would be no self-characteristic of true enlightenment that could be spoken of.
This explanation of the gateway of arising is based upon the *tathāgatagarbha*. Above, the meaning of awakening was clarified;

first, its principle was revealed in general, followed by a detailed enumeration of the meanings of initial awakening (*ādikṣaya-bodhi*) and ultimate awakening (*niṣṭhā-bodhi*). Here, the meaning of non-awakening is clarified;

likewise, it first presents delusion in general, and then further opens up the characteristics of the three subtleties and six coarsenesses. Thus, one should know that the contrast between delusion and awakening, whether presented generally or specifically, is not different.
What is called the meaning of "non-awakening" refers to not knowing, as they truly are, that the *tathatā* (suchness) is a single reality.

This is because one does not understand the essence of the Great Universal Dharma-gate of the One Dharma-realm. That is to say, if there is a "suchness" external to wisdom, then sentiment arises and wisdom is obstructed;
thus, correct wisdom is inverted into delusive thought. If there is a "wisdom" external to suchness, then appearances change and the essence becomes distinct. Thus...
When suchness is inverted, it is termed "name" and "mark"; collectively, this refers to True Suchness not maintaining its own nature.

With a single moment of deluded movement, one fails to realize that the fundamental substance of phenomena before one is naturally as-it-is; thus it is said, "non-awakening arises, and with it, thought.
This non-awakened mind is none other than true wisdom becoming obscured and darkened, having no separate essence of its own; therefore, it is said, "thought has no self-nature."

Because the characteristics do not depart from fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), they are likened to one who is lost regarding direction not departing from the directions themselves, or a mind that is deluded not departing from the nature of awakening.
As stated in the preceding text, "it is by depending on fundamental enlightenment that non-awakening exists.

Because there is the deluded mind of non-awakening, the following section clarifies true awakening in contrast to the false; this serves as a reverse demonstration that delusive thoughts do not depart [from true awakening].
The nature of awakening also, because of non-awakening, suddenly awakens to self-reflection and is able to know the name and meaning of True Suchness (Tathatā);
therefore, it is said that true awakening is what was previously referred to as "beginning awakening" based on non-awakening.
Thus we know that apart from fundamental awakening, there is no mind of non-awakening; and apart from non-awakening, there is no intrinsic characteristic of true awakening that can be described.
Furthermore, based on non-awakening (*abodha*), three kinds of characteristics arise; they are associated with and inseparable from that non-awakening. What are these three?
First is the characteristic of the activity of ignorance (*avidyā-karma-lakṣaṇa*). Because it depends on non-awakening, the mind moves; this movement is called "activity.

If there were awakening, there would be no movement; if there is movement, there is suffering. This is because the fruit is never separated from its cause. Second is the characteristic of the capacity for seeing (*darśana-lakṣaṇa*). This arises because it depends on movement.
Therefore, when one is able to see that there is no movement, the three kinds of objective appearances do not exist;
it is because of the capacity for seeing that objects falsely manifest, and apart from seeing, there are no objects.

As for the statement that "the three kinds of appearances arise based on non-awakening," this means that the three subtle states arise from the non-awakening of ignorance (*avidyā*). Because there is... [text ends]

Luminosity (*vidyā*) is the essence and the three subtle states are the characteristics; since the characteristics do not depart from the essence and the essence does not differ from the characteristics, it is said that they are associated with and inseparable from that non-awakening (*a-vibodha*).
First, regarding the "karmic characteristic of ignorance" (*avidyā-karma-lakṣaṇa*):

because one does not know the single reality of *tathatā* as it truly is, the mind arises through non-awakening and possesses mentation; therefore, it is said that the mind moves, and this mentation moves.
Although at that time no objective realm manifests, the causes of the ten dharma realms all take this as their initial sign;

therefore, it is called "karma. Within true nature (*dharmatā*), there is fundamentally no characteristic of movement, such that both delusion and awakening are transcended and both defilement and purity are forgotten.
Because the mind arises through non-awakening, the causes and effects of ordinary beings and sages are established from this point onward; hence it is said: "When there is movement..."

There is suffering because its fruit does not depart from its cause; thus, karma is the cause and suffering is the fruit. Because cause and effect are linked in a continuous cycle like a cluster of *akṣa* fruits, it is said that these two are inseparable.
As for the second, the characteristic of the perceiver, this is the characteristic of transformation (*vivartana-lakṣaṇa*).

Because one does not know reality as it is, when a single thought-moment moves, there arises what is falsely termed "luminous awareness. Once that which is falsely established comes into being, [the subsequent characteristics arise].
You falsely claim that it can form the characteristic of seeing; thus you say that because it moves in reliance upon the mind, it is able to see.

This means that it transforms in reliance upon the prior characteristic of karma to become the faculty of seeing. However, if one relies on the gate of the purity of nature, there is no such thing as seeing.
By implication, seeing must rely on the meaning of movement; therefore, it is said that if there is no movement, there is no seeing. Third is the characteristic of the objective field.

This refers to the manifestation of appearances. It is because once true wisdom (*tathatā-jñāna*) is inverted to become the "perceiving subject" (*darśana-lakṣaṇa*), the principle of true reality (*bhūta-tattva*) follows that perceiver and manifests as the "objectified realm" (*viṣaya-lakṣaṇa*).

What is meant is that when true wisdom becomes obscured, the principle of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*) turns accordingly into "stolid emptiness" (*jaḍa-śūnyatā*); therefore it is said: "Because of the perceiver, the false realm appears"—that is, it appears based on this inversion.

The marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are able to manifest objects; however, if one relies on noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) to depart from views, since these objects no longer exist, one should know that these objects definitely arise from views.
This is because if there were no dreaming mind, there would be no dream-objects; thus it is said that "if one departs from views, then there are no objects.
Nevertheless, these three marks all suddenly manifest due to a single thought of ignorance (*avidyā*); they do not possess a sequence of before and after.
It is said that the substance of the eight consciousnesses is fundamentally lucid and pure; this is precisely what is called the *amala-vijñāna* (stainless consciousness) or the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Because it is perfumed by ignorance (*avidyā*), it is able to give rise to all conditions, transforming its entirety as the self-witnessing portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) into the two divisions of seeing and appearance (*darśana-bhāga* and *nimitta-bhāga*).
At the moment of this initial transformation, it is termed the "phase of the karma of ignorance" (*avidyā-karma-lakṣaṇa*), once the seeing-portion has been established.
That which is called the "aspect of the seeing faculty" (darśana-bhāga) is precisely what is termed the "aspect of the objective realm" (nimitta-bhāga);

for it is by depending on the seeing faculty that the aspect of self is grasped, and by depending on the aspect of phenomena that the dharmas are grasped. From this, the six kinds of coarse aspects further arise.
Because there are objective conditions (*ālambana*), six further types of characteristics arise. What are these six? First, the characteristic of the basis of cognition (*jñāna-nimitta*):

based upon the objective field, the mind gives rise to discrimination between the pleasant and the unpleasant. Second, the characteristic of the basis of continuity (*anubandha-nimitta*): based upon cognition, feelings of suffering and pleasure arise;
the mind gives rise to thoughts that correspond [to those feelings] in an uninterrupted succession. Third, the characteristic of the basis of grasping (*upādāna-nimitta*)...

First, the characteristic of the continuity of objects: because the mind gives rise to attachment toward suffering and pleasure while dwelling upon and maintaining objects through continuous recollection. Second, the characteristic of the dependence on false grasping: because one relies on deluded attachments and conceptualization to falsely grasp at the characteristics of provisional names and signs. Third, the characteristic of the dependence on names and signs: because one relies on names and signs to seek out and grasp them, thereby creating various kinds of karma. Because retribution is not autonomous, one should know that ignorance can give rise to all defiled dharmas,
for all defiled dharmas are characterized by non-awakening (*abodha*).
As for the statement that "the conditions of objects give rise to six kinds of characteristics," this means that objects serve as conditions to develop the six coarse aspects.

Because it possesses both the subjective faculty of cognition and the objective referent, and because cause and effect are simultaneously manifested, it is termed "gross. Regarding the "single characteristic of cognition":
based upon an object, the mind gives rise to discrimination between the pleasant and the unpleasant; thus, the "object" refers precisely to the aforementioned characteristic of the object-field.

Although the characteristic of the object-field manifests above [in the preceding stage], no discrimination arises there; however, based on that object, one further gives rise to attachment and defilement.

Although thoughts of attachment and the like arise within equanimity (*upekṣā*), because one does not grasp at them, it is called "wisdom" (*jñāna*). Regarding the second characteristic, the characteristic of continuity:

because one relies upon wisdom, the mental concomitants of the perceptions of suffering and pleasure arise and continue without interruption; thus, "wisdom" refers to the characteristic of superior wisdom (*adhiprajñā*).
Although thoughts of attachment and the like arise within this characteristic of superior wisdom, one remains unbound by the perceptions of suffering and pleasure.
This mind, moreover, arises from attachment to what is pleasant and gives rise to suffering through non-attachment to what is unpleasant.
Because this single type of mind is associated with non-forgetfulness, it is called "continuity" (*saṃtati*). Third, regarding the characteristic of grasping (*upādāna-lakṣaṇa*):

because the mind that experiences pleasure and pain arises through attachment, sustained by the mental application (*manasikāra*) toward the continuity [of objects], the "continuity of mental application" refers precisely to the aforementioned characteristic of continuity. This is the characteristic of continuity mentioned above.

Although one does not forget suffering and pleasure, one still does not give rise to attachment toward them; yet, while dwelling in this state, one develops a profound sense of weary detachment (*nirveda*) toward suffering, whereas one develops intense defiled attachment toward pleasure.

Therefore, these are called the "four modes of grasping" (*upādāna*). As for the characteristic of names and words (*nāma-pada-lakṣaṇa*), it arises because conventional designations (*prajñapti*) are established based on false grasping and discrimination;
thus, false grasping and discrimination are precisely the aforementioned characteristic of grasping (*upādāna-lakṣaṇa*). This refers to the aforementioned grasping...
Although the grasping of marks gives rise to attachment, it still does not establish conventional designations (*nāma-paññatti*).

This further relies on deluded grasping and discrimination to provisionally establish and designate the characteristics of form; therefore, it is called "reckoning the mark of names. Fifth, the mark of the arising of karma:
because one creates various kinds of karma based on names, one relies upon these names—that is, the aforementioned reckoning of names.
The "characteristic of names" (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*) refers to the fact that although names and conventional designations (*prajñapti*) are established, one does not yet create karma.

This [next stage], however, is called the "characteristic of initiating karma" (*karma-samutthāna-lakṣaṇa*) because, based on those names and conventional designations, one engages in discursive thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), grasps at signs (*nimitta*), and thereby creates various kinds of karma. Regarding the "characteristic of suffering bound by the six types of karma" (*ṣaḍ-karma-bandhana-duḥkha-lakṣaṇa*):
it arises because, depending on karma, one experiences retribution and lacks autonomy. "Depending on karma" refers precisely to the aforementioned characteristic of initiating karma.
Although the preceding section clarified karma, it had not yet made explicit its results;

this [section] clarifies that based on karma, one undergoes retribution and transmigrates through the three realms with no mastery over the mind, and is therefore termed "suffering bound by karma. One should know that the following is a summary:

the characteristics of the three subtle and six coarse [delusions] all manifest due to the non-awakening of ignorance (*avidyā*), thereby demonstrating that ignorance is the cause of all defiled phenomena.
The dharma of defilement is the characteristic of ignorance; apart from ignorance, there are no characteristics of the three subtleties or six coarsenesses.
Apart from the dharma of defilement, there is no essence of ignorance. Therefore, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "Those characteristics are faults, all of which arise from the mind's bondage.
They are deluded thoughts that have no knowledge of dependent origination. Deluded thoughts [arise] regarding dependent origination.
Furthermore, there are two aspects to awakening and non-awakening. What are these two? First, the common aspect;
second, the distinct aspect.
The above has already explained both meanings of awakening and non-awakening; here, they are further clarified.

Regarding the two kinds of characteristics: as stated previously, the non-arising and non-ceasing [of the true nature] is in conjunction with arising and ceasing [of the false], being neither identical nor different; this is what is termed the *ālaya-vijñāna*. Although it was previously indicated that they are "neither identical nor different," this passage now explicitly clarifies it. Being "not identical" refers to the characteristic of difference (*bheda-lakṣaṇa*), while being "not different" refers to the characteristic of sameness (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). The reason the true and the false are called the characteristic of sameness is as follows: [the true nature] is the essence of the false, and [the false] is the function of the true. Because their essences are not distinct, they are termed the characteristic of sameness. Furthermore, because the false arises from the true and returns to the true, they are termed the characteristic of sameness. Moreover, because the false is originally empty and identical to the true, they are termed the characteristic of sameness. Finally, because the false is the very substance of the true, they are termed the characteristic of sameness. Therefore, although the true and the false are conventionally distinguished, in reality they are not two separate things. This is why they are called the characteristic of sameness. As for the characteristic of difference: although the false arises from the true, its arising does not exhaust the true; although the false returns to the true, its returning does not destroy the true. Thus, the true remains eternally constant while the false undergoes change; therefore, they are termed the characteristic of difference.
