This means that while True Suchness (tathatā) remains unchanging as it follows conditions, its substance is empty due to the formation of phenomena through deluded thought (vikalpa).
It is also called "differentiation" because, while True Suchness remains unchanging as it follows conditions, the substance of deluded thought is empty yet forms phenomena.

Thus, one knows that while the essence of the true and the deluded is identical, their functions differ, hence they are named differently. This is also because of what was previously explained regarding awakening.

Furthermore, it is said that non-enlightenment (abodhi) is contrary to enlightenment (bodhi), yet it is also said that delusion depends upon enlightenment and is not separate from original enlightenment (mūla-bodhi).
If one says they are different, how can delusion depend upon enlightenment? If one says they are the same, why are defilement and purity not equal?

Moreover, if they were fixedly the same or fixedly different, there would be no gateway for spiritual cultivation. Why is this? If they were the same, then ordinary beings and sages would be identical.

When delight and aversion are both severed, the distinct states of defilement and purity proceed in opposition, and delusion and awakening are forever separated; therefore, one uses identity and difference to analyze and explain in order to eliminate this confusion.
As for the aspect of identity (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*):
for example, various earthenware vessels are all identical in their nature and characteristics as mere dust particles; likewise, [all things] are thus without outflows (*anāsrava*).
It clarifies that the various illusory manifestations of karma are all identical in their nature and characteristics to True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Therefore, based on this meaning, the *Sūtras* state that all sentient beings are originally and eternally abiding in the entry into *nirvāṇa*; the Dharma of Bodhi is neither a characteristic to be cultivated nor a characteristic to be produced.
It is ultimately unattainable, and while there are no color-forms (*rūpa*) to be seen, yet there is the seeing of color-forms.
These marks are merely produced by the illusory activity of following defilement; they are not the mark of the non-empty color of wisdom, because the marks of wisdom are invisible.
This reveals that the essential natures of awakening and non-awakening are fundamentally identical, just as various earthenware vessels, though they may exist or not, [share the same substance].
The ultimate distinctions of all measures are identical to the nature and characteristics of atoms, for there is no separate substance apart from atoms.

Although the illusions of outflow-free states, ignorance, and karma differ, they are in fact identical to the nature and characteristics of True Suchness (*tathatā*), because the substance of all phenomena is established through the mind.
Thus, the outflow-free state has the meaning of awakening, while ignorance has the meaning of non-awakening.
The various illusory manifestations of outflowing karma are precisely the mark of the purity of wisdom and the mark of inconceivable karma;

the various illusory manifestations of the karma of ignorance are precisely the marks of the three subtleties and six coarsenesses. Although these marks of defilement and purity differ according to whether they involve outflow-free or ignorant states, ultimately they all return to the self-nature.
Within this self-nature, there is but a single mark and a single flavor, which is ultimate.
Because they are equal, they are said to be "the same. Therefore, a sūtra is cited as proof to clarify that the dharmas of nirvāṇa and bodhi are primordially and eternally abiding;
they are not characteristics that can be cultivated, nor are they characteristics that can be produced. Ultimately, there is nothing to be attained, nor is there any form or characteristic visible.
Regarding the statement that they are "not characteristics that can be cultivated, nor characteristics that can be produced," this is because they are untainted (*anāsrava*).

Since it is the very nature and characteristic of True Suchness (*tathatā*), there is no contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) to be cultivated, nor is there any Buddha-way (*buddhamārga*) to be constructed.

As for the statement that "no form or characteristic can be seen," it is because ignorance (*avidyā*) is itself the nature and characteristic of True Suchness; thus, there is no deluded dharma to be discarded, nor is there any form or characteristic to be perceived.
That which is called the true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*); it is an illusory transformation and empty.

The body is itself the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Since its nature and characteristics are equal and no characteristic can be perceived, yet one still perceives material forms (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*), these are merely illusory realms produced by the delusions of karma;

they are not the non-empty nature of the wisdom-form (*jñāna-rūpa*), because the characteristics of that wisdom are themselves unperceivable. As the *Prajñāpāramitā* says: "Form is itself emptiness. How could this be otherwise?
The nature of the substance of wisdom can be perceived.

As for their differing characteristics, they are like various earthenware vessels, each being distinct; likewise, due to the differentiation of the illusory manifestations following defilement and the differentiation of the illusory manifestations of ignorance, there is the differentiation of the nature of the outflows-free state.
This demonstrates that the functions and characteristics of awakening and non-awakening are inherently distinct. It is also like various earthenware vessels:

although they share the same nature and characteristics as fine dust particles, they do not obstruct one another and instead differ according to the shape of each vessel. Likewise, although the untainted (*anāsrava*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) share the same nature and characteristics as True Suchness (*tathatā*), they do not obstruct one another;
rather, according to the differences in their defiled and illusory natures, distinct characteristics manifest, just as [the differences] exist in the case of the untainted.
According to the nature of the distinctions between the marks of the purity of wisdom and the inconceivable marks, there arise the differences of the three bodies, the four wisdoms, the ten powers,
the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;
whereas according to the marks of the distinctions between the three subtle and six coarse [ignorances] of nescience, there arise the five aggregates, the six sense bases, and the twelve spheres.

One certainly knows that while the distinctions between the eighteen realms, the three miserable paths, the six destinies, and the twenty-five states of existence are solidly established, their essential substance is fundamentally the same, differing only due to their phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
If one can remove the vessel [of attachment] and contemplate emptiness, both sameness and difference will vanish.
Furthermore, regarding the causes and conditions for arising and ceasing: it is said that sentient beings evolve in dependence upon mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
How is this meaning established? It is explained that based on the *ālayavijñāna*, there arises ignorance (*avidyā*) through non-awakening;
because it can perceive, manifest, and grasp objects, and because it gives rise to a continuous stream of mentation, it is called "thought" (*manas*).

The preceding section concludes the explanation of the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*). This section is the formal exposition of the causes and conditions for arising and ceasing;
the causes and conditions for cessation will be explained later in the passage concerning the six types of defiled mind. Here, we first clarify the causes and conditions for arising.

To clarify the causes and conditions for arising is to explain the meaning of "non-awakening" (*a-bodhi*) mentioned above—the dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) of the three subtleties and the six coarsenesses. However, the essence of the *ālayavijñāna* is not...

Maintaining one's own nature (*svabhāva*) is the cause for the arising of the three subtle states; external false objects stirring up waves of consciousness is the condition for the arising of the six coarse states.

Although there are these causes and conditions for the arising of the delusions—both subtle and coarse—they all take the essence of the *ālaya* mind as their support, with the sixth and seventh consciousnesses serving as the pivot.
Therefore, it is said that [the mind] evolves based on the mind, thought, and consciousness.

Therefore, as for the meaning of this passage: "How is it so?"—this interrogative phrase serves to clarify that [the mind] evolves in dependence upon the mind, the thought, and the mental consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*).
It is said that there is ignorance (*avidyā*) by depending on the *ālayavijñāna*; this explicitly clarifies that [the mind] evolves in dependence upon the *citta*.
Because the *tathatā* (Suchness) is perfumed by ignorance, this *ālaya* is formed; and this very *ālaya* acts as the basis for that ignorance. This is the activity of ignorance.
The characteristic of manifestation arises from this characteristic of karma due to ignorance;

because one does not realize that the phenomena of *tathatā* are one, one is able to see, able to manifest, and able to grasp objects, giving rise to a continuous succession of thoughts. This correctly clarifies the transformation based on the manas.

"Able to see" refers to the characteristic of seeing; "able to manifest" refers to the characteristic of objects; and "able to grasp objects" refers to the characteristic of cognition (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*). Thus it arises.
The continuity of thought (*smṛti-saṃtati*) is precisely the characteristic of continuity;

although there are five distinct characteristics, they all manifest within a single moment of deluded movement, and thus are collectively termed "mind" (*manas*). This "mind" is precisely the characteristic of thought.

Furthermore, these five characteristics are none other than the two innate attachments to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*), as well as the discriminative attachment to phenomena. Arising from non-awakening (*a-prabodha*), they are capable of seeing and perceiving.

The manifestation of the innate grasping at dharmas (*sahaja-dharma-grāha*) that arises toward objects and continues as a stream of thought constitutes both the discriminative grasping at dharmas (*vikalpa-dharma-grāha*) and the innate grasping at self (*sahaja-ātma-grāha*).

The reason the discriminative grasping at self is not listed here is that it is subsumed under the "characteristic of grasping" (*grāhaka-lakṣaṇa*) within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) discussed in the following text;
thus, among the six types of defiled minds mentioned below, it has already been addressed from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onward.

Prior to this, one distances oneself from the arising of the continuity of thoughts regarding the objects of grasping; from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onward, one distances oneself from the arising of the capacity to see and manifest through non-awakening.

This precisely accords with the verse on the eight consciousnesses concerning the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*). Prior to the Immovable Stage, one merely abandons the storehouse-consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*);

after the Vajra Path, one abandons the maturation (*vipāka*) in the stage of emptiness. Prior to that, one abandons the storehouse; at that point, one truly abandons the attachment to the storehouse as "I" (*ātma-grāha*).
"Consciousness is empty" and "true emptiness" both refer to the innate clinging to dharmas (*sahaja-dharma-grāha*). Question:

It was stated above that based on awakening there is non-awakening, and by the power of this non-awakening, the substance of the mind is moved, causing the union of arising and ceasing so that the *ālaya*-vijñāna, its karmic marks, and so forth, come to exist.
Why, then, is it said here that based on the *ālaya* there is ignorance (*avidyā*)? Answer: This is the primary intent [of the present passage].
This passage takes up only the meaning of the true mind following conditions (*pratyaya*), for this meaning of "following conditions" is difficult to name directly.

Thus, sometimes it is explained that ignorance (*avidyā*) exists based on the *tathatā* (suchness) prior to its arising; alternatively, it is explained that ignorance exists based on the *ālayavijñāna* once it has been fully established and arisen.
Only through these two designations is the full meaning exhausted; therefore, the text expresses them in various ways, alternating between the former and the latter.
Furthermore, this mind has five names. What are these five? First, it is called the *karma-vijñāna* (act-consciousness), because by the power of ignorance, the mind moves without awareness.
Second, it is called the *pravṛtti-vijñāna* (evolving consciousness), because depending on the moving mind, it is able to perceive objective appearances.
The third is called the *pratibhāsa-vijñāna* (manifesting consciousness), which means it is able to manifest all objective realms, just as a clear mirror manifests forms and images;

the manifesting consciousness is likewise, appearing immediately as each of the five sense-objects encounters it, without any sequence of before or after, because it arises spontaneously at all times and is always present.
The fourth is called the *jñāna-vijñāna* (cognitive consciousness), which refers to the discrimination of defilement.
The fifth, called the *saṃtati-vijñāna* (continuing consciousness), is so named because it is associated with mindfulness and is uninterrupted.

These five names correctly explain how, through non-awakening, there arises the ability to see, the manifestation [of objects], and the grasping of objective spheres, resulting in the continuity of the arising of mindfulness.
The first is called the *karma-vijñāna* (action-consciousness); this refers to the arising of the aspect of karma (*karma-lakṣaṇa*) from non-awakening. This is clear.

Consciousness does not arise of itself; it is stirred by the delusion of ignorance. Once stirred, there is suffering, and thus it is called "karma. Previously, the characteristics of karma were explained;

here, consciousness is explained to show that consciousness is the active producer (*janaka-lakṣaṇa*) and [the characteristics] are the produced (*janya*). Since we are now clarifying the cause of production, it is called "consciousness.
Furthermore, it is shown that the characteristic is none other than consciousness, as they do not have two separate meanings. Consciousness is that which discerns and distinguishes.

The "causal basis of meaning" refers to the characteristics (*nimitta*) by which discernment (*vijñapti*) arises; it is not otherwise, for apart from conditions, there is no form—what then would consciousness be used for?

This collectively reveals that the arising of dharmas is due to the mind, and the arising of the mind is due to dharmas; the meanings of these preceding and following passages are seen in mutual correspondence. The four types of consciousness mentioned in the subsequent text are all explained according to this principle.
Second, they are called "transforming consciousnesses" (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), which means they are the seeing aspect (*darśana-bhāga*). This is because they depend upon the mind.
When movement arises, the capacity for seeing is formed; if there were no ignorance, the mind would not move, and thus the characteristic of seeing would not exist.

The third is called the "manifesting consciousness" (*darśana-vijñāna*), which is the characteristic of objective realms (*viṣaya-nimitta*). Because it relies upon the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), objective realms falsely appear.
Although all objective realms appear, they are not yet discriminated; therefore, it is likened to a bright mirror manifesting various forms.

Furthermore, reflections appear in a mirror; because these reflections fundamentally lack any distinction of before or after, it is said that the manifesting consciousness (*nirmita-vijñāna*) is likewise.
It appears according to the five sense objects as they encounter it, without any sequence of before or after.

The reason there is no distinction of before or after is that this manifesting consciousness functions spontaneously and is always present in the foreground. Fourth is what is called the cognitive wisdom-consciousness (*jñāna-vijñāna*). That is to say—

The characteristic of cognition (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*): Because it gives rise to thoughts of purity, defilement, and so forth based on the objects manifested by the manifesting consciousness (*ādarśa-vijñāna*), and because although it engages in discrimination, it does so spontaneously and subtly, it is called "cognition.
Fifth, the continuous consciousness (*saṃtati-vijñāna*) is the characteristic of continuity:

Because it gives rise to feelings of suffering and pleasure based on the cognition-consciousness (*jñāna-vijñāna*) which discriminates all phenomena of purity and defilement, one acquires the characteristic of growth.
Because it continues by its very nature without interruption;
because it maintains the virtuous and non-virtuous karma of immeasurable past lives and so forth, ensuring they are not lost;

and because it can bring to fruition the retributions of suffering and pleasure in the present and future without error; it is able to cause [one to remember] events already experienced in the present.
Suddenly, one thinks of future matters and unconsciously gives rise to deluded anxieties; therefore, the three realms are false and illusory, produced solely by the mind.
Apart from the mind, the objects of the six sense-fields do not exist. Why is this so?

Because all phenomena arise from the mind and are born of deluded thoughts; all discrimination is simply the discrimination of one's own mind. The mind does not see the mind, for there is no [separate] mind.
One should know that all worldly objects can be perceived because they are sustained by the ignorant, deluded mind of sentient beings.
Therefore, all phenomena are like images in a mirror; they have no substantial essence that can be apprehended. They are merely the false imaginings of the mind.
Because when the mind arises, various phenomena arise; and when the mind ceases, various phenomena cease.
The preceding section clarified the characteristics of the five mental activities; this section clarifies the functions of the five mental activities.

Because the substance of the mind inherently possesses the perfuming of the karma-consciousness of ignorance, it forms seeds; therefore, it is able to maintain and sustain past karmas, whether wholesome or unwholesome.
"Maintaining and sustaining" (zhuchi) carries the meaning of grasping and upholding. Wholesome and unwholesome karmas refer to wholesome and unwholesome seeds. By means of these wholesome...
Because the seeds of evil are constantly continuous like a torrential stream, it is said that they cause [the results] not to be lost.

Since the essence of the mind contains both the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*), it is further able to mature the retributions of suffering and pleasure in the present and future.
Due to past virtuous karma, one experiences the retribution of pleasure in the present and future; due to past non-virtue...
Because of karma, one invites the retribution of suffering in the present and future; because the causal factor of karma is not lost, the retribution likewise does not deviate.
Because the essence of the mind possesses wisdom-consciousness (*jñāna-vijñāna*), it enables one to suddenly recollect events that have already passed in the present.
Because it possesses the consciousness of continuity (*saṃtati-vijñāna*), it enables one to [anticipate] events that have not yet occurred in the future.

By awakening to deluded movement, one clarifies that the karma of the past and the retribution of the present and future reveal the law of cause and effect across the three periods of time as nothing other than one's own mind.

By clarifying what has already occurred and reflecting upon what has not yet occurred, one reveals that the thoughts of arising and ceasing throughout the three periods of time likewise do not depart from one's own mind. Therefore, [the text] concludes:
Xian says: "The three realms are false and illusory, produced solely by the mind. Because all phenomena arise from deluded thoughts, they are called 'false and illusory.
Since they do not exist apart from the mind, they are said to be 'mind-only.
As these phenomena are themselves the mind, that which discriminates is precisely the discrimination of one's own mind. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "One's own..."
The mind grasps at its own mind; it is through non-illusion that illusion is formed. If the mind does not grasp, then nothing can be attained;
that which cannot be seen is precisely what is not grasped. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "If one does not grasp, there is nothing that is not illusion.

Since even non-illusion does not arise, how can illusory phenomena be established? Or it is said: "Since the mind is itself the dharma, why do you not see the mind? Therefore, it is called "non-existence" (*wu*).

"Characteristics can be apprehended"—one should know that this concluding statement summarizes the preceding intent so that one may understand that all phenomena are fundamentally non-existent and are established solely based on the deluded mind of ignorance.
Just as the images within a mirror have no substantial reality, it is said: "When the mind arises, phenomena arise;
when the mind ceases, phenomena cease. This refers to the arising of the mind-source as the mind moves according to its habitual perfuming.

Regarding the statement that "extinction" refers to returning to purity: if one is apart from a mind of pure detachment, how could any phenomena ever have arising or extinction? That which is called non-arising and non-ceasing, when conjoined with arising and ceasing, is named the Ālaya-vijñāna.

Its half that is non-arising and non-ceasing is termed the "True Aspect" (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*), which is the essence of the eight consciousnesses; its half that is arising and ceasing is termed the "Karmic Aspect" (*karma-lakṣaṇa*).

If this were not the mind (*manas*), what else could it be? Furthermore, the essence of the eight consciousnesses is subtle and self-luminous; if it were not the mind serving as their underlying substrate, how could this be so?
Since ignorance is utterly incapable of seeing or manifesting anything, one should know that all such seeing and manifesting are the fault of this mental faculty (*manas*).
Therefore, this treatise attributes the three subtle states to the mental faculty; how could this contradict other sūtras and śāstras?

Furthermore, because this mental faculty constantly and critically examines the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as the self, the five sensory consciousnesses arise from it.
There are five causes for the transformation [of consciousness]: because the five consciousnesses grasp the shadows of external objects, there are six consciousnesses;

once the five consciousnesses have transformed, they immediately infuse the *bhāga-lakṣaṇa* (objective aspect) of the eighth consciousness; once the sixth consciousness has transformed, it immediately infuses the two divisions—the *darśana-bhāga* (subjective aspect) and the *lakṣaṇa-bhāga* (objective aspect)—of the eighth consciousness.

Thus, the reception of perfuming, the maintenance of seeds, and the accumulation that gives rise to resultant phenomena occur without interruption; all this is due to the faculty of mind (*manas*) clinging to a self.
For this reason, if the seventh consciousness does not grasp [objects], then the five and six consciousnesses do not arise.
Since the five and six consciousnesses do not arise, there is no sense of "perfuming" (vāsanā) regarding the two divisions of the perceived (nimitta) and the perceiver (darśana).

If the principle of perfuming does not exist, how could there be the names of the *ālayavijñāna*—the storehouse consciousness that receives perfuming, maintains seeds, and accumulates the fruit—and the *vipākavijñāna* (maturation consciousness)? Therefore...
This treatise attributes the perfuming of seeds and the maturation of retribution to the *manas*; thus, it does not contradict other sutras and śāstras.
We know for certain that the explanation of the three subtle states clarifies that within the substance of the eight consciousnesses, there is a partial aspect of arising and ceasing;
how could there ever be non-enlightenment (*avidyā*) capable of seeing and manifesting apart from the eight consciousnesses?

Furthermore, as for what is called "mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*): it is this very evolving consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) which, based upon the deep-seated grasping and attachment of ordinary beings, gives rise to various false attachments of "self" and "what belongs to self.
Following after objects and discriminating among the six sense-fields, it is called mental consciousness; it is also called the "separating consciousness" (*prativikalpavijñāna*).
Furthermore, it is termed the "consciousness that discriminates phenomena" (*vastuprativikalpavijñāna*). This consciousness increases in dependence upon the afflictions of views and craving.
Because it has the meaning of "long" (*dīrgha*).

This is the correct explanation that it evolves based on the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). This consciousness derives its name from depending upon the mind (*manas*); therefore, it is called "based on the continuous consciousness.

Its grasping and attachment evolve more deeply, and as it clings to objects according to their specific characteristics, it is named "mental consciousness. The continuous consciousness is precisely the mind (*manas*).

This manas, by constantly and critically examining the principle of non-self among the noble ones, causes every thought-moment to become purified and ensures that the mental consciousness never again evolves [into a self-grasping state].

However, by constantly and critically examining the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses as "self" and the manifested image-division (*nimitta-bhāga*) as "mine" among ordinary beings,
it deeply adheres from within, thereby giving rise to various kinds of deluded attachments externally.
Because it turns according to the objects of the six consciousnesses, this is the "characteristic of grasping," which is precisely the discrimination of self-clinging;
it is also called the "consciousness of separation" because the faculties and objects of this sixth consciousness are coarse and manifest, constantly changing and altering.
Furthermore, it is called the "consciousness that discriminates phenomena" because this consciousness conditions objects in the same manner as the five [sensory] consciousnesses.

The object consists of the grasping of the sensory realms of form, sound, odor, taste, and touch; if separated from the five consciousnesses, it further discriminates the reflected images of these five objects.
Furthermore, because it can take as its object phenomena of the three periods of time—whether possessing substance or lacking substance—it is called the "discriminating consciousness of things.
Although this consciousness evolves based on the mental faculty (*manas*), it increases through reliance upon the afflictions of views and craving. Thus, views are obtained.
The eighty-eight afflictions of the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are called the "ground of abiding in all views.

The eighty-one grades of the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) are called the "ground of abiding in desire-attachment," the "ground of abiding in form-attachment," and the "ground of abiding in formless-attachment.
These four grounds of abiding cause the mind to be clouded and disturbed by afflictions; they cause the collection of mental factors to waver within and rush outward toward external objects.
It is called "increase.
That consciousness which arises based on the perfuming of ignorance cannot be known by ordinary beings, nor can it be realized through the wisdom of the two vehicles;
rather, it is that which Bodhisattvas, from their initial stage of right faith, observe upon generating the mind of enlightenment, and which they attain partially upon realizing the Dharma-body.
Partial knowledge extends even to the ultimate stage of a bodhisattva, yet it cannot be fully known; only a Buddha realizes it completely. Why is this?
This mind has been pure by its very nature from the beginning, yet it possesses ignorance. Being defiled by ignorance, there arises a defiled mind.
Although there is a defiled mind, it is ever-constant and unchanging. Therefore, this meaning can be known only by a Buddha.
That which is called the nature of the mind is eternally without thought, and thus it is termed "unchanging.
Because one does not penetrate the single Dharma-realm, the mind becomes dissociated [from its true nature], and thoughts suddenly arise; this is termed "ignorance" (avidyā).

This further clarifies that the consciousness arising from ignorance is understood only by a Buddha; it serves as the basis for the subsequent explanation of the principle of the cessation of causes and conditions.
The consciousness produced by the permeation of ignorance is a portion of the eighth consciousness, which is the meaning of "non-awakening" (*abodhi*);
it is precisely the *karmic-consciousness* (*karma-vijñāna*) within the *manas*. However, when ignorance permeates True Suchness (*tathatā*), this is the activity of the true aspect.
The mutual harmony [of these factors] is termed the "partial aspect of karma" (*karma-lakṣaṇa*) of the *ālayavijñāna*, which is precisely what is called "karmic consciousness" (*karmavijñāna*).
This is the ground of the dwelling of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*). It is something that ordinary beings cannot know and is not realized by those of the Two Vehicles;

for the contemplative wisdom of the Two Vehicles can only comprehend the four grounds of dwelling in afflictions (*kleśa-catur-vāsabhūmi*), while it is precisely this ground of the dwelling of ignorance that they must suppress.
Because it is *nirvāṇa*, they are unable to awaken to it. Even from the initial stage of correct faith and the arousal of the bodhicitta, when one observes, one is still unable to know it;

this is because their dualistic attachments to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*) have not yet been severed, and they still abide in the rank of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), being unable to awaken to and penetrate the realm of all Buddhas.
If one realizes the *dharmakāya* and attains a partial knowledge of it, it is because they have already abandoned [those attachments].

Because the two innate attachments to a self and to phenomena are gradually suppressed and gradually severed, and one partially realizes the ten kinds of true suchness (*tathatā*), one attains partial knowledge as one progresses through the stages (*bhūmi*).

Even at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), one has not yet exhausted all knowledge, because there remains one obstacle and two delusions that have not yet been completely severed; thus, one cannot know it exhaustively. Only... [the Buddha knows it exhaustively].
Because the Buddhas have exhausted the five stages of dwelling and eternally extinguished the two obstacles, they are able to thoroughly comprehend that this mind has been so from the very beginning;
this is the correct elucidation of the principle of its difficulty to know. Because this mind is unchanging yet follows conditions, it is said to be "intrinsically pure while possessing ignorance.
Nevertheless, although it follows conditions, its essence does not change; therefore, it is said that "although there is a defiled mind," [it remains intrinsically pure].
Because it is eternal and unchanging, if one observes it through ignorance (*avidyā*), it does not hinder its being entirely true;
if one seeks realization through that which is true and eternal, it does not hinder its essence being intermingled with ignorance.
Therefore, this meaning can only be known by a Buddha, as the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* says: "The intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara-citta*) is difficult to comprehend; that mind..."
It is difficult to fully comprehend even the afflictions, and so on, until the conclusion states: "Only a Buddha can know what is called the nature of the mind.
This concludes by generally explaining the two meanings of the true and the delusive. Because the nature of the mind is eternally without thought, it is termed "immutable";

this concluding statement reveals the True [Nature]. Because one realizes that the dharma of *tathatā* (suchness) is one, wisdom and principle are as they were originally—without the characteristic of thought.

The nature that is eternally constant is termed "original enlightenment" (*mūla-avabodha*); because one does not penetrate the single dharma-realm (*eka-dharmadhātu*), delusion is manifested and bound.
Because the self-mind is non-enlightened and follows along with defiled conditions, and because one does not penetrate the oneness of the *tathatā*-dharma, wisdom contradicts principle;
thus, thoughts suddenly arise, which is termed "ignorance" (*avidyā*).

There are six kinds of defiled minds (*saṃkliṣṭa-citta*). What are the six? First, the defilement associated with grasping (*parigraha-saṃprayukta-kleśa*), which is removed through the liberation of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) and by departing from the stage of faith-association (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*).

Second, the defilement associated with non-interruption (*anupaccheda-saṃprayukta-kleśa*), which is gradually abandoned through the cultivation of skillful means on the stage of faith-association and attained through ultimate detachment upon reaching the stage of pure mind (*śuddha-citta-bhūmi*). Third, the defilement of partial... [text truncated]

1. The defilement associated with the distinct cognition (*pratisaṃvid-jñāna*) is gradually abandoned from the stage of possessing the precepts (*śīla-bhūmi*) up until its ultimate abandonment at the stage of the means of signlessness (*animitta-upāya-bhūmi*).
2. Fourth, the defilement dissociated from manifested form (*rūpa*) is abandoned by means of the stage of mastery over form (*rūpa-vaśitā-bhūmi*). 3.
Fifth, the defilement dissociated from the perceiving mind (*citta*) is abandoned by means of the stage of mastery over mind (*citta-vaśitā-bhūmi*). 4. Sixth, the fundamental karma...

Because those who are not yet free from the defilements dissociated [from the mind] can enter the Tathāgata stage upon reaching the final stage (*kṣayabhūmi*) of the Bodhisattva, they are able to abandon them;

whereas those who do not understand the meaning of the single dharma-realm (*ekadharmadhātu*) proceed from the stage associated with faith (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*) through observation and training to sever [defilements], entering the pure mind stage (*śuddhacittabhūmi*),
where they attain partial abandonment, until finally attaining ultimate abandonment at the Tathāgata stage.
The above concludes the explanation of the causes and conditions for arising; this now correctly explains the causes and conditions for cessation.
That which is ceased herein is the realm of delusive conditions—the defiled cause of ignorance—which is capable of causing those causes and conditions to cease.

That which serves as the cause for this cessation is the internal permeation of True Suchness (*tathatā*), while the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas serve as the external conditions. To clarify these causes and conditions for cessation is precisely to investigate [the nature of reality].
The meaning of "luminous awareness" refers to the coarse and subtle afflictions severed by the Bodhisattvas of the Three Sages, the Ten Stages, and Equal Enlightenment.
Having clarified the former meaning, it is now joined with the characteristics of the three subtleties and six coarsenesses;

in principle, this encompasses nine types, yet these are opened into six because the latter three among the six coarsenesses are what ordinary beings must abandon—though they may still be called "awareness," they are nonetheless [delusion].

Because they are not perceived, these are not listed here; furthermore, within the context of the causes and conditions for arising, the mental consciousness (*manas*) has five types and the mental cognition (*mano-vijñāna*) has one type, which are distinguished by their arising and ceasing, and thus are termed "six.
First is the defilement associated with grasping (*saṃprayukta-kleśa*), which is precisely the characteristic of grasping (*parigraha-lakṣaṇa*).
This characteristic of grasping is the discriminative grasping of a self (*ātma-grāha*) that arises within the mental cognition, manifesting as the appearances of its own mind.

Conceptualizing and deliberating, one clings to this as a real self; since those of the Two Vehicles have already realized the true emptiness through liberation from the grasping at self, they abandon these marks.

Furthermore, even when Bodhisattvas have perfected the ten stages of faith and observe with *śamatha* that the nature of pervasive conceptualization does not arise, they are likewise able to distance themselves from these two. As for the second, the "defilement of uninterrupted association," it is as follows:
This is the characteristic of continuity. This characteristic of continuity arises within the mental ground (*manobhūmi*) as the conceptualization of the grasping at dharmas;
it discriminates and calculates the appearances of one's own mind, clinging to them as real entities.

From the stage of initial right faith up to the stage of application (*prayoga*), one practices the contemplation of the emptiness of dharmas, gradually suppressing and gradually eliminating [this grasping] until, upon entering the first moment of the first bhūmi, it is ultimately abandoned and purified.
The "ground of mind" (*citta-bhūmi*) is the first ground (*prathamā bhūmi*). When entering the first ground, the sixth and seventh consciousnesses both undergo transformation;

the inferior-grade wisdom is attained, and the dual attachments to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*) are both abandoned—namely, the two obstacles of discrimination (*parikalpita-āvaraṇa*), which are utterly absent in the stage of "Extreme Joy.
Third, the defilement associated with discriminative wisdom is the "characteristic of wisdom" (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*); this characteristic of wisdom is precisely the innate [defilement].
The grasping at a self within the mental ground (*manobhūmi*) involves subtle deliberation;

from the second ground through the eighth ground, one enters the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and repeatedly eliminates it—that which is called "effortless practice" (*anābhoga-caryā*), which I constantly crush.

The stage of possessing precepts (*śīla-bhūmi*) is the second ground; the stage of the skillful means of signlessness (*animitta-upāya-bhūmi*) is the eighth ground. Fourth is the manifestation of form (*rūpa*).
The non-associated defilement is precisely the characteristic of the objective realm (*ālambana-nimitta*).
This characteristic of the objective realm arises spontaneously within the mental ground (*manobhūmi*) as the innate grasping at phenomena as real (*sahaja-dharma-grāha*).

It can only be abandoned by Bodhisattvas of the ninth stage, who exclusively enter the *tathatā* of the emptiness of phenomena, realize that all phenomena are like illusions, and attain mastery over phenomena. Fifth, this is the non-associated defilement of the perceiving mind.
This is precisely the characteristic of the "seer. This characteristic of the seer is also called the "obstruction of knowledge" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*);

because it arises subtly within the stage of mind (*manobhūmi*), Bodhisattvas of the ten stages must complete their cultivation of the perfected nature of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasunyatā-pariniṣpanna*). When they have finished this practice, the wondrous cloud of the shade of compassion covers the ocean of *nirvāṇa*, and they achieve all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Because they attain the eye of the mind and forever achieve liberation from [this obstruction], this is the sixth.
The defilement that is fundamentally non-associated with karma is precisely the karmic aspect of ignorance (*avidyā-karma-lakṣaṇa*).

This karmic aspect consists of the seeds of the two innate grasps (*sahaja-grāha-dvaya*), which subtly permeate the mental ground (*manobhūmi*) and constantly maintain their presence within the substance of the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).

This continues until the final moment of the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), when the Vajra Wisdom arises; at that point, the ripening consciousness becomes empty through the wisdom of a single moment of correspondence (*ekakṣaṇa-pratipatti-jñāna*).
By severing that root ignorance, one enters directly into the ocean of the fruit of wondrous enlightenment, attaining ultimate liberation;

this is because of the failure to comprehend the single dharma-realm. The following summary establishes the preceding meaning: because of the failure to comprehend the single dharma-realm, these six kinds of defiled minds arise.
Now, from the stage of Worthiness (*śaikṣa*), relying on semblance-enlightenment, one gradually studies and severs them until reaching the stage of the Ten Sages (*daśārya*).
From the stage of partial awakening up to the entry into the ground of the Tathāgata, one is finally able to achieve ultimate and eternal cessation;
thus we know that the noble stages are established based on a defiled mind. If one were apart from a defiled mind, what would there be for the so-called "noble" or the designation "ordinary"?
These are all merely empty sounds; their extraordinary features and inferior forms are all illusory appearances.

Regarding the meaning of "correspondence" (*saṃprayoga*): it refers to the fact that although the mind, mental factors (*citta-caitta*), and phenomena (*dharma*) have different bases and differ in their defiled or pure aspects, they are identical in their characteristics of cognition (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*) and their characteristics of objective conditions (*ālambana-lakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the meaning of "non-correspondence" (*asaṃprayoga*): it refers to the fact that the mind itself, being unawakened, is eternally without distinction, and thus does not possess the characteristics of cognition or the characteristics of objective conditions as distinct entities.
This explains the meaning of the three types of association and the three types of non-association within the six preceding defiled minds. Regarding the meaning of "association":
although the mind (citta) and mental factors (dharma) are distinct, they are associated because their characteristics of cognition and their objects are identical.

"Mind" refers to the characteristic of intellection (jñāna-lakṣaṇa), the characteristic of continuity (anubandha-lakṣaṇa), and the characteristic of grasping (parigraha-lakṣaṇa). "Mental factors" refer to the characteristic of objective environment (viṣaya-lakṣaṇa) among the three subtle states.

Although the characteristic of cognition (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of continuity (*saṃtati-lakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of grasping (*udgraha-lakṣaṇa*), and the characteristic of the object (*viṣaya-lakṣaṇa*) are distinct, it does not prevent the mind from arising as either attachment or non-attachment, or as sensations of suffering and pleasure, in accordance with those objects.

Therefore, it is said that because the characteristics of cognition and the characteristics of the objects are identical, the characteristic of cognition is precisely the mental activity (*citta-manasikāra*), and the characteristic of the objects is precisely the phenomena (*dharma*). This clarifies that apart from conditions, there is no mentation.

Thus, regarding the meaning of "associated" and "non-associated": because it is based on the single thought-moment of non-awakening within original enlightenment that ignorance is designated, this very single thought-moment of ignorance suddenly manifests the three subtle states (*trisūkṣma*). Since there is absolutely no external object acting as a condition, it is said to be "not the same" as the preceding [state of] knowing;
for while the characteristics of the object are the same, the mode of association differs. In this way, associated and non-associated are clearly distinguished.

The term "associated" (*saṃprayukta*) is used to manifest the characteristics of the coarse and the subtle, because it refers to the mutual orientation of mind and object, wherein subject and object stand in opposition.
Thus, among the six coarse states, those from the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*) onward are all capable of being completely severed.

As for the "non-associated" (*viprayukta*), this refers exclusively to the sudden manifestation of their characteristics through the very ignorance of the mind itself; they do not exist as mutually dependent entities.
For this reason, they are called the "three subtle [evolutions]"; it is therefore only from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onward, up to the stage of Tathāgata, that they can be completely severed.

Furthermore, regarding the meaning of the defiled mind, it is termed the "hindrance of afflictions" (*kleśāvaraṇa*), because it can obstruct the fundamental wisdom of *tathatā* (suchness); thus, it is ignorance (*avidyā*).
"Meaning" (*artha*) refers to that which obstructs wisdom and hinders the natural activity of worldly wisdom. Why is this so?
Because by relying on a defiled mind, one is able to see and manifest objects through false grasping, thereby contravening the nature of equality.
Since all phenomena are eternally quiescent and devoid of the characteristic of arising, ignorance fails to awaken and falsely opposes the Dharma; thus, one is unable to attain accord with it.

Because all worldly objects are known in their various forms, based on the aforementioned clarity of intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*), there exists ignorance (*avidyā*). Being defiled by this ignorance, there is a "defiled mind" (*kliṣṭa-citta*);
this correctly explains the meaning of how the defilement of the mind by ignorance acts as an obstruction, and it also reveals the departure from the six kinds of defiled minds.
There is nothing other than severing these two obstacles and realizing the two kinds of fruits; thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"By severing the afflictive obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*) that cause the continuity of rebirth, one realizes true liberation (*vimukti*); by severing the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that hinder omniscience, one attains Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
That which is called the "affliction-obstacle" refers to the afflictions of the four stages of abiding in views and craving, which are capable of continuing [the cycle of existence].
The obstacle of the segmentary cycle of birth and death obstructs the true suchness (*tathatā*) of self-emptiness, preventing the principle of *nirvāṇa* from ever manifesting;
therefore, it is said that this can obstruct the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) of true suchness. Fundamental wisdom is itself *nirvāṇa*.

Because self-nature *nirvāṇa* is originally devoid of arising and ceasing, it is termed fundamental wisdom. Ignorance (*avidyā*) is called the "obstruction to wisdom" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), which refers precisely to ignorance.

The Dwelling Grounds (*bhūmi*) can perpetuate the cycle of *pariṇāmi-vaipākika-janma* (transformative birth-and-death) and obstruct the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), thereby preventing the wisdom of bodhi from ever manifesting;
thus, they are said to "obstruct the natural wisdom of worldly activity. This natural wisdom of activity is itself bodhi.
Because the body of bodhi-wisdom manifests within the sensory realms and the Buddha-fields, all things therein are the wondrous power of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
Because they are accomplished with mastery, they are called the "worldly knowledge of spontaneous karma. What is the meaning of this? Below, both meanings are interrogated together.
"By relying on the defiled mind" explains the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). "Because all phenomena... explains the obstruction of knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Because one is able to see and manifest by falsely grasping at objects, this contradicts True Suchness (*tathatā*), which is without seeing and without manifestation.
Because the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) is characterized by non-appropriation and equality, it is called the "obstruction of afflictions" (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Since all phenomena are eternally quiescent and devoid of the characteristic of arising, they constitute the domain of wisdom (*jñāna*).

Because [the mind] fails to awaken due to ignorance and thus moves delusively, it stands in mutual opposition to that eternally quiescent reality; therefore, it is called the "obstruction of wisdom" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Below, he himself explains the meaning of this opposition, stating: "It is not..."
Because it can conform to all worldly objects through various forms of cognition, it is truly said that one does not know the single *tathatā*-dharma as it really is.
Regarding the phrase "obstruction of wisdom" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*): it is not that wisdom itself possesses an obstruction;

rather, because ignorance obstructs wisdom and thus the function of wisdom is not manifested, it is called the "obstruction of wisdom. Question: Of the six types of defiled minds, the first type belongs to the [first]...

The six consciousnesses are followed by five types [of afflictions] that all belong to the seventh mental faculty (*manas*). However, once the six types of defiled minds are completely severed, one enters the stage of the Tathāgata.

How then can it be said that only the sixth and seventh consciousnesses are transformed, while the five consciousnesses and the eighth consciousness are not? Answer: As stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, both the conceptual and innate dual attachments to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*) reside within the sixth and seventh consciousnesses. Therefore, when these two types of attachment are eliminated, the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) occurs. Since the five consciousnesses lack these attachments, they do not undergo transformation independently; rather, they follow the transformation of the seventh consciousness.

Thus, although the eighth consciousness remains as the support for the pure dharmas, it is the sixth and seventh consciousnesses that are specifically "transformed" because they are the locus of the defilements to be abandoned. Consequently, there is no contradiction in saying that only the sixth and seventh are transformed.

Within the two consciousnesses, one gives rise to the discrimination and conceptualization of the marks of one's own mind, grasping them as a real self and real dharmas; thus, self-grasping is the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and dharma-grasping is the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
It is firmly known that by severing these two hindrances and realizing the two fruits, one merely exhausts the sixth and seventh consciousnesses.

Furthermore, for a Bodhisattva to cultivate [the path] throughout three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas—[is this not so?]— *Note: The original text appears to be a fragment, likely from a commentary on Yogācāra doctrine (such as the *Cheng weishi lun*). The final clause "is this not so? is an inference based on the context of the preceding argument regarding the cessation of the seventh and sixth consciousnesses.*
It is not that one transforms these two consciousnesses—the sixth and the seventh—only upon reaching the first asaṃkhyeya-kalpa to enter the first bhūmi;

rather, it is the transformation of the lower-grade wisdom of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses. Upon practicing during the second asaṃkhyeya-kalpa to enter the Immovable Bhūmi (Acalā-bhūmi), there is the transformation of the middle-grade wisdom of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses.
Only upon practicing during the third asaṃkhyeya-kalpa does one reach the culmination of Equal Enlightenment (Samyak-saṃbodhi) and transform the sixth [consciousness].

The seventh and second consciousnesses are superior-grade wisdom (*adhimātra-jñāna*). However, the five consciousnesses and the eighth consciousness have as their objective condition (*ālambana*) the nature of phenomena and persons which are non-existent;

their subjective conditions (*ālambaka*) are direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and because they do not transform during the causal stage, it is said that "the sixth and seventh transform during the causal stage, while the fifth and eighth are perfected in the resultant stage.

For this reason, within the context of the causes and conditions for arising, only the manas and mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) are explained, whereas regarding the causes and conditions for cessation, [only] the eighth consciousness is addressed.
In this context, it is only the six types of defiled minds within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that are ceased; it is not that the mind itself is absent.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of characteristics regarding arising and ceasing. What are these two? First, those that are coarse because they are associated with the mind;
second, those that are subtle because they are dissociated from the mind. Moreover, the coarsest among the coarse are the objects of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
The coarse within the coarse and the subtle within the subtle are the spheres of the Bodhisattvas; the subtle within the subtle is the sphere of the Buddhas.
These two kinds of arising and ceasing depend upon the permeation of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsanā*). That which is called "depending on causes" has the meaning of non-awakening (*abodha*);
that which is called "depending on conditions" has the meaning of falsely constructing objective realms. If the cause is extinguished, [the conditions are likewise extinguished].
Thus, because the conditions for cessation and the causes for cessation cease, the dissociated mind ceases; because the conditions cease, the associated mind ceases.
Although the preceding section clarified the causal conditions for arising and ceasing, it did not yet distinguish between the characteristics of arising and ceasing.

This [section] precisely explains and clarifies that the coarse characteristics of the realms of ordinary beings and sages correspond with the mind, while the subtle characteristics do not correspond with the mind.
The explanation is as stated above: that which is the "coarse within the coarse" refers to the latter four characteristics among the six coarsenesses.
Because ordinary beings rely upon these to grasp at words, give rise to karma, and undergo retribution, this is called the realm of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

Furthermore, those who perceive these four characteristics are also termed ordinary beings because they do not awaken to the source of the mind. That which is the "subtle within the coarse" refers to the six... [text fragment ends].
The first two of the three coarse [aspects] are the coarse within the subtle; these correspond to the latter two of the three subtle [aspects].

When Bodhisattvas are at the stage of the three stages of worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*) and prior to the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*), they are free from the subtlety within the coarse. From the eighth stage onward, they comprehend the coarseness within the subtle;
therefore, this is called the "Bodhisattva realm. The subtlety within the subtle refers to the first of the three subtle [aspects], which is non-existence (*abhāva*).
It is explained that one who is free from these marks of karmic activity enters the stage of the Tathāgata; therefore, this is called the Buddha’s realm.
Having clearly elucidated the departure from these coarse and subtle marks, it is understood through the passage concerning the six kinds of defiled minds.

Below this section on the two types of arising and ceasing, the preceding intent is summarized to clarify that [arising and ceasing] proceed from causes and conditions. However, all phenomena are fundamentally...
Non-arising depends upon the perfuming of ignorance to undergo arising and ceasing.
That which is called "depending on causes" refers to the meaning of non-awakening; taking non-awakening as the cause, the three subtle marks arise.
That which is called "depending on conditions" refers to the meaning of falsely constructing objective realms; taking objective realms as the condition, the six coarse marks grow. As it is said:
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "Inconceivable perfuming and inconceivable transformation are the causes for the arising and abiding of the flow of the manifesting consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

The grasping of various objects and the perfuming of beginningless false discrimination are the causes for the arising and abiding of the characteristics of the consciousness that discriminates phenomena (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
In that sutra, "arising from the flow" refers to the three subtle stages, while "arising from characteristics" refers to the six coarse stages; this is indeed so.

Knowing that when ignorance is abandoned, there is no cause for the arising and abiding of the three subtle states, and that when objects are extinguished, there is no condition for the growth of the six coarse states;
therefore it is said: "Because the cause is extinguished, the non-corresponding mind is extinguished; because the condition is extinguished, the corresponding mind is extinguished.
This is also as stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*: "If that reality is obscured, then all manner of unrealities and various delusions arise."
When [the signs] cease, all sense-faculties and consciousnesses cease; this is called the cessation of signs. As for the cessation of continuity:

when the cause of continuity ceases, continuity itself ceases. One should know that the statement in that sutra regarding the "cessation of signs" refers to the cessation of associated mind, while the "cessation of continuity" refers to the cessation of dissociated mind.
Question: If the mind ceases, how can it be continuous? If it is continuous, how can one speak of its ultimate cessation? Answer:

That which is called "cessation" refers only to the cessation of the mind’s characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), not the cessation of the mind’s essence (*svabhāva*). It is like wind that exists by depending upon water and possesses the characteristic of movement;
if the water were to cease, then the characteristic of the wind would be severed, as it would have no basis for support. Since the water does not cease, the wind [does not cease].

Regarding the continuity of characteristics, it is solely because the wind ceases that the characteristic of motion also ceases; it is not that the water itself ceases. Ignorance (*avidyā*) is likewise: it moves based upon the substance of the mind.
If the substance of the mind were to cease, sentient beings would be cut off and have no basis for support. Because the substance does not cease, the mind is able to continue.
It is solely because delusion (*moha*) ceases that the characteristics of the mind cease accordingly; it is not that the cognitive wisdom of the mind ceases.
Because the preceding section clarified that when causes cease, conditions cease, and once causes and conditions have ceased,

both the associated mind and the dissociated mind likewise cease— appearing to be a state of total annihilation— it is therefore provisionally established through this dialogue to demonstrate that it is the characteristics of ignorance and the mind that cease,
not the characteristics of the essence of mind and wisdom. Within this, water is used as a metaphor for the essence of mind.

The wind is used as a metaphor for ignorance; the characteristic of movement serves as a metaphor for the three subtle and six coarse states. The analogy is self-evident and can be understood according to the text.

*Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra-sukhārtha* (An Easy Compendium of the Treatise on the Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna), Fascicle Lower.
Composed by Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa;

Prince Vasuṇa. Translated by the Sramana Ming of Mount Lu, Zhengyuan. Commentary:
Furthermore, because there are four kinds of dharmas that have the nature of perfuming (*vāsanā*), the arising of defiled and pure dharmas continues without interruption. What are they?
Regarding the four [categories], the first is the pure dharma, which is called *tathatā* (suchness). The second is all causes of defilement, which is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
The third is the deluded mind, which is called the karma-consciousness (*karmavijñāna*). The fourth is the deluded objective realm, namely the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).
As for the meaning of "perfuming" (*vāsanā*), it is like a worldly garment that originally has no fragrance; yet, because a person perfumes it with incense, it then comes to possess it.
The fragrance is likewise so with this True Suchness (tathatā): the pure dharma is truly free from defilement, yet because it is perfumed by ignorance, the appearance of defilement arises.
The defiled dharma of ignorance is truly devoid of pure activity, yet because it is perfumed by True Suchness, the function of purity arises.

Although the preceding section clarifies the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing, if there were no principle of perfuming (*vāsanā*) such that delusion would immediately cease upon arising, how could there be the nature of saṃsāra through the long night of ignorance?

And if there were no principle of perfuming such that wisdom would immediately vanish upon arising, how could there be the constant cultivation of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) to fulfill the realization of the fruit? Therefore, this section sets forth and elucidates the four kinds of perfuming.

This reveals that the dharmas of defilement and purity are each uninterrupted. First, the perfuming of pure dharmas explains the meaning of the aforementioned "awakening," as well as the two aspects of purity up to the distancing from the six types of defiled minds and the increase of pure dharmas.
Second, the perfuming of the causes of defilement. Third, the perfuming of the deluded mind explains the meaning of the aforementioned "non-awakening" and the growth of the three subtle states.
The fourth is the perfuming of false objects (*vitatha-viṣaya-vāsanā*), which explains the increase of the six coarse defiled phenomena (*ṣaḍ-audārika-kleśa-dharma*).

That is to say, seeds produce the manifest, and the manifest perfumes the seeds; thus the manifest continues without interruption. This is the meaning of the perfuming of causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-vāsanā*).
The dharma and its metaphor are self-evident, as can be understood from the text. Question: When the defiled and the pure are contrasted, why is it that only the pure function has a single type?

Question: Are there three distinct types of defilement? Answer: Because these defiled phenomena differ in their intrinsic natures and rely upon various causes and conditions, they are fully explained as being threefold.
Although pure phenomena are established in relation to defilement for the purpose of forming the meaning of perfuming (*vāsanā*), their essence and function have never been separate;
therefore, they are clarified as being one. Question: Why do defiled and pure phenomena both possess the capacity for mutual perfuming?

Question: Are the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of defiled phenomena called the function (*vṛtti*) of pure phenomena? Answer: When defilement perfumes the pure, it reveals that the True [Nature] is without characteristics (*animitta*), yet it manifests characteristics according to that perfuming.
Furthermore, because it reveals that false phenomena have no substantial essence, one speaks only of "characteristics.

Moreover, since these defiled phenomena lack the function of flowing back toward the source, one speaks of "characteristics" and not "function. This explanation is given in terms of the meaning of non-enlightenment as it follows the flow.

In the sutras, regarding the statement that the *tathāgatagarbha* is perfumed by evil habits and so forth—whereby it is said to be defiled by purification—although this pertains to the *tathatā* within the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpādavyaya-mukha*), because one intends to emphasize that its essence (*svabhāva*) is primordially pure, there is in fact no sense of being perfumed.

However, with respect to its essence and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), because it internally perfumes [the mind], it brings about the function of turning away from defilement and conforming to the truth; thus, it speaks of "function" (*vṛtti*) and not "characteristic."

This is also explained in terms of the meaning of the awakening that flows against the current; it explains how, because the *tathāgatagarbha* exists, one can become weary of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and joyfully seek *nirvāṇa*.

How do the perfumations (*vāsanā*) give rise to defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśadharma*) such that they are not severed? It is said that this occurs because, based upon the *dharmatā* of True Suchness (*tathatā*), there exists [the potential for] non-existence.
It is explained that because ignorance (*avidyā*) is the cause of defiled phenomena, it perfumes the *tathatā* (suchness).

Because of this perfuming, there arises the deluded mind (*vikalpa-citta*). Because the deluded mind exists, it perfumes ignorance; because it does not comprehend the reality of *tathatā*, non-awakening thoughts arise, manifesting deluded objects.
Because these deluded objects serve as the conditions for defiled phenomena, they in turn perfume the deluded mind, causing it to...
Because of this clinging thought, one creates various karmas and undergoes all manner of suffering of body and mind.
This clarifies the meaning of the permeation (*vāsanā*) of defiled phenomena: it is said that because one relies upon the *tathatā* (Suchness), there is ignorance;
this refers to the "karmic aspect of ignorance. This text reveals that delusion has no self-substance and is established in dependence upon the True Suchness. Thus, the text makes this explicit.
Regarding the meaning of the mutual permeation (*vāsanā*) between the defiled and the pure: if these were fundamentally opposed in their movement, permeation would be impossible;

therefore, it is said that [the defiled] "depends" [upon the true]. Since it arises by depending on the True [Suchness], it in turn permeates True Suchness to give rise to the characteristic of the "perceiving subject.

Thus, it is said: "Because of the dharma of permeating True Suchness, there exists the deluded mind. This deluded mind is precisely the characteristic of the perceiving subject. However, this deluded...
The mind is itself ignorance; it has no separate substance, but is designated as "ignorance" based on the initial movement of a single thought-moment.

Furthermore, because it possesses the power of perfuming (*vāsanā*), it is called the "deluded mind. Thus, it was said previously that one is able to perceive appearances by relying on the moving mind;
were there no movement, there would be no perception. Since the deluded mind exists in reliance upon ignorance, it in turn perfumes [it].

Because one habituates ignorance to give rise to the appearance of objects, it is said that through the perfuming of the deluded mind upon ignorance, one fails to realize that the *tathatā* (suchness) and phenomena are one;
thus, non-enlightened thought arises, and deluded objects arise. However, these objects have no substantial reality;
they are merely provisionally established based on the perfuming of ignorance by deluded thoughts. Therefore, as stated previously: [...with the perfuming of ignorance...]
Because there is a perceiving subject, objects falsely appear; apart from this perception, there are no objects.

Since objects manifest based upon the deluded mind, they in turn perfume (karmically influence) that deluded mind, thereby prolonging the characteristics of the six coarse stages. Therefore it is said:

"Because there are conditions consisting of defiled dharmas, they perfume the deluded mind, causing it to become attached through recollection and to create various kinds of karma, whereby one undergoes [retribution]."

Causing all sufferings of body and mind to be clung to through mindfulness is the characteristic of wisdom, the characteristic of continuity, the characteristic of grasping, and the characteristic of calculating names.
The performance of various karmas is the characteristic of initiating karma. The undergoing of all sufferings of body and mind is the characteristic of suffering bound by karma.
Furthermore, that which arises in the three periods of time through the permeation of ignorance upon True Suchness is...
Because the mind arises, various phenomena arise; with the objective realm as a condition, the six coarse factors—craving, defilement, suffering, pleasure, and so forth—are prolonged.
That which is called "mind" arises precisely because of these phenomena, whereby various states of mind are produced.

Thus we know that from the subtle to the coarse, mind and phenomena mutually perfuse one another to form the marks of defilement; truly, it is said that false delusions arise together, serving as seeds for one another in succession.
Furthermore, regarding the meaning of the perfuming of these delusive objects, there are two kinds. What are the two? First, the perfuming that increases conceptualization;
second, the perfuming that increases grasping. Regarding the meaning of the perfuming of the delusive mind, there are also two kinds. What are they?

First, there is the fundamental perfuming of the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*), which enables the experience of the suffering of birth and death by Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and all Bodhisattvas.

Second, there is the perfuming that increases the discerning consciousness of phenomena (*viṣaya-vijñapti-vijñāna*), which enables the experience of the suffering bound by the karma of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
There are two meanings to the perfuming of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsanā*). What are these two? First, the fundamental perfuming...

First, because the habituation [of ignorance] can accomplish the meaning of the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*); second, because the habituation of views and craving that arises therefrom can accomplish the meaning of the discerning consciousness of objects (*viṣaya-vijñāna*).
Above, this was a general clarification of the perfuming of defiled dharmas from the subtle to the coarse; here, it specifically clarifies the perfuming from the coarse to the subtle.
The subtle phrasing and intent are presented alternately to exhaustively clarify their meaning. Regarding the two kinds of meaning for the perfuming of false objects (*bhrānta-viṣaya*):
this specifically explains the preceding text, stating that because there are defiled dharmas as conditions consisting of false objects, they perfume the deluded mind (*bhrānta-citta*), and so forth.

First is the perfuming that increases mindfulness (*vṛddhi-smṛti-vāsanā*), which refers to the perfuming within the stage of the mental faculty (*manobhūmi*) that differentiates between attachment and non-attachment.
First, the arising of craving for suffering, pleasure, and so forth, which causes the mental factors of cognition and the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) to continue in succession without interruption;
second, the increase of grasping and perfuming, which is the perfuming within the mental consciousness that gives rise to attachment, falsely establishes names and conventions,
and causes the characteristics of grasping and the calculation of names and so forth to have no end— this is the meaning of the perfuming of the deluded mind.
Regarding the "two kinds," this specifically clarifies the preceding passage concerning how the existence of the deluded mind perfumes ignorance and so forth.

First, the fundamental perfuming of the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) refers to half of the eighth consciousness—the karmic aspect (*karma-lakṣaṇa*)—which is the karmic consciousness within the first five [consciousnesses] and the manas.

Because it serves as the support for the perfuming of the abiding ground of ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*), it causes the long-flowing stream of birth and death to continue, thereby sustaining these three.

The noble ones experience subtle suffering that does not cease within their bodies of transformation; this is the fundamental root of karmic consciousness, namely the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*).

Because it is perfumed by this, it can give rise to the two aspects of the evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and the manifesting consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*). Since this is not severed by Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas, they must follow along with its transformations.
Furthermore, from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onward, Bodhisattvas gradually subdue this ignorance until the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*).
Because the final mind alone is able to sever [ignorance] completely, we know that everything prior to perfect enlightenment proceeds in dependence upon this ignorance.
Second, the habituation of the *vikalpa-vastu-vijñāna* (discriminative consciousness of phenomena) increases;

that is, within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), it serves as the sustaining condition for the four abidings (*catur-upādāna*) and afflictions, causing the characteristic of arising and ceasing to grow, which enables ordinary beings to receive the body of segmented birth (*paricchinna-śarīra*) without ever ceasing.

O Elder, in contrast to the fundamental [nature], because this discriminative consciousness-mind provides the nourishment for the afflictions, grasps through attachment, and gives rise to karma, it brings about the marks of suffering bound by the karma of ordinary beings. Regarding the meaning of "the perfuming of ignorance," there are two aspects:
specifically clarifying the preceding text, it means that because there is the cause of defiled dharmas—namely, ignorance—it perfumes the *tathatā* (suchness).

First, regarding "the fundamental permeation": this refers to the meaning of the fundamental ignorance permeating True Suchness (*tathatā*) to bring about the karma-consciousness (*karmavijñāna*), as previously stated: "Because it relies on non-awakening, it is called 'karma'.

Although the essence of True Suchness is pure, it does not preclude its susceptibility to the permeation of ignorance, thereby forming defiled functions; this is what is termed "inconceivable" (*acintya*).
There are two types of perfuming and inconceivable transformation: secondly, the perfuming of views and craving that arises is based upon fundamental ignorance;

it gives rise to the perfuming of afflictions of views and craving within the *karmic consciousness* (*ālayavijñāna*), which in turn can accomplish the *discriminating consciousness of objects* (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
As stated previously, this consciousness increases in dependence on the afflictions of views and craving; for this reason, it is called the sixth mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
It is associated with all mental factors (*caitta*) in defiled states. Question: All ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) possess both types of suffering;
why is it that here only the suffering bound by karma (*karmabandhana-duḥkha*) is attributed specifically to ordinary beings? Answer:
Although all ordinary beings possess both types of suffering, this [suffering] alone is designated as "the suffering bound by karma" merely in terms of coarse and subtle awareness.

This is said in reference to those who have not yet attained awakening. Because the noble ones of the Three Vehicles have transcended birth-and-death through segmental divisions and are thus free from gross suffering, they are associated only with subtle suffering.
Although ordinary beings possess subtle suffering, it is entirely unperceived because it is overwhelmed by gross suffering;
for this reason, it is not mentioned. Nevertheless, it is not that subtle suffering does not exist.
How does the perfuming that gives rise to pure dharmas continue without interruption? It is because the *tathatā* (suchness) exists that it can perfume ignorance;
by the power of these causes and conditions of perfuming, it causes the deluded mind to grow weary of the suffering of birth and death and to joyfully seek *nirvāṇa*.
Because this deluded mind possesses the causes and conditions of weariness and seeking, it immediately perfumes the *tathatā*, whereby one gains self-confidence in one's own nature.
Knowing that the mind’s false movement has no external objects, one cultivates the dharma of seclusion.
Because one knows with suchness that there are no external objects, one gives rise to compliant practices through various skillful means—neither grasping nor recollecting them.
Eventually, through the power of long-term cultivation, ignorance is extinguished. Because ignorance is extinguished, the mind does not arise; because it does not arise, there are no objects.

Because they cease together with their causes and conditions, the characteristics of the mind are all exhausted; this is called attaining *nirvāṇa* and accomplishing spontaneous activity (*svayambhū-karma*).
This generally clarifies the meaning of the perfuming of pure dharmas: namely, because the *tathatā* dharma exists, it is able to perfume ignorance (*avidyā*).
This is precisely the perfuming that extinguishes the aspect of karma. It is the direct opposite of the previously explained perfuming of defilement, which relies upon...
Because True Suchness (tathatā) exists, ignorance (avidyā) appears before it; since ignorance has no self-nature, it is said that ignorance exists in dependence upon True Suchness.
This demonstrates that True Suchness possesses the power of pure function, and thus it is said that True Suchness can permeate (vāsana) ignorance.
When the power of internal permeation takes True Suchness as its cause, it causes the deluded mind to become weary of the suffering of birth and death.
Seeking the attainment of nirvāṇa with joy is precisely the subduing and extinguishing of the characteristic of the perceiving subject (*darśana-lakṣaṇa*).
