This directly reverses the prior defiled perfuming (*saṃkleśa-vāsanā*), because since there exists the cause of defiled dharmas such as ignorance (*avidyā*), the perfuming of true thusness (*tathatā*) results in the cause of the deluded mind.
Perfumed by ignorance, the deluded mind grows and tends toward the suffering of birth and death, obscuring nirvāṇa; this [process] now proceeds through the perfuming of true thusness.
As ignorance fades, the deluded mind gradually ceases and pure function daily arises; thus, one comes to loathe birth-and-death and joyfully seeks nirvana.

Because this deluded mind possesses the causes and conditions of aversion and seeking, it immediately perfumes the *tathatā* (suchness), leading one to have self-confidence in one’s own nature and to know that the mind is a deluded movement with no external objects before it.
This is precisely the perfuming that extinguishes the characteristics of objective realms; it is the overturning of the preceding state of defilement.
Within the process of perfuming, because there is a deluded mind, it perfumes ignorance;

because it does not understand that the Dharma of True Suchness is one, non-awakening arises, and thoughts give rise to the false manifestation of objective realms. Thus, one knows that these realms are fundamentally empty.

Since this false manifestation appears as if existing due to the arising of non-awakened thoughts, once one uses the causes of aversion and seeking to perfume True Suchness, one then gains faith in one's own nature.

Originally pure and fundamentally free from deluded thoughts, if one were separated from all phenomena, what could there be? Therefore, one cultivates the practice of seclusion to purify defiled perceptions.

By knowing things as they truly are, one understands that within the nature of *tathatā* (suchness) there is no realm of delusion; it is based upon this that various methods [of cultivation] arise. Below, the detailed explanation clarifies the cultivation of the dharma of seclusion.
By knowing the nature of *tathatā* as it truly is, one realizes there is no deluded objective sphere, and thus various skillful means are established accordingly.
One then invokes True Suchness (*tathatā*) and practices in accordance with it, neither grasping nor conceptualizing; this is the stage of the three provisions (*tri-sambhāra*).

Because the three stages of the *śaikṣa* (the three levels of worthiness) rely on a semblance of awakening, one does not grasp at the grasped (*grāhya*) or the grasper (*grāhaka*), and correctly realizes that the very act of mindfulness is itself empty. This means that although one is mindful, there is no subject who minds nor any object to be minded;
this is called "conformity. This continues until, through the power of long-term cultivation and habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*), [realization is attained].

Ignorance is extinguished through traversing three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas until, at the final thought-moment of equal enlightenment, one severs that ignorance by means of the wisdom associated with a single thought-moment.
That is to say, if one is free from discursive thought (*smṛti*), it is called "attaining entry.

Because ignorance is extinguished, the mind does not arise; thus, the aspect of karma is extinguished, and there is no longer the aspect of a perceiving subject—the mind itself [is no longer a subject].
Seeing arises from the capacity for seeing, whereby objects falsely manifest. Since the capacity for seeing does not arise, the characteristics of objects are extinguished.
Once the three subtle states are extinguished, the six coarse characteristics have no basis upon which to attach.

Because the characteristics of the three subtle and six coarse states are found to be utterly unobtainable, it is called attaining Great Nirvana and accomplishing spontaneous karma; this is spontaneous karma.
This is precisely Bodhi.
Regarding the meaning of the perfuming of the deluded mind, there are two kinds. What are these two?

First is the perfuming of the *parikalpita-vijñāna* (discriminative consciousness of phenomena), which relies upon ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles who, weary of the suffering of birth and death, proceed gradually toward [enlightenment] according to their respective capacities.
Regarding the unsurpassed path, there are two types of mental perfuming (*manas-vāsanā*): first, that which causes all Bodhisattvas to resolve with vigor and swiftly proceed toward Nirvana;
second, the perfuming of *tathatā*. There are two meanings to the perfuming of *tathatā*. What are these two? First, perfuming by its own essential nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*);
second, perfuming by its activity (*vṛtti*). Regarding perfuming by its own essential nature: from time immemorial, it has been endowed with the untainted (*anāsrava*).
The Dharma possesses the nature of acting as the objective sphere for inconceivable karma; based on these two meanings, it constantly perfumes [the mind] with power,
thereby enabling sentient beings to weary of the suffering of birth and death, to joyfully seek nirvana,
to have confidence that their own bodies possess the *tathatā* dharma, and to resolve to practice.
The preceding section generally clarifies that the perfuming of pure dharmas proceeds from within to without;
this section specifically clarifies that perfuming also proceeds from without to within, such that the textual intent of both parts mutually illuminates one another to fully exhaust their meaning.

Regarding the statement that "the perfuming of the deluded mind has two kinds of meanings," this is a detailed explanation of the preceding text, as this deluded mind possesses the causes and conditions of aversion and seeking, which in turn perfume the *tathatā* (suchness) and so forth.

This correctly translates the fundamental熏習 (kṣaṇa-vāsanā) of the *karmic consciousness* (*karma-vijñāna*) within the aforementioned defiled熏習, as well as the熏習 of the *discriminative consciousness of phenomena* (*vastu-vijñapti-vikalpa-vijñāna*).
First, regarding the熏習 of the discriminative consciousness of phenomena:

this refers to the sixth consciousness performing the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-darśana*),熏習ing the dharma of non-self and thereby abandoning the grasping at signs; therefore, it is said that "it relies upon all ordinary beings. Second...

Because those who ride the vehicles (yāna) weary of the suffering of birth and death and gradually progress toward the Unsurpassed Way according to their respective capacities, and because the wisdom of contemplation of the two vehicles does not fully comprehend the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), there remains birth and death that can be loathed;

thus, according to their own intellectual power, they realize the *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder), or they may turn their minds toward the path of Unsurpassed Enlightenment. This is still [the case for those of] dull faculties...

Because the essence of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is so vastly different [from the ultimate], it is said that one gradually approaches the unsurpassed path of awakening, which is *bodhi*.
Second, regarding "mental perfuming" (*manas-vāsanā*): "mind" here comprehensively encompasses the first five types of mind;

that is, the seventh consciousness constantly contemplates non-self and pure phenomena, thereby perfuming and transforming the karmic, evolving, and cognitive aspects within the essence of the eighth consciousness.

Because they continue their characteristics to fulfill the *dharmatā* of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-tathatā*), it is said that these bodhisattvas, through the courage and vigor of their resolve, swiftly proceed toward *nirvāṇa*. These bodhisattvas are those who have realized the resolve for enlightenment;

because they advance with profound wisdom and heroic diligence, their realization of the illusory nature of phenomena accords perfectly with the principle of non-arising. Therefore, it is said that they "swiftly proceed," as previously stated.
The phrase "unsurpassed path" refers to *nirvāṇa*; the meaning of these terms is mutually illuminating.
It does not mean that one heads toward the unsurpassed path while not tending toward *nirvāṇa*, nor that one tends toward *nirvāṇa* while not heading toward the unsurpassed path.
Regarding the two kinds of meanings for the permeation of *tathatā*, this is a detailed explanation of what was stated above: because the *dharmatā* of *tathatā* exists, it is able to permeate.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) directly corresponds to the fundamental perfuming and the perfuming of views and craving that arise within the aforementioned defiled perfuming.
First, regarding the perfuming of the essential nature and characteristics (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa-vāsanā*): first, we clarify the meaning of "nature" and "characteristics.

This refers to those who have possessed untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) since beginningless time; it demonstrates that the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is fully endowed with pure dharmas.

The essence of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*) refers to the nature that is fully endowed with the capacity to manifest inconceivable karma as its objective sphere; this clarifies the characteristic of non-emptiness.
Regarding "inconceivable," it means that the dharma of self-nature acts as a supreme objective sphere, manifesting great radiance that universally illumines the *dharmadhātu*.
This cannot be fathomed or deliberated upon by the thinking mind, nor can it be grasped by contemplative wisdom.
The preceding discussion was based on these two meanings; hereafter, the text correctly clarifies the meaning of perfuming (*vāsanā*).

This essence and its characteristics serve as the internal pure cause, constantly perfuming to give rise to pure function. By the power of this pure function, one is able to become weary of birth-and-death and joyfully seek nirvana.
Furthermore, it is said that by gaining confidence that one’s own body possesses the *tathatā* dharma, one resolves to cultivate practice.

This clearly elucidates the intent of practicing according to reality as it is. If one merely feels aversion toward birth and death and seeks nirvana, one still falls within the realm of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
Because one has confidence that one’s own body inherently possesses *tathatā* (suchness), one no longer rushes outward in search of it;
only then can one directly enter the realm of all Buddhas from this very point. Question: Regarding the aforementioned "perfuming by the mind" (*manas-paribhāvanā*), [how does it function]?
It has already been clarified that the Bodhisattva’s courageous resolve leads swiftly toward Nirvana;
this True Suchness (tathatā) perfuming is also said to enable sentient beings to weary of the suffering of birth-and-death and joyfully seek Nirvana—is this not redundant?
Answer: There are two types of perfuming: first, original perfuming; second, newly acquired perfuming. To clarify, the perfuming of True Suchness is precisely the substance of ignorance itself.
Because the internal permeation of the marks causes the formation of pure karma, one comes to loathe birth-and-death and delight in nirvana; this is the original permeation.
To clarify, the permeation of the true suchness by the mental consciousness means that one borrows this pure function to reflexively permeate the true suchness, thereby increasing its power;
thus, it causes one to advance toward nirvana—this is the new permeation. Since there is one original and one new, they do not overlap.

Question: If this is the meaning—that all sentient beings possess *tathatā* (suchness) and so forth, and that all are permeated by it—then why are there immeasurable distinctions between those with faith and those without faith, and why do these differences occur sequentially rather than simultaneously? Should they not all know at once that they possess the *tathatā*-dharma and diligently cultivate skillful means to enter *nirvāṇa*? Answer: Although *tathatā* is fundamentally one, it manifests in immeasurable ways. It is like the great ocean: though its nature is one, it contains immeasurable waters. Furthermore, it is like the single space (*ākāśa*): though it is one, it accommodates immeasurable forms. Moreover, although the *tathatā*-nature is one, the afflictions (*kleśa*) of sentient beings are immeasurable; thus, the cultivation of counteractive qualities (*pratipakṣa*) is also immeasurable. Because the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) are weak, the power of the afflictions is strong; because the roots of goodness are strong, the power of the afflictions is weak.

Therefore, there are immeasurable distinctions in the degrees of faith and lack of faith, as well as in the sequence of their development. Consequently, they do not all attain entry into *nirvāṇa* at the same time. Furthermore, although the *tathatā*-nature is one, the capacities of sentient beings are diverse; thus, the teachings and practices are also diverse. For this reason, there are immeasurable distinctions. It is like a single sun shining upon the world: although the light is one, the vessels that receive it are diverse. It is also like a single rain falling from the sky: although the water is one, the seeds that receive it are diverse. Therefore, although the *tathatā*-nature is one, there are immeasurable distinctions in the cultivation of the path. Thus, there is no fault in the fact that they do not all enter *nirvāṇa* simultaneously.

Because the nature and distinctions of ignorance (*avidyā*) at the limits of existence have been different in their thickness from the very beginning—like sands beyond the Ganges—the various higher afflictions arise based on ignorance;
the various afflictions of self-view, attachment, and defilement arise based on ignorance.
In this way, all such afflictions arise depending upon ignorance, with infinite distinctions between preceding and succeeding states.
Because only the Tathāgata can know it.
The above clarifies the essence of internal causal perfuming;

here, a question and answer are established to clarify that one must rely on the function of external conditions for perfuming before one can gradually sever the two obstacles and realize the two kinds of fruits. If this is the meaning...
This refers to the meaning of internal causal perfuming within the essential nature and characteristics of the aforementioned True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Since this essence and characteristic of True Suchness neither increases in the state of the noble ones nor decreases in the state of ordinary beings, and since all sentient beings fully possess the essence and characteristics of True Suchness and so forth, and all are perfumed such that they diligently cultivate skillful means to enter nirvāṇa together—why is it that some have faith while others do not? Why is there no [distinction]?
The distinctions between the preceding and succeeding stages arise from not knowing that True Suchness (tathatā) is fundamentally identical; they exist because of obstructions.
Specifically, while True Suchness is originally one, there are immeasurable and boundless *avidyā*—namely, the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)—which exceed the sands of the Ganges in number;

the "dust-like" afflictions, which are the superior afflictions; and the afflictions of self-view and attachment, namely the two types of delusion: the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) consisting of views and thoughts. These three...

The various types of delusions collectively clarify the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*); since this hindrance arises from the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), it is said to arise based on ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because there are differences in the thickness or thinness of these two hindrances, they differ from the single essence and equality of *tathatā* (Suchness).

Consequently, there is a distinction between those who have faith and those who do not, as well as the difference between earlier and later stages. These two hindrances exist only for [beings other than] the Buddha.
One who is able to know this must rely upon the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as external conditions for guidance in order to sever these hindrances;
only then can one exhaustively eliminate them, realize true liberation, and attain great bodhi.
Furthermore, all Buddha-dharmas have causes and conditions; only when causes and conditions are fully assembled are they accomplished.

For example, the nature of fire within wood is the direct cause of fire, yet if no one knows it and it does not rely on skillful means, there is no possibility that it could spontaneously burn the wood.
Sentient beings are likewise: although they possess the power of the direct cause of permeation, if they do not encounter the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas...
It is impossible for those such as virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) to serve as conditions by which one can personally sever afflictions and enter *nirvāṇa*.

Even if there is the power of external conditions, if the internal pure dharmas lack the power of habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*), one will still be unable to ultimately weary of the suffering of birth and death or joyfully seek *nirvāṇa*.
When causes and conditions are fully complete—namely, oneself...

Because there is the power of habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) and because they are protected by the compassionate vows of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, they are able to give rise to a mind that loathes suffering, believe in the existence of *nirvāṇa*, and cultivate roots of goodness.

Through the maturation of these cultivated roots of goodness, they encounter Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who provide instruction, benefit, and encouragement; thus, they are able to advance toward the path of *nirvāṇa*.

Because it was explained above that all afflictions can be known only by the Tathāgata, this analogy is cited to clarify that one must rely upon the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as conditions (*pratyaya*) for them to be realized.

Thus, the true cause of the Buddha-dharma is like the nature of fire within wood, while the pure conditions of the Buddha-dharma are like the expedient means of drilling and friction; only then can the fire emerge from the wood.
If fire, even though it possesses the nature of burning, could burn wood of its own accord without the application of skillful means, such a thing is impossible.

Likewise, although sentient beings possess the true cause of *tathatā*, if they are obstructed by ignorance and afflictions, it is impossible for them to sever their afflictions and enter *nirvāṇa* on their own without relying upon the guidance of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Thus it is said:
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that one must possess three kinds of causes before being able to enter the ocean of the Buddha-dharma:

first, the direct cause (*nidāna-hetu*); second, the contributory cause (*pratyaya-hetu*); and third, the revealing cause (*vijñapti-hetu*). The direct cause is this very *tathatā* (suchness) acting as an internal cause through its permeating influence (*vāsanā*).
The contributory cause consists of these Buddhas and Bodhisattvas acting as external conditions for guidance and instruction. The revealing cause arises from what exists internally.
Because there is a primary cause that is assisted by external conditions, and by means of these causes and conditions one exhausts all afflictions (*kleśa*),

realizes the ultimate exhaustion of ignorance, and attains *nirvāṇa* without remainder and the perfection of unsurpassed *bodhi*, it is called "realization" (*jñāna*). The above clarifies that while the primary cause exists,
if there were no Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to serve as external conditions, one would be unable to spontaneously sever the afflictions and advance.

Regarding the transition to nirvana: although there may be the power of external conditions, this section below clarifies that even if Buddhas and Bodhisattvas serve as external conditions, if the internal cause is not cultivated, one cannot yet weary of the suffering of birth and death or seek nirvana.
Only when causes and conditions are fully present and both internal and external cultivation have taken place can one finally transcend the cage of ordinary beings and enter the state of a sage.

It is encompassed such that, when conditions are fully satisfied—namely, through the manifestation of the direct cause (*hetu-pratyaya*), the contributory cause (*pratyaya-hetu*), and the revealing cause (*vyañjana-hetu*)—one is able to achieve them and advance toward the path to *nirvāṇa*.
Specifically, the power of one's own habitual permeation (*vāsanā*) is the direct cause;
furthermore, because one is protected by the compassionate vows of all Buddhas, this is the contributory cause. By possessing these two...

Because of these causes and conditions, one is able to give rise to a mind of revulsion toward suffering, believe in the existence of *nirvāṇa*, cultivate roots of goodness, and even progress toward the path to *nirvāṇa*;
this is the "revealing cause" (*yuan-yin*). Question:

When the Tathāgatas and others manifest themselves to sentient beings, why is it that those who first cultivate roots of goodness are merely sustained by the protection of their vows, while it must wait for those whose roots of goodness have matured before the Buddhas reveal themselves?

The teaching for the benefit and joy [of beings] answers that there is no distinct cause for the Buddhas other than the difference between the purity and impurity of the mirror-like minds of sentient beings.
Because of this, the reflections of the Buddhas appear to some as manifest and to others as unmanifest.

Since sentient beings have not yet forgotten their conceptual discriminations when they first resolve to attain enlightenment, they are unable to personally encounter the Buddhas; yet, because the Buddhas do not abandon sentient beings, they do so through their compassion.
Having given rise to the mind through compassionate protection and mindfulness of sentient beings, one gradually enters the stages of the three worthies and ten sages;

as the two types of grasping are progressively subdued and severed, one increasingly accords with the principle of True Suchness (Tathatā), and thus personally encounters the Buddhas who provide instruction,
benefit, and joy.
That which functions as perfuming is the power of external conditions for sentient beings. Such external conditions have immeasurable meanings;
briefly stated, there are two kinds. What are these two? First, differentiated conditions; second, equal conditions.
This correctly explains the function of the two aforementioned types of perfuming.

Although Buddhas and Bodhisattvas manifest universally according to the various capacities of sentient beings as external conditions to perform all Buddha-works, there are immeasurable varieties; yet, summarizing their beginning and end, they do not transcend these two types.
Regarding the "differentiated condition," it refers to what is seen and heard by the practitioner according to their own faculties and nature.
There are distinctions in the speed with which beings receive the Path, ranging from slow to immeasurable;

however, that which serves as the equal condition is that what is seen and heard by the practitioner within right concentration is without distinction. Therefore, one should know that the Buddhas have no different causes, yet there are differences according to the faculties and natures of the practitioners.

Regarding the specific condition (*viśeṣa-pratyaya*): this person, relying upon the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others, from the time they first resolved their minds to seek the Path until they attained Buddhahood—whether seeing them or recollecting them during that interval, whether as kinsmen, parents, or relatives; or as servants; or as friends;
or as enemies; or through the four means of attraction (*saṃgraha-vastu*), and so forth, including all such things.

By performing immeasurable practices as conditions, one generates the power of the perfuming of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), which enables sentient beings to increase their roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) and obtain benefit through either seeing or hearing [the teaching]. These conditions are of two kinds. What are the two?

First, the proximate condition, by which they attain liberation swiftly; second, the remote condition, by which they attain liberation after a long period. These are the two types of proximate and remote conditions.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of discernment (*vikalpa*). What are the two? First, the condition for the increase of practice; second, the condition for receiving the Path.
This clarifies how a practitioner, relying upon all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, begins by generating the resolve to seek the Path, and continues until the attainment of Buddhahood.
In the midst of its conclusion, some may see the physical marks and features of the Buddha or hear the Buddha’s voice, taking these as external conditions for perfuming;
or it may be like the World-Honored One manifesting as parents for Rāhula as an external condition for perfuming;
or it may be like the World-Honored One acting as an external condition for Yaśodharā, Ānanda, Cunda, and other kinsmen and attendants.

The influence of external conditions through habitual perfuming may be like that of the World-Honored One in a previous life as the seer Asita, who performed menial tasks such as gathering firewood and drawing water;
or it may be like that of Yantou, Xuefeng, Yunyan, and Daowu, who acted as companions through the influence of external conditions;
or it may be like Devadatta, who was the sworn enemy of the World-Honored One Śākyamuni throughout their lifetimes.
Through the external conditions of perfuming by means of giving, kind words, beneficial conduct, and cooperation,

these immeasurable causal conditions— whether favorable or adverse— are all brought together through the power of great compassion to cause all sentient beings to increase their roots of goodness and obtain benefit.
Thus, these immeasurable causal conditions may be like the transformative guidance of Mañjuśrī.
It is because the Dragon Girl swiftly attains perfect enlightenment and quickly achieves liberation;

or, as the World-Honored One taught and instructed the great disciples that they had developed the causes for the Mahāyāna under the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū and subsequently attained the fruit of the One Vehicle at the assembly on Vulture Peak, thereby achieving liberation after a long period.
Thus, the conditions for this attainment of liberation do not exceed two types. First:

First, the condition for increasing practice causes the practitioner to proceed from initial right faith to the stage of the Dharma-body, extensively performing the ten thousand practices so that their roots of goodness may increase;

second, the condition for receiving the Way also causes the practitioner to progress through successive stages from beginning to end regarding the Great Dharma-Eye Treasury. Thus, the condition for increasing practice causes one to cultivate the Way.

This means that by clarifying the conventional through the ultimate, one is unimpeded regarding phenomena, thereby fulfilling the limb of merit (*puṇya-saṃbhāra*) and enabling practitioners to receive the conditions for the Path;
by clarifying the ultimate through the conventional, one does not contradict principle, thereby fulfilling the limb of wisdom (*jñāna-saṃbhāra*).

Once principle and phenomena are perfectly integrated and both merit and wisdom are cultivated, one can then avoid deviating onto divergent paths within this state, whereby all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas benefit sentient beings.
How could one ever repay such grace?
As for the condition of equality, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas vow to deliver all sentient beings;

through natural permeation, they never abandon them, manifesting their activities according to what is seen or heard by responding to their needs, by virtue of the power of the wisdom of identical essence.
This means that because sentient beings rely upon samādhi, they attain the equal vision of all Buddhas.
This reveals that the compassion which is identical in essence with wisdom constantly perfumes sentient beings through the power of external conditions;
yet, by virtue of their fundamental great vows, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not allow even a single sentient being to fail to enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
Therefore, whenever sentient beings encounter and perceive these manifested inconceivable karmas, they are permeated by them;
although these inconceivable karmas are without distinction, they are necessarily perceived as equal only when the practitioner abides in right concentration.
This truly means that one unites the non-discriminating mind with the principle of non-conceptualization.
This differentiation of the perfuming of essence and function further consists of two kinds. What are these two?

First is that which is not yet associated (*asaṃprayukta*), referring to ordinary beings, followers of the Two Vehicles, and Bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds. Because they perfume [the mind] by means of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and rely on the power of faith, they are able to practice;
however, because they have not yet attained non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-citta*) that is associated with the essence, they have not yet attained mastery.

Because the cultivation of karma accords with its function, these two are already in accord; that is to say, Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body attain non-conceptual wisdom and accord with the functional wisdom of all Buddhas.
Relying solely on the power of the Dharma, they naturally cultivate practice, perfuming True Suchness (Tathatā) and thereby extinguishing ignorance.
The above concludes the separate clarification of essence and function.

This section, which collectively reveals the two meanings of the correspondence and non-correspondence between essence and function, serves to distinguish the differences in what is perceived by those of the three stages of worthiness (*śaikṣa*) and the ten stages of sagehood (*ārya*).
It also clarifies that what is perceived at the stage of worthiness consists of differentiated conditions, whereas what is perceived at the stage of sagehood consists of equal conditions.

First, those who are not yet in accord—namely, ordinary beings and followers of the two vehicles—cannot harmonize with the principle of non-discrimination because they have not yet transcended the mind, thought, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*).
Furthermore, Bodhisattvas from the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*) up through the four stages of application (*prayoga*) cultivate practice based solely on the power of faith;
thus, although they gradually suppress the dual grasping of discrimination within the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, they are unable to transform these two consciousnesses.
Because they have not yet been severed, they do not accord with the principle of non-conceptualization.

Since they do not correspond with the essence, their functions naturally diverge and differ. For Bodhisattvas at the stage of Worthiness (Śaikṣa), whose cultivation of the six perfections still belongs to the characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), how could they possibly accord with sovereign karmic function? This is because they do not correspond with the essence.
Therefore, they cannot realize the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) of all Buddhas equally, because their activity is not in accord with it;
nor can they fully perceive the physical marks and adornments of the Reward-body (saṃbhogakāya) of all Buddhas.

As for "accordance," it refers to Bodhisattvas on the stages (bhūmi) who have already transformed the sixth and seventh consciousnesses and have completely severed the two types of conceptual grasping; thus, they are in accord with non-conceptual [wisdom].

Since principle and its application correspond, their function should likewise be so; for by relying solely on the power of the Dharma, one naturally practices, perfuming True Suchness (tathatā) and thereby extinguishing ignorance.
From the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onward, because the mind and dharmas are mastered, they correspond to both essence and function.
Even prior to the eighth stage, although the mind and dharmas have not yet attained mastery, [the practice continues] by means of...
The wisdom of wondrous observation enters the contemplation of the twofold emptiness, gradually severing the two types of innate grasping and partially realizing *tathatā*;
therefore, it also accords with both essence and function.
Furthermore, defiled phenomena have been continuously perfumed since beginningless time, persisting until the attainment of Buddhahood, after which they cease to exist.
Regarding the statement that the perfuming of the dharmas of cessation and purity is never exhausted in the future: how is this so?

Because the dharma of *tathatā* (suchness) constantly perfumes, the deluded mind is extinguished and the *dharmakāya* manifests; because the perfuming that gives rise to activity [is present], there is no exhaustion.

This passage provides a general distinction between the meanings of defiled and pure perfuming (*vāsanā*) to demonstrate that while delusive phenomena can be severed, the pure aspect is eternally abiding.
Since these defiled dharmas exist because of delusion and perish through awakening, the cause and effect within the realm of sentient beings are clearly manifest;
yet, upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood, they appear like flowers in the sky. Therefore, it is said: "up until the attainment of Buddhahood."
Subsequently, there is the cultivation of the pure mind through severance; because its presence or absence does not depend on delusion or awakening, there is nothing further to be severed.

Since the pure essence of True Suchness constantly cultivates within the causal stage, causing the deluded mind to cease and the Dharma-body to manifest, then in the resultant stage, one gives rise to functional cultivation based upon that Dharma-body, manifesting as both the recompense-body and the transformation-body.
Because it brings benefit and happiness to sentient beings until the end of the future, it is never interrupted.

Furthermore, as for the essential nature and characteristics of True Suchness (*tathatā*): it neither increases nor decreases for any ordinary beings, *śrāvakas*, *pratyekabuddhas*, bodhisattvas, or Buddhas;
it is not born in the past limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) and does not perish in the future limit (*aparākoṭi*); it is ultimately eternal and constant, having existed from the very beginning.
The self-nature is fully endowed with all merits, namely: the sense that its own essence possesses the meaning of great wisdom and luminosity;
the sense that it universally illumines the Dharma-realm; the sense of true and authentic cognition; the sense of the self-nature of the pure mind;
the sense of permanence, bliss, self, and purity; and the sense of coolness, immutability, and sovereignty. It is thus endowed with [merits] exceeding those of the Ganges.
Because the sands are not separate from, not severed from, and not different from the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas, and because they fulfill them without any deficiency,
it is called the Tathāgatagarbha and also the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata.

This is the correct explanation of the "substance-greatness" (*tattva-mahat*) and "characteristic-greatness" (*lakṣaṇa-mahat*) from the section on Establishing the Thesis, which fully elucidates the "Revealing the Correct Meaning" from the section on Detailed Exposition.
It also clarifies in detail the meaning of the internal causal perfuming within the "True Suchness as Self-Substance and Characteristic" mentioned in the preceding text;
that is to say, "all ordinary beings" refers to the six classes of mundane beings, while "śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas" refers to...
The four noble ones clarify that this true suchness (*tathatā*) itself neither increases nor decreases amidst the dharmas of ordinary beings and sages.
This is not [the case] regarding the prior limit; the following section correctly clarifies the meaning of its non-increase and non-decrease:

while all phenomena arise through the defilements of ordinary beings, the *dharmatā* does not arise; while all phenomena cease through the wisdom of the sages, the *dharmatā* does not cease. Since there is no prior...

When subsequent arising and ceasing are extinguished, one transcends the measure of ordinary beings and sages; there is ultimate equality and the eternal abiding of the single mind, which is precisely the self-substance of *tathatā*.
The passage beginning with "From the very beginning" (*yongben yilai*) correctly elucidates the self-characteristic of *tathatā*.

Because there are no characteristics external to its substance, it is said that its "self-nature is replete with all merits. The phrase "That which is called" (*suoyi wei*) provides a detailed clarification of this unity.
Because all merits possess the significance of the great radiance of wisdom and the significance of universally illuminating the dharma-realm, they constitute the virtue of *prajñā*.
In Sanskrit, *prajñā* is translated here as "wisdom" (*zhìhuì*). It is termed "wisdom-radiance" in contrast to the obscurity of ignorance and delusion;
for while "knowledge" (*zhì*) possesses the function of discernment, "wisdom" (*huì*) possesses the utility of illuminative realization.

Therefore, it is named "Pervading Illumination of the Dharma Realm" because it signifies the meaning of true cognitive awareness (*tathatā-jñāna*) and the meaning of the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-viśuddha-citta*);

this is precisely the virtue of the Dharmakāya. "True cognitive awareness" refers to the stainless consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*), for since it realizes that all phenomena are suchness (*tathatā*), it is called "true.
Because this mind of intrinsic nature is unstained even while enmeshed in bondage, it is called "pure," as stated in the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*:
Second, the originally pure essence of the Nirvana of bodhisattvas from time immemorial is precisely your present consciousness-essence, the primordial clarity;
you should certainly know that the essence of Bodhi and Nirvana is the Dharma-body. This consciousness-essence, the primordial clarity, is true cognitive awareness.
Because it possesses the meanings of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, and because it possesses the meanings of coolness, immutability, and sovereignty, it is—
This refers to the virtue of liberation (*vimukti-guṇa*). Liberation is itself *nirvāṇa*, and *nirvāṇa* possesses four kinds of wondrous, pure virtues:
permanence, bliss, self, and purity. "Permanence" means that it does not change throughout the three periods of time; "bliss" means that one is not disturbed even while amidst manifold sufferings;

"self" means that one is not constrained even while dwelling within the six realms of existence; and "purity" means that one is not defiled even while passing through the nine stages of decomposition. Thus, *nirvāṇa* stands in contrast to...

Regarding the afflictions (*kleśa*), they obscure and disturb the mind so that it cannot attain coolness (*sītala*); because one receives retribution according to karma, one lacks sovereignty (*vaśitā*).
Having realized *nirvāṇa*, one emerges from the obstacle of afflictions and the mind is naturally cool; therefore, it is called "cool and unchanging.
Since one has emerged from the obstacle of afflictions, one no longer receives retribution dependent on karma; thus, it is termed "sovereignty" (*vaśitā*) in meaning.
Being fully endowed with such qualities, this general summary reveals that the virtues of *tathatā* (suchness) transcend all numerical measure.

"Not separate" means that by citing any single virtue, the entire nature of reality is encompassed. "Uninterrupted" means it is not born in the past limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) nor does it perish in the future limit (*aparākoṭi*).
"Non-different" means that *tathatā* is itself the virtues, and the virtues are themselves *tathatā*. "Inconceivable" means that while it is of a single nature...
There are many meanings, yet within these many meanings there is complete oneness; it cannot be measured by a limited mind, for it is where mental activity ceases and the path of language is cut off.
Regarding the "Buddha-dharma": "Buddha" refers to the awakened mind, wherein all supreme virtues are entirely the dharma of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
Thus, as the *Vajra* [Sūtra] says: "All dharmas are Buddha-dharmas. This is called "Suchness" (*tathatā*).
In the section on the *tathāgatagarbha*, the conclusion summarizes the two meanings of essence (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*):

the *tathāgatagarbha* is summarized as the greatness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇamahattva*), and the *tathāgata-dharmakāya* is summarized as the greatness of essence (*svabhāvamahattva*). Because suchness (*tathatā*) is fully endowed with the three virtues of the *dharmakāya*, *prajñā*, and liberation, it perfumes sentient beings;
thus, they are able to abandon the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and realize true liberation, and sever the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

When one realizes the Great Prajñāpāramitā, the two obstacles are exhausted and the two forms of emptiness do not arise; proceeding directly to Bodhi, one returns to non-attainment and perfectly realizes the Dharmakāya.
Otherwise, practicing in vain for vast eons will ultimately yield no accomplishment—just as cooking sand can never produce rice, for it is not its fundamental substance.
Question: It was stated above that the essence of *tathatā* (suchness) is equal and free from all characteristics;

why, then, is it further said that its essence possesses such various virtues? Answer: Although these meanings of various virtues do indeed exist in reality, they lack any characteristic of differentiation;
they are identical in a single flavor, being nothing other than *tathatā* alone. For what reason? Because it is non-conceptual and free from distinctions.
Because their distinct characteristics are thus non-dual, by what further meaning can one speak of differentiation?
It is shown by way of the arising and ceasing of the *karmic consciousness*. How is this shown? Because all phenomena are fundamentally only mind, and in reality there is no thought;

yet, through the lack of awakening, a deluded mind arises and gives rise to thoughts, perceiving various objective realms. Therefore, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*). That the nature of the mind does not arise is precisely [the state of awakening].
Because it is the meaning of the light of great wisdom, if the mind gives rise to views, there is the characteristic of non-seeing;
because the nature of the mind is free from views, it is the meaning of universally illuminating the Dharma-realm. If the mind has movement, it is not true cognition;
it lacks self-nature, and being neither permanent, nor blissful, nor self, nor pure, it is characterized by feverish affliction and decay, and thus is not sovereign, even unto its full extent.

Because there are meanings of delusory defilements exceeding those of the sands of the Ganges, when the nature of the mind is unmoving in contrast to these meanings, then the characteristics of pure merits exceeding those of the sands of the Ganges are manifested.
If the mind were to arise and further perceive prior phenomena as objects of recollection, then there would be something lacking;
thus, these immeasurable merits of pure dharmas are seen within the single mind, and nothing more exists beyond it.
Because that which is contemplated is thus fulfilled, it is called the Tathāgata-garbha, the Dharma-body.

This section of question and answer extends back to the preceding discussion on essence and characteristics to clarify that, from the beginning, there is a single suchness (tathatā) without increase or decrease;
this serves as a commentary for the previous chapter. However, because all merits do not possess a separate substance but manifest in accordance with the nature (dharmatā), it is so stated.
Regarding the meaning that all are equal in flavor as the single, unique suchness (*tathatā*), the following section investigates and explains the intent behind this "single, unique suchness":
because there is no conceptualizing mind, there is no distinction between the eight mental factors and the fifty-one mental concomitants;
because there are no conceptualized marks, there is no distinction between the eleven form-phenomena, nor between the manifest and unmanifest, nor between the substantial and non-substantial.

This distinction arises because both form and mind are simultaneously extinguished; therefore, there is no duality. Furthermore, by what principle does the following clarify the meaning of differentiation?

It is to manifest that while the True Source is fundamentally without difference, it is established in contrast to the delusory. Thus, in contrast to the "phase of karma" (*karmalakṣaṇa*) of ignorance, it is called the "great light of wisdom";
in contrast to the "phase of the perceiving subject," it is called the "universal illumination of the Dharma-realm"; and in contrast to the "objective realm"...

Because the characteristics, meanings, and manifestations of all pure merits—more numerous than the sands of the Ganges—are shown forth, one knows that through these three characteristics there arise distinct names;
it is like a *maṇi* jewel which manifests various colors according to the direction from which it is viewed, yet the *maṇi* itself does not actually possess five colors.
When the mind arises, the lower fetters are revealed; this is the meaning of the term "Tathāgatagarbha" as the Dharmakāya.
Furthermore, this is said in contrast to the non-universality of deluded thoughts; for when deluded thoughts arise, one immediately recalls a previous state.
Since there is a prior state to be recalled, one recollects this while neglecting that, and thus it is not all-encompassing and lacks something.
To address this meaning, the characteristic of being free from thought is revealed: although it possesses immeasurable pure qualities, it is equal to the realm of empty space.
Virtue is precisely this single mind, free from further conceptualization; therefore, it is complete. Because of this completeness, it is called the Tathāgatagarbha.
Because this single mind is all-pervasive, it is called the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, as for the function of True Suchness (tathatā), it refers to the fact that all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, while originally on the stage of the causal ground, gave rise to great compassion and cultivated the various pāramitās to gather and transform sentient beings.

They established great vows, desiring to deliver and liberate them until the realm of sentient beings is exhausted, without limit as to the number of kalpas, extending to the end of the future; this is because they regard all sentient beings as their own bodies.
Furthermore, one does not grasp at the mark of sentient beings. What is the meaning of this?
It means that one knows, according to reality, that all sentient beings and one’s own body are equal in *tathatā* (suchness) and without distinction.

Because there exists such great wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*), ignorance is eliminated, and one perceives the fundamental *dharmakāya*; thus, inconceivable activities and various functions arise spontaneously.
It is equal to True Suchness (tathatā) and pervades all places; furthermore, no characteristic of activity can be apprehended therein. Why is this?

It is because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are solely the body of the Dharma-body and the characteristic of wisdom, the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), which possesses no realm of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
Being free from deliberate activity, it is only said to possess "activity" because sentient beings obtain benefit according to what they see and hear.

This commentary establishes the section on the "Function of the Great" (*mahā-vṛtti*), which also clearly elucidates the aforementioned power of external conditions as the熏習 (*vāsanā*) for sentient beings, whereby all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas rely upon True Suchness (*tathatā*). The passage beginning with "All Buddhas...

clarifies the compassionate mind of their original practice in the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*). The passage beginning with "Establishing the great vow... clarifies the profundity of their original vows in the causal stage.
It is the mind, yet it does not grasp at the marks of sentient beings in order to clarify the wisdom-mind of perfect enlightenment.
What is the meaning of this? Below, the text interrogates and explains the reason why the wisdom-mind does not grasp at the marks of sentient beings:
because one knows, in accordance with reality, that the essence of sentient beings and Buddhas is equal and without distinction; it is precisely by means of this great equality...
Wisdom, within the context of self-benefit, eliminates ignorance and perceives the fundamental dharmakāya;
it further awakens all sentient beings through this wisdom, manifesting various inconceivable functions. However, these functional manifestations do not depart from the fundamental essence.
Since the essence is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), no functional manifestation can be apprehended. Why is this? [The following section] interrogates and clarifies this point.
The meaning of "no functional characteristics can be apprehended" is that although the Buddhas manifest various bodies, they do not move from the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*);
and although they preach various dharmas, they eternally abide in the principle beyond words.

Therefore, it is said that they possess only a body of the dharma-body and the aspect of wisdom, which is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) free from conditioned activity; this is precisely "ever-quiescent while illuminating. Although true...
The principle of wondrous wisdom is fundamentally and eternally quiescent, yet it does not obstruct its responsive benefit according to the capacities of beings;
thus, it is said that "it merely accords with the seeing and hearing of sentient beings to bring about benefit, and is therefore called 'function'.

This is precisely "quiescence while constantly illuminating. Because it is illuminated while constantly quiescent, the immeasurable becomes one; because it is quiescent while constantly illuminating, the one becomes the immeasurable.
"Measure" (pramāṇa) truly means that while responding to conditions and meeting with sentient beings without exception, one constantly remains upon this seat of Bodhi.

This function is of two kinds; what are these two? First, that which is seen by the minds of ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles, based on the *vikalpa-vastu-vijñāna* (the consciousness of discriminating phenomena), is called the *nirmāṇakāya* (Emanation Body).
Because they do not know that it is manifested from the *pravṛtti-vijñānas* (evolving consciousnesses), they see it as coming from outside and grasp at it [as external].

Because its boundaries of form cannot be fully known, there are two [aspects]: first, it relies on the *karmic-consciousness* (*karmavijñāna*), meaning that what is perceived by the minds of Bodhisattvas from their initial resolve (*prathamacittotpāda*) up to the ultimate stage of a Bodhisattva is called the *saṃbhogakāya*.

This body possesses immeasurable forms; each form possesses immeasurable marks (*lakṣaṇa*); each mark possesses immeasurable secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*); and the resultant environment upon which it rests is likewise immeasurable.
The various adornments, manifesting as they appear, are infinite and inexhaustible;
free from the marks of limitation, they are able to constantly sustain and maintain themselves without decay or loss according to their respective functions.
Such merits are all accomplished through the perfuming of the untainted practices of the *pāramitās* and the inconceivable perfuming, and are thus fully endowed with the immeasurable.

Because it possesses the characteristic of pleasure, it is called "retribution" (*vipāka*); furthermore, that which is perceived by ordinary beings is its coarse form, which appears differently according to the six realms of existence as various distinct types;
because these do not possess the characteristic of experiencing pleasure, they are called "correspondence" (*nirmāṇa*).

First, that which is perceived by the minds of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) is called the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body), which is in fact the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body).

Because ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles have not yet forgotten their conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), they perceive only the coarse marks of the *nirmāṇakāya* and do not see the subtle and wondrous adornments of the *saṃbhogakāya*.

Therefore, it is said that this is based on the *vijñapti-matram-vastu-vijñāna* (consciousness of objects through conceptual discrimination). Because they rely on this consciousness of objects through conceptual discrimination, they are unable to comprehend [the true nature].

The objective realm is precisely the mind’s vision; because one perceives the Buddha’s response-body (nirmāṇakāya) as coming solely from the outside, one grasps it through physical marks and seeks it through sound.
Failing to realize that all marks are non-marks is to fail to see the Tathāgata. Thus it is said: "To grasp the boundaries of form is to be unable to know it exhaustively.
To be unable to know it exhaustively means not knowing that form is like the mind—having no boundaries. Because of this... [text ends]
Because one perceives only the limits [of this state], it is not yet exhaustive. Second, that which is perceived by the various Bodhisattvas and others is called the *saṃbhogakāya* (Enjoyment Body).

From the stage of initial right faith up to the stage of the provisions (*sambhārāvasthā*), although the evolving consciousnesses have not yet been emptied, because they practice the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā-darśana*) and are able to contemplate the principle of the signless nature of *tathatā* (Suchness), they are able to perceive it slightly and with equanimity.

Because the Reward Body (*sāmbhogika-kāya*) and the Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*) purely enter the wisdom of signless contemplation (*animitta-vipaśyanā*) and partially realize *tathatā*, they perceive the Reward Body;
this perception becomes increasingly superior stage by stage until, at the level of Equal Enlightenment (*samābodhi*), one perceives the Buddha’s most supreme body.

This is like seeing the moon through a gauze screen; all of this is due to the fact that the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) has not yet been exhausted. Therefore, it is said that [the perception] "depends upon the karmic consciousness. If this were exhausted...
Consciousness has no visible form or characteristics, yet the body possesses immeasurable colors; this explains below the meaning of the *saṃbhogakāya*.

Since these primary and secondary rewards (*pratyaya*) and their immeasurable adornments are all manifested by the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*), they are without limits and accord with what is appropriate.
This refers specifically to the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) experienced on the [Buddha] grounds; that is, the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*).
Because it is detached from these objects, it is said to be "constantly able to maintain, neither destroying nor losing. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"There is not a single dharma that is not Vairocana Buddha; there is not a single speck of dust that is not the Flower Treasury World-Ocean.
Such merits are all due to the perfuming of the profound practice of the ten pāramitās, as well as the inconceivable perfuming of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya*).
Because these two causes are fully endowed with the characteristics of bliss, it is called "retribution.

Furthermore, for the sake of explaining the meaning of the *saṃbhogakāya* (Enjoyment Body) to ordinary beings, it is said that these three types of *nirmāṇakāya* (Emanation Bodies) manifest through the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (Wisdom of Accomplishing Tasks);

they appear differently according to the faculties and dispositions of sentient beings, and are not identical to the self-enjoyment (*svasaṃbhoga*) which is fully endowed with the characteristics of bliss—just as [the hells consist of] glowing coals and boiling cauldrons.
Because there is no teaching that does not accord with the capacities [of beings] in such places, it is called "appropriate" (*yathābhavya*). Question:
Why is it said that the manifestation of the bodies of all Buddhas depends upon the mind and consciousness of sentient beings? Answer:

As explained in treatises such as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the power of the Buddhas' compassion and wisdom acts as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), while the seeds of the responsive resonance of sentient beings act as the immediate cause (*hetu-pratyaya*), upon which [the manifestation] relies.
Because the Buddha is essentially the reflected image manifested by one's own mind, it is said to exist within one's own consciousness;
this is what is meant by the statement that the Buddhas within the minds of sentient beings attain liberation from time to time.
Furthermore, that which is seen by bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds upon enlightenment is seen only partially because they have deep faith in the dharma of *tathatā* (suchness).
They perceive those matters of the adornment of physical forms as being without coming or going, free from spatial limits, and manifesting solely in dependence upon the mind;
yet they do not depart from *tathatā*. Nevertheless, these bodhisattvas still engage in conceptual discrimination because they have not yet entered the stage of the *dharmakāya*.

Therefore, if one attains a pure mind, that which is perceived becomes subtle and wondrous, and its function becomes increasingly superior until it reaches its ultimate consummation at the end of the Bodhisattva stages.

If one is free from the karmic consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), there is no phenomenon of seeing; for the Dharma-body of all Buddhas has no such phenomena of color or form through which they might see one another.
This clarifies the meaning of the *nirmāṇakāya* (retribution body) as perceived by Bodhisattvas based on the *karmic consciousness*:

from the initial stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*) up to the four stages of application (*prayoga*), because they deeply believe through the *tathatā-samādhi* that all phenomena do not depart from suchness,
they know that matters such as physical marks and adornments all manifest from the locus of the *manifesting consciousness* (*darśana-vijñāna*), having neither coming nor going.

Although one may believe that all phenomena are mind based on the characteristics of their respective limits, one has not yet awakened to the cessation of the *vyañjanā-vijñāna* (the consciousness of perceived objects) through discrimination;
thus, one sees only partially. This is because the obstacle of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) has not been removed and one has not yet entered the Ground of Pure Mind (*śuddhabhūmi*).

This is what was referred to in the preceding text as "semblance-awakening" (*pratirūpa-bodha*). Bodhisattvas on the grounds (*bhūmi*) have already awakened to and severed the two types of grasping through discrimination.
Because they have realized the ten kinds of *tathatā* (suchness), what they perceive is subtle and their function is increasingly superior;

yet they still cannot exhaust its limits, for their *karmic consciousness* (*karmavijñāna*) has not yet been overturned—this is what was referred to in the preceding text as "awakening according to one's portion.

It is only upon reaching the stage of the Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi-bodhisattva*) that they begin to see the ultimate, because their *karmic consciousness* is about to be exhausted; thus, there is no longer any obstruction, as stated in the preceding text.
This refers to ultimate awakening. If one were to depart from the *ālayavijñāna* (karmic consciousness), it would be the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) that clarifies the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*).

However, because one relies upon the *ālayavijñāna*, there exist the two aspects of transformation and manifestation. If one were to depart from ignorance and the *ālayavijñāna*, these aspects would not exist;
there would be only True Suchness (*tathatā*), like space merging with space or water poured into water, where all things are unimpeded and all phenomena are equal.
Therefore, because those without form do not see one another, it is as stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: "Even seeing is detached from seeing;
seeing cannot reach it.
Question: If the Dharma-body of all Buddhas is devoid of form and characteristics, how can it manifest form and characteristics? Answer:
This very Dharma-body is the essence of form; therefore, it can manifest as form. That is to say, from the very beginning, form and mind have been non-dual.
Because the nature of form is itself wisdom, the essence of form is formless and is called the Wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*).
Because the nature of wisdom is itself form, it is called the Dharma-body. Pervading all places, the forms it manifests have no boundaries, appearing in accordance with the mind.
It is able to manifest the infinite bodhisattvas, infinite reward bodies (*vipākakāya*), and infinite adornments within the worlds of the ten directions,
each distinct and yet without limitation or mutual obstruction; this cannot be known through the discrimination of mind and consciousness,
for it is due to the principle of the sovereign function of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
In this dialogue, it is clearly revealed that the Buddha’s true *dharmakāya* is like empty space; it manifests forms in response to objects, like the moon reflected in water.
The meaning is this: since the *dharmakāya* is without marks (*animitta*), there are no such phenomena as manifesting a body or preaching the Dharma.

How, then, can various physical forms (*rūpalakṣaṇa*) be manifested from within that which is markless? One must realize that while the essence of empty space is not comprised of any manifold characteristics, yet...
It is able to accommodate the manifestation of manifold characteristics because the *dharmakāya* is not a physical form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) yet can manifest all forms;
this is because the truth of the *dharmakāya* is the very substance of all phenomena.

Regarding the statement "form and mind are non-dual," the following section precisely clarifies that the truth of the *dharmakāya* is the substance of all phenomena. Since form has no self-nature, it is entirely form...
Since nature is itself wisdom, matter (*rūpa*)—being identical to wisdom—is called the Wisdom Body (*jñānakāya*);

and since wisdom is the mind, wisdom has no separate substance apart from the total essence of wisdom, which is matter. Thus, wisdom being identical to matter is termed the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*), which pervades all places.
Since the Dharma Body is all-pervasive, the Reward Body (*sambhogakāya*) manifested by the Dharma Body likewise has no spatial limitations.
The manifested primary and secondary retributions throughout the worlds of the ten directions, and their respective forms and characteristics, do not obstruct one another.
Such merit transcends the realm of mind and consciousness because it manifests solely based upon the nature of wisdom (*jñatā*).
Therefore, it is said that this cannot be known through the discrimination of mind and consciousness, as it pertains to the meaning of the sovereign function of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Furthermore, it demonstrates how one enters the gate of True Suchness (tathatā) directly from the gate of Arising and Ceasing (utpāda-nirodha):

namely, by investigating the five aggregates (skandhas), one finds that both form and mind, as well as the objects of the six sense-fields, are ultimately without thought. Because the mind has no form or characteristics, even if one searches for it throughout the ten directions, it can never be found.
Just as a person who is deluded might take the east to be the west while the direction itself does not actually change, so too it is with sentient beings.

Because of the delusion of ignorance, one takes the mind to be thought; yet the mind is in reality unmoving. If one can observe and know that the mind is without thought, one will immediately attain compliance and enter the gate of True Suchness (Tathatā). Therefore.
This is a sudden demonstration of the skillful means for entering reality, revealing that the two gates of arising-and-ceasing and true-suchness (*tathatā*) are not mutually exclusive.

Because the meaning of superior awakening is cultivated gradually from the level of ordinary beings to the state of sainthood, various levels of awakening—such as "resemblance" and "partial"—are enumerated.

This [teaching], however, causes one to enter directly into the realm of the *dharmakāya* without passing through successive stages; therefore, it is called "immediate entry. Furthermore, for all sentient beings...
Sentient beings constantly dwell within birth and death because they falsely cling to the body and mind, regarding them as truly existent.

To demonstrate that this is a delusion and to lead them back to the truth, he causes them to observe that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are all empty. Furthermore, it is said: "Matter and mind are distinct," which separately explains the five aggregates.
"Matter" refers to the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); matter comprises eleven dharmas, namely the five sense organs (*indriya*) and the six sense objects (*viṣaya*). This is based on...

The "sentient being's physical body" refers exclusively to the five sense faculties (*indriya*). "Mind" refers to the four aggregates (*skandha*) of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;

it includes the eight mind-kings (*citta-rāja*) and the fifty-one mental factors (*caitta*). The "six objects of the sensory realms" refer to the external objective fields that serve as the conditions for the aforementioned faculties and mind.
Through such observation, one realizes that both the internal body and external objects lack any intrinsic nature (*sva-lakṣaṇa*).
Ultimately, because there is no thought-moment that connects the subject and object, one seeks through mental reflection alone and can never find a "mind" capable of manifesting;
since the manifesting mind cannot be found, how could the manifested aggregates and dharmas possibly exist?

Not only does awakening extinguish delusion so that awakening does not give rise to further delusion, but even if one has not yet ceased their madness, what exactly have they lost? Therefore, it is likened to being lost.
The "direction" is actually not turning; the deluded mind is actually not moving.
If one can observe in this way until there is neither delusion nor awakening, one will be able to enter the realm of True Suchness instantaneously.
Regarding the remedy for false attachments: all false attachments depend upon the view of a self; if one is free from the self, there are no false attachments.
This view of a self is of two kinds. What are these two? First, the view of a personal self (*pudgala-ātman*); second, the view of a phenomenal self (*dharma-ātman*).
This correctly explains the second point from the preceding heading: the counteracting of false attachments.

Because one does not understand the characteristics of true suchness (*tathatā*) and dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), one becomes deluded regarding the principle and gives rise to two kinds of attachments according to one's own sentiments. Both of these attachments are established upon the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*);
because one fails to realize that the dharmas of non-self are fundamentally and originally of one suchness, one falsely gives rise to a perceiving subject and an perceived object.

The characteristics of the elements (dhātu) thus give rise to attachment to phenomena (dharma-grāha); because of this attachment to phenomena, conceptual discrimination (vikalpa) arises again, whereby attachment to a self (ātma-grāha) is formed.
Regarding the view of a person (pudgala-dṛṣṭi), it is said that there are five types based on ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana).

Although there are five types of self-grasping, they all refer to the grasping at teachings and the grasping at principles by beginners in the Mahāyāna, and are not the same as the grasping of sentient beings toward the characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*).
What are these five? First, hearing the *sūtras* state that the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is ultimately quiescent; yet...
Just as space is not understood because it is taken to be a refutation of attachment, one then claims that space is the *tathāgatagarbha*.
How is this countered? It is clarified that the characteristic of space is a false phenomenon whose essence is unreal; it exists only in relation to form (*rūpa*).

Because it possesses this visible characteristic, it causes the mind to undergo birth and cessation. In reality, all phenomena of form are fundamentally the mind itself, and there is no external form at all.
If there were no form, then there would be no characteristic of space; that which is called "all objective realms" exists only because the mind falsely arises.
If the mind is free from false movement, then all objective realms cease, and only the single true mind remains, pervading everywhere.
This is what is meant by the ultimate meaning of the Tathāgata’s vast intrinsic wisdom; it is not like the characteristic of empty space.
This clarifies the virtues of the *dharmakāya*. By citing the *sūtra*, it is shown that the meaning elucidated by the Master of the Treatise does not exceed the original intent of the Tathāgata.
As previously stated, "that which is free from the marks of thought is equal to the realm of empty space and is all-pervading" refers precisely to the Tathāgata’s equal *dharmakāya*;
therefore, the *sūtra* is cited as proof, stating: "the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata."
Ultimate stillness is like empty space; this clarifies the principle of the Dharmakāya as being like empty space, thereby revealing that the Dharmakāya is without marks.

Fearing that ordinary people—who stubbornly cling to the five aggregates, body, and mind as being real form—will fail to understand this and mistakenly grasp the Dharmakāya as having real characteristics such as empty space, he demonstrates the Middle Way as an antidote.
To eliminate false attachments, one first contemplates that space has no substantial reality; it is manifested only through form. If separated from form, the characteristic of space does not exist.
This is because all objective realms arise solely from the deluded activity of the mind;

thus, this correct teaching prevents one from clinging to the provisional. Although delusive phenomena originally lack a true nature, they are not extinguished; therefore, it is said that they are "one."
When all objective realms are extinguished, there remains only the single true mind, which is omnipresent; this is precisely what is meant by "not clinging to emptiness.
Since both emptiness and the provisional are non-clinging, and both existence and non-existence are simultaneously discarded, this is the ultimate meaning of the Tathāgata’s vast nature-wisdom.
How could it ever be illustrated by the false appearances of empty space?

Second, when one hears the sūtras state that all worldly phenomena are ultimately empty in essence, and even the dharmas of nirvāṇa and *tathatā* are ultimately empty—being primordially empty and free from all marks—one may fail to understand this as a refutation of attachment and instead claim that the nature of *tathatā* and nirvāṇa is merely emptiness. How is this to be remedied? To clarify the truth: [the text continues with the following: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are two kinds of emptiness: first, the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*);

second, the emptiness of self-nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*). What is the emptiness of non-existence? It refers to the non-existence of things such as a rabbit’s horns, a tortoise’s hair, a barren woman’s son, or a flower in the sky; because these do not exist, they are called empty. This is called the emptiness of non-existence. What is the emptiness of self-nature? It refers to the fact that all phenomena, from form up to consciousness, are each devoid of their own intrinsic nature. Because they are devoid of their own intrinsic nature, they are called empty. This is called the emptiness of self-nature. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the emptiness of self-nature refers to the fact that all phenomena are devoid of the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing.

Because they are devoid of the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing, they are called empty. This is called the emptiness of self-nature. [The text concludes: "Therefore, Mahāmati, you should not say that the nature of *tathatā* and nirvāṇa is merely emptiness. Why? Because *tathatā* and nirvāṇa are the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the true nature (*dharmatā*), and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). They are not like the emptiness of non-existence, which is merely the absence of something. If one were to say that *tathatā* and nirvāṇa are merely emptiness, one would be slandering the Buddha-dharma and falling into the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*). Therefore, Mahāmati, you should abandon such views and cultivate the wisdom of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-prajñā*) to realize that while all phenomena are empty of self-nature, the ultimate reality of *tathatā* and nirvāṇa is neither existence nor non-existence, transcending all conceptual extremes."
Because the very essence of the Dharma-body is not empty and is fully endowed with immeasurable intrinsic merits.

This clarifies the virtue of liberation; as stated above, all sentient beings are primordially and eternally abiding in entry into nirvāṇa—it is neither a characteristic to be cultivated nor a characteristic to be produced, ultimately being without perception and without form or appearance.

Because it can be accepted, the scripture is cited as proof, stating: "The essential nature of all phenomena in the world is ultimately empty, even down to the *tathatā* (suchness) of *nirvāṇa*, which is also ultimately empty.
This reveals that both mundane and supramundane phenomena are, in their very substance, true emptiness, free from the marks of defilement and purity;
it serves to shatter the attachment of ordinary beings who loathe birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and seek *nirvāṇa*. Lest this be misunderstood...

Realizing that this erroneous attachment takes *nirvāṇa* to be the characteristic of a void of annihilation, [the teaching] demonstrates the contemplation of the provisional as an antidote to reveal that the self-substance of *tathatā* is,
in its true nature, not empty, but fully endowed with immeasurable merits in accordance with its own nature,
lest it be understood through a void of cessation and extinction.

Third, when hearing the sūtras state that the Tathāgata-garbha neither increases nor decreases and that its essence is fully endowed with all dharmas of merit, one fails to understand this and instead claims that the Tathāgata-garbha possesses the distinct characteristics of material and mental dharmas. How is this countered?
It is because it is taught solely in terms of the meaning of True Suchness (tathatā), while the aspects of birth, death, and defilement are merely manifested for the sake of instruction.
This is because it explains the distinctions [of the qualities].
This clarifies the virtue of *prajñā*: the characteristic of all merits is precisely the functional activity of the wisdom of *bodhi*.
As stated above, regarding "the permeation of the essential nature," since beginningless time, one has possessed untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas and is fully endowed with them.
Because the nature of the sphere of activity produced by conceptual thought is such, a sutra is cited as proof:
"The Tathāgatagarbha neither increases nor decreases, its essence being fully endowed with all dharmas of merit. This clarifies that the Tathāgatagarbha is replete with all merits;
it is taught so as to refute the ordinary person’s view of annihilationism, for fearing they might not understand, [the text] speaks of the sphere of all wondrous functions.

Because [beings] erroneously perceive the characteristics of form, mind, and so forth, the meaning of emptiness is taught as an antidote to clarify that within the essence of True Suchness (*tathatā*), all things are empty according to reality;
however, distinctions are spoken of based on the meaning of arising, ceasing, and defilement, as stated above:
"In contrast to ignorance, great wisdom and so forth are spoken of."

Fourth, when hearing the sūtras state that all worldly phenomena of birth and death and defilement exist in dependence upon the tathāgatagarbha, and that all dharmas do not depart from true suchness (tathatā), one may—due to a lack of understanding—claim that the very essence of the tathāgatagarbha inherently possesses all worldly phenomena such as birth and death.
How is this to be remedied? [It is by understanding that] the tathāgatagarbha, from the very beginning...
Since beginningless time, there have existed only pure merits exceeding the sands of the Ganges, which do not depart from, cease, or differ from the meaning of *tathatā* (suchness).
This is because the defiled dharmas of afflictions exceeding the sands of the Ganges exist only as false appearances;
their nature is fundamentally non-existent, and from the beginningless past, they have never been associated with the *tathāgatagarbha*. If the essence of the *tathāgatagarbha* possessed falsity...
It is impossible for the Dharma to cause one to realize and meet [the truth] such that delusions are eternally stilled.
This clarifies that the deluded dharmas of ordinary beings are fundamentally empty and quiescent from the beginning.

Because it was stated above that "all deluded thoughts do not depart from original enlightenment" and that "the three realms are false and constructed solely by the mind," a scriptural passage is cited as proof: "One..."
All the defiled phenomena of birth and death in the world exist in dependence upon the *tathāgatagarbha*; all dharmas do not depart from suchness.

This clarifies that the nature of delusion has no substance of its own and is established in dependence upon the True. This is taught to shatter the attachment of ordinary people who seek purity by abandoning defilement;
for they might otherwise fail to understand that it is the *tathāgatagarbha* itself which truly possesses these defiled phenomena of birth and death.
