This tranquility arises from delusion and confusion; however, such phenomena as those manifested and spoken of are actually summoned by the spiritual awakening of those who practice dhyāna.
If one awakens to Bodhi, all of these are merely floating thoughts.
For this reason, a practitioner should always observe with wisdom so as not to allow this mind to fall into the net of error;
one should diligently maintain right mindfulness and neither grasp nor cling, whereby one will be able to remain far removed from all such karmic obstructions.
This explains in detail the meaning of extinguishing [the afflictions] by reflecting that all objective realms are but the mind alone.

Since all demonic activities arise from ignorance, one should employ wisdom to observe them, whereby the net of delusion will naturally be removed—just as a torch dispels darkness or boiling water melts ice.
The principle of such observation is to maintain right mindfulness, neither grasping nor clinging; once these are absent, [the demons vanish].
Grasping and attachment are termed "wrong reception" (*asamādhi*); when right reception (*samādhi*) manifests before one, the activities of Māra naturally recede.

As a verse in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "If one discriminates the characteristics of objects, this is the net of Māra; to be unmoving and non-discriminative is called the Seal of the Dharma (*dharmamudrā*).

Since we are speaking here in terms of the fundamental cause, it is called a "karmic obstruction. Second, if one falls into the net of the heterodox, it constitutes a karmic obstruction, for demons delight in such things.

Since objects are the mind itself, there is nothing to enter and nothing to emerge from;

thus, when entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one does not dwell upon the extraordinary signs perceived within that state, nor does one dwell upon the marks of peace and bliss attained therein.
Even after emerging from concentration, one remains as if still abiding in it; because of this lack of laxity or pride, afflictions gradually diminish and wholesome conduct increases.
The passage beginning with "If one is like ordinary worldlings" exhorts practitioners to cultivate through the samādhi of true thusness (*tathatā*).
The passage beginning with "By cultivating the various worldly meditative concentrations" admonishes practitioners not to encounter divergent paths,
ensuring that they ultimately return to perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, for one who diligently and single-mindedly practices this samādhi, ten kinds of benefits shall be obtained in the present life.

Regarding the question of being startled by sound: once one has attained the samādhi of right reception (*samāpatti*), one no longer undergoes any sensations;
why then do you single out sound as that which cannot move one? The answer is: this very Dharma-body of the true teaching is pure within hearing.
If one wishes to attain *samādhi*, one must truly enter through the faculty of hearing. Therefore, it is cited that sound—the sense-object (*viṣaya*)—cannot move it.

Regarding those who, due to past [faults], practice the meaning of *śamatha*: because they perceive the principle of true emptiness as being devoid of all conceptualization, they speak of "sinking.

This is precisely the aforementioned mind of great compassion.
As the *Awakening of Great Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* says: "Transforming various illusions to open up for illusory multitudes; by giving rise to illusion..."
Therefore, one is able to inwardly give rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). All bodhisattvas initiate their practice from this point, gradually increasing it.
By giving rise to such vows, [the text] below correctly clarifies that they act in accordance with the aforementioned compassionate vows.
Because they have established profound vows and great compassion, they are capable and competent to undertake all wholesome deeds at all times and in all places.
Seeing all sentient beings—whether they follow the path or go against it—he constantly maintains a mind intent on delivering them without ever succumbing to indolence.

Only while seated does he distinguish between the specific practices of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). However, when entering meditative absorption, he cuts off all conceptual discrimination and remains free from all conditioned activity;
therefore, he focuses his mindfulness exclusively on *śamatha*. When emerging from absorption, he contemplates all phenomena as being like illusions; though he understands these phenomena...
Because illusion does not obstruct the fact that its very substance is empty, stillness (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) are practiced together.
This refers to the essential principle of practicing stillness and insight simultaneously: to contemplate that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is unarisen is stillness;

yet, to further contemplate the retributions of causes and conditions—such as good and evil, suffering and pleasure—is insight. Thus, one contemplates the retributions of the causes and conditions of good and evil.
It is precisely contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), yet it is also precisely the non-apprehensibility of the nature of mindfulness (*smṛti-svabhāva-anupalabdhi*), which is cessation (*śamatha*).

Cessation is elucidated by way of the meaning of "not being existent," while contemplation is elucidated by way of the meaning of "not being non-existent. Because these two are non-dual, they are said to be "precisely" one.

This is because that which is not existent is precisely that which is not non-existent; thus, one is able to cultivate contemplation without abandoning cessation. That which is not non-existent is precisely... [that which is not existent].

Because [the object] exists, one is able to cultivate *śamatha* (calm abiding) without abandoning *vipaśyanā* (insight). This is not merely the non-duality of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, but also the identity of mind and object.

That is to say, by using non-conditioning wisdom (*anālambana-jñāna*) to take a signless object (*animitta-viṣaya*), and by the signless object taking non-conditioning wisdom as its object, object and wisdom are identical in a single true reality (*eka-tattva-lakṣaṇa*).
Only then can it be called the Perfect and Sudden *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. Third, True Suchness (*tathatā*).
It is obscure.
If one cultivates *śamatha* (calm abiding), it serves as an antidote to the ordinary person’s attachment to the mundane world and allows for the relinquishing of the timid views of the two vehicles;

if one cultivates *vipaśyanā* (insight), it serves as an antidote to the two vehicles’ failure to give rise to great compassion and their inferior mental faults, thereby distancing oneself from the state of an ordinary person.
Because they do not cultivate the roots of goodness for this reason, these gates of śamatha and vipaśyanā assist and perfect one another, never being separated;
if śamatha and vipaśyanā are not complete, one will be unable to enter the path to bodhi.

The above provides a detailed explanation of the meaning of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight). This section specifically clarifies how they serve as remedies for the mental defects of both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
These two gates of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* together remedy these two types of faults. As for *śamatha* remedying the two faults:

it primarily remedies the ordinary being’s attachment to a self (*ātman*) and their greedy grasping for worldly things, ensuring that they do not become attached; it also concurrently remedies the two-vehicle practitioner’s clinging to the phenomena of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and their views.
"Generating fear toward suffering causes one to realize that dharmas are empty and originally unarisen; observing this cures the two faults.

This means it correctly remedies the inferior and base mind of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas by causing them to universally contemplate all sentient beings and give rise to great compassion, while simultaneously remedying the mark of indolence in ordinary worldlings by causing them to contemplate impermanence and diligently cultivate wholesome deeds. This concludes the summary of the two contemplations.
It is revealed that one must practice both contemplations simultaneously before transcending the Small Vehicle and being able to enter directly onto the path of unsurpassed enlightenment.
Furthermore, when sentient beings first study this Dharma and seek to attain right faith, their minds become timid and weak;
dwelling in this Sahā world, they fear they will not be able to constantly encounter the Buddhas to personally receive and make offerings to them, and they dread that their faith might falter.
For those who find it difficult to achieve [the goal] and whose resolve wavers, you should know that the Tathāgata possesses a supreme skillful means to protect and sustain their faith.

That is to say, by means of the causal condition of single-mindedly recollecting the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*), one will be born according to one's vow in a Buddha-land in another direction, where one constantly beholds the Buddha and is forever separated from the evil realms.
As stated in the Sūtra: "If a person single-mindedly recollects the Western World of Ultimate Bliss..."
If one dedicates the roots of goodness cultivated under Amitābha Buddha with the vow to seek birth in that world, one will immediately attain birth;

because one constantly beholds the Buddha, there shall never be any regression. If one contemplates the Tathatā-Dharmakāya of that Buddha and constantly and diligently practices it, one will ultimately attain birth and abide in the stage of Right Certainty (samyaktva-niyāma).

This is the correct explanation of the seven [practices] within the section on causes and conditions (*nidāna*). They are presented to demonstrate that by means of the skillful method of single-minded mindfulness, one will be born before the Buddha and will certainly not regress from the faith of non-retrogression.

Since the preceding section clarified the two meanings of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* as remedies for the faults of the ordinary, narrow mind, it is feared that there may be those unable to cultivate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*;
therefore, the Dharma-gate of mindfulness of the Buddha is shown to inspire faith.

"Non-retrogression of the mind" refers to the birth of those with medium faculties and medium grade through the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha with single-minded devotion; this is explained below.
"If one contemplates that Buddha’s True Suchness Dharma-body" explains the birth of those with superior faculties and superior grade; this is explained below.

This causal condition of mindfulness of the Buddha is like a mother thinking of her child and the child thinking of his mother; the causal conditions between mother and child do not conflict or distance themselves, for the Buddha likewise thinks of the multitude.
When sentient beings are born [in the Pure Land], their minds open naturally through mindfulness of the Buddha; they are reborn according to their vows and attain the vision of the Buddha.

Regarding those who are reborn, there are approximately three stages: first, like a lotus flower that has not yet opened, when faith and practice are not yet perfected, one is not yet called "non-retrogressive," yet because one dwells in a place devoid of conditions for retrogression, one is termed "non-retrogressive. Second, when the stage of faith is fully perfected...

First, by discarding the flowers and opening [the mind] to see the Buddha, one enters the stage of the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*), attaining a slight vision of the *dharmakāya* and dwelling in the stage of correct determination (*samyaktvaniyāma*).

Second, having fulfilled the stage of the three worthies (*trividha-ārya*), from the entry into the first ground (*prathamabhūmi*) onward, one realizes the all-pervading *dharmakāya* and is born into boundless Buddha-lands.
Within this context, "ultimate" and so forth refer to the latter two stages, because those of inferior grade and inferior birth do not [attain them].

Because one is able to contemplate the Buddha’s Dharma-body, the section on the cultivation of faith has already been explained; next, the section on the benefits of exhorting cultivation will be explained.

Thus, I have already provided a general exposition of this Mahāyāna, the secret treasury of all Buddhas. If there are sentient beings who wish to attain [realization] within the profound realm of the Tathāgata...

Having given rise to right faith, one should distance oneself from slander and enter the path of the Mahāyāna; one should uphold this treatise, contemplate it, and practice it, so that ultimately one may reach the unsurpassed way.
This is the section on the correct circulation [of the teaching], which also explains the eighth point within the section on causes and conditions as an exhortation to demonstrate its benefits.
Because of practicing [the path] in this way, the Mahāyāna—this section below restates the meaning of the main body of the treatise. "If there are sentient beings...
and so forth, which correctly clarifies the exhortation to practice in order to manifest its benefits.

If a person, having heard this Dharma, does not give rise to fear or weakness, you should know that this person will certainly succeed to the lineage of the Buddhas and will surely receive the prediction of enlightenment from all the Buddhas.

Even if someone were able to transform all sentient beings filling a trichiliocosm, causing them to practice the ten wholesome paths of action, it would not equal the merit of a single person who, for the duration of one meal, correctly contemplates this Dharma; the latter surpasses the former.

The merit is beyond comparison. Furthermore, if a person receives, upholds, contemplates, and practices this treatise for even a single day and night, the resulting merit is immeasurable, boundless, and cannot be described;
even if all the Buddhas of the ten directions were each to praise that merit for immeasurable, boundless *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they would still be unable to exhaust it.
Why is it said to be inexhaustible? Because the merit of the *dharmatā* is inexhaustible, the merit of this person is likewise without limit.

If there are sentient beings who slander and do not believe this treatise, they will receive the retribution for their sins by undergoing great suffering and affliction for immeasurable kalpas. Therefore, sentient beings should simply look up to it with faith and should not disparage it.
To slander [this Dharma] is to deeply harm oneself and also to harm others; it severs the seeds of the Three Jewels,
for all Tathāgatas attain nirvāṇa by relying on this Dharma, and all Bodhisattvas, through it, practice and enter the Buddha-wisdom.
This clearly explains the weighing of the offenses and blessings of faith and lack of faith, so that sentient beings may receive and uphold [this teaching].
Because this Dharma-nature is inconceivable, those who practice by invoking this Dharma likewise obtain inconceivable merit;
yet those who slander this Dharma also incur immeasurable billions of karmic retributions, as they likewise invoke its nature.
For kalpas one shall undergo great suffering and affliction, like a diamond cloud; the meaning of this sutra is inconceivable, and its karmic retribution is likewise inconceivable.

Therefore, one should below [this point] exhort others to give rise to faith and distance themselves from slander, for all those on the path of cause and those on the path of fruition attain ultimate realization by relying upon this Dharma. Those who slander it sever the continuity of the Triple Gem.
For those of such a disposition, there will ultimately be no occasion to see the Buddha or hear the Dharma.
One should know that past bodhisattvas have already attained pure faith by relying on this Dharma;
present bodhisattvas are now attaining pure faith by relying on this Dharma; and future bodhisattvas shall attain pure faith by relying on this Dharma. Therefore:
Sentient beings should diligently practice and study this.
This passage correctly clarifies the meaning of how all bodhisattvas, through causal cultivation, attain entry into the Buddha-wisdom;
it is a formal exhortation for sentient beings to practice in reliance upon this. As the Heart Sūtra says: "Bodhisattvas rely on prajñāpāramitā..."
Because of the perfection of wisdom, the mind is without hindrance; there is no fear, and one is far removed from inverted dreams and delusions, attaining ultimate nirvana.
It can even eliminate all suffering; it is true and not false.
"The profound and vast meaning of all Buddhas, I now explain in accordance with it through this dhāraṇī;
may the merit of this, like the nature of reality (dharmatā), universally benefit the entire realm of sentient beings.
This summarizes the intent of the entire treatise: the first phrase concludes the meaning, the second phrase concludes the text, and the final two phrases [conclude the dedication].

This concludes the fundamental purpose of composing this treatise. Furthermore, the first two lines conclude the four sections consisting of the causal conditions, the establishment of the doctrine, the explanation, and the practice of faith;
the latter two lines conclude the section on the benefits of exhorting others to practice.
In sum, it is seen that by explaining the fundamental meaning of the Tathāgata, one enables sentient beings to leave behind all suffering and attain ultimate bliss.
Because of seeking worldly fame, profit, and honor.

Postscript.
This treatise is the essential core for healing the minds of all sentient beings; though its text is brief, it encompasses vast meaning.

Since the time Master Zidi translated it, although several commentaries have appeared, regarding those that grasp the main framework and the vital points while explaining the symbols and clarifying the meanings, only the commentary by the Master of Yanmen is truly swift and essential.
In the autumn of the Xinyou year, I inquired about the Dharma with Venerable Shisheng at Kuangshan and received [this work].

Having thoroughly investigated its meaning until every point was clear, I could not bear to set aside the volume; thus, I have drawn upon my resources to join with the assembly in re-engraving this work to broaden its dissemination.
It is my hope that all who see or hear it will bring an end to birth and cessation, realize True Suchness (*tathatā*), and attain the fundamental state of the Tathāgata.
In this way, I shall not fail the single-minded devotion of Master Aśvaghoṣa, nor shall I fail the timely commentary of the late Master of Yanmen.
The meaning of this explanation was composed by the junior disciple Da Yuanzhenzhi. Postscript.
